PREFACE 

This book is the result of a suggestion made to me by the Honorable Harold P. Williams of our Superior Court that a book on the Massachusetts Law of Damages was urgently needed by the Bar and the Bench, and I gratefully acknowledge his friendly inspiration and advice. 

The original sources in our decisions present a wealth of material which does not readily appear in the Digests and it has been my main effort to present this material in such a way that it can be speedily located by the busy practitioner.

It was my original plan to present with each chapter a brief synopsis of the settled law on the subject. This cannot be done. The law of Damages has not grown on any consistent theory at all, but simply represents the earnest efforts of a succession of able judges to do justice in each particular case, with the result that there are many quite inconsistent decisions in our books. Some of these decisions may possibly be distinguished by the facts in each case, while others represent a change in the view of the court, and all the textbook writer can do is to present the cases as they are, leaving the attorney to make his own deductions. 

If this book proves to be of some service to the Bar in the solution of the many perplexing problems arising out of questions of damages, then all the labor spent in its preparation will be well justified. The subject is difficult to handle, touching as it does the whole law, and I ask the charity of the Bar for any errors or omissions which they may discover.

September 1, 1942. 

ARTHUR W. BLAKEMORE.

THE LAW OF DAMAGES IN MASSACHUSETTS. 

PART I. 

GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS. 

CHAPTER I. 

IN GENERAL. 

1. The fundamental rule of damages. 

2. The law of damages is practical rather than logical. 

3. The word "damages" includes all factors. 

4. Special damages defined. § 5. Actions brought for benefit of third party. 

§ 1. The Fundamental Rule of Damages. The law of dam ages is simple in theory and complicated in application, and a succession of very able courts in this State have been struggling for over a hundred years to apply the principles to various complicated bundles of facts. The fundamental principle in all assessment of damages is an effort to place the plaintiff in the same position as if no wrong had been done to him,¹ and in actions of contract this usually is reduced to a mathematical problem; but the problem is quite insoluble by such a test in most actions of tort except that for conversion. Who is to say what is the money value of the loss of an eye or an arm or a leg? On such questions both the courts and the legislature have evaded responsibility 1 "The rule of damages in an action against a tortfeasor is that the plaintiff shall recover an amount commensurate with the wrong done him." Per 

Knowlton, J., in Nash v. Minnesota Title Insurance & Trust Co., 163 Mass. 

574, 581.

Damages in actions of contract are based on the theory of placing the plaintiff in the same position in which he would be if the contract had been performed. Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway Co. v. Union Street 

Railway Co., 269 Mass. 329; Cragin v. Jones, 283 Mass. 474. To the same effect see Rockwood v. Allen, 7 Mass. 254.

$2 

by leaving these problems to the mercies of an untrained jury with little supervision, with the results which might be expected. General guiding principles could easily be formulated, as has been done in the workmen's compensation law, but this has not been done in this State except in actions for death, with the result that the findings for damages for personal injuries are unpredictable and often influenced by imponderables which should have no effect whatever.

In this connection what was said by Lord Halsbury in 

The Mediana, [1900] A.C. 113, 116, is very pertinent: “Of course the whole region of inquiry into damages is one of extreme difficulty. You very often cannot even lay down any principle upon which you can give damages; nevertheless it is remitted to the jury, or those who stand in place of the jury, to consider what compensation in money shall be given for what is a wrongful act. Take the most familiar and ordinary case: how is anybody to measure pain and suffering in moneys counted? Nobody can suggest that you can by arithmetical calculation establish what is the exact amount of money which would represent such a thing as the pain and suffering which a person has undergone by reason of an accident.”’2 

§ 2. The Law of Damages is Practical rather than Logical. 

The learned reader who looks in this book for a statement of clear, logical, consistent rules of damages is doomed to disappointment, and this is no criticism of our court, but is rather commendation. He will find here something perhaps more valuable-reports of the earnest efforts of shrewd judges to find workable, reasonable answers to the many puzzling problems presented to them.

If the rule is followed strictly that the plaintiff should be placed in the same position as if no wrong had been done to him, then the plaintiff's lawyer's bill should be awarded 

2 C. W. Hunt Co. v. Boston Elevated Railway Co., 199 Mass. 220, 236.

§§ 3, 

3 

IN GENERAL 

as much as his doctor's bill, and there is no reason why the defendant should not be charged with interest if he breaks the plaintiff's leg as much as if he breaks the plaintiff's contract. The Spade case, noted hereafter in § 896, is perhaps quite illogical, but it represents the honest endeavor of a wise court to thwart malingerers, and it is certainly good law although it may be bad in theory. Of course the strict intellectual logician would say that the man who left a lantern too near Mrs. O'Leary's cow should pay for the whole damage done by the Chicago fire, if he could-which makes nonsense although technically correct. There are many inconsistent decisions noted in chapter V on proximate and remote consequences and possibly many of them are illogical, but these decisions represent attempts to reach results which are practical rather than theoretical. 

If the reader will bear in mind that the law of damages is a practical rather than an exact science, is reasonable rather than logical, he will better understand the decisions here noted. As Judge Holmes said once: "The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience."3 

§ 3. The Word "Damages" Includes All Factors. "The word 'damages' is often used . . . to comprehend all factors going to make up the total amount which the plaintiff may recover under correct principles of law."4 

§ 4. Special Damages Defined.5 The expression "special damages" as distinguished from general damages has been defined in various ways at different times by our court, depending on the circumstances of each case, and seems to comprehend all damages peculiar to the plaintiff in the action not necessarily resulting from the act complained of. Special damages have been defined to be "damages 

3 Holmes, The Common Law, p. 1. 

4 Per Rugg, C.J., in Binder v. Harris, 267 Mass. 162, 165. 

5 See also §§ 360-367. 

6 Special damages are further considered post, § 918.

$5 

which the law does not imply from the facts alleged in the declaration." "Special damage, in trover, is that which the plaintiff sustains beyond the mere loss of his property by its conversion." Special damages are "such damages as are not implied by law, because they do not necessarily arise from the act complained of." Hence it has been held that evidence that the plaintiff was a schoolteacher, as bearing on her damages for personal injuries, could not be admitted unless specially alleged in the declaration. This decision, however, seems to have been overruled by later cases bearing on impairment of earning capacity.¹ 10 Special damages have been defined as being "some damage of such a character, that it might be given in evidence, to aggravate the damages, in one action, or be itself the substantive cause of action, as in the case of trespass quare clausum, and carrying away plaintiff's goods; the carrying away the goods may be a ground of special damage, or be the cause of a separate action." 11 Special damages in this view will not include damages directly incidental only to the main cause of action and dependent upon it. 

§ 5. Actions Brought for Benefit of Third Party. One who has a legal cause of action but no beneficial interest and brings suit for the benefit of another is still entitled to recover full damages. It is proper but not necessary to state in the writ the fact that the action is brought for the benefit of another.12

CHAPTER II. 

WHAT LAW GOVERNS. 

§ 9. Interest. 

§ 6. Contracts. "The general rule is that the validity of a contract is to be determined by the law of the state in which it is made," while the law of the place of performance governs the rights and obligations of the parties under it. So, where a contract was signed in Massachusetts and sent abroad where it was accepted and the acceptance was sent by telegram to the defendant in Boston, damages for its breach must be governed by the law of Massachusetts, as it did not become a contract until the defendant in Boston was notified of the acceptance and the contract is to be performed in Massachusetts. Also, where a contract to convey to the plaintiff certain real estate in Massachusetts was executed and to be performed in New York, the rule of damages is governed by the law of New York. In this State substantial damages will be given, while in New 

York, which follows the English rule, only nominal damages can be recovered where there is a defect in the title, in the absence of bad faith.¹ 3

Torts. In actions of tort the substantive rights of the parties, including the right to damages, depend on the law of the State where the tort took place. Actions for Death. Our court has consistently taken the position that the ordinary action for death is remedial rather than penal in nature, and will therefore enforce a death statute of another State. The action for death is not criminal but has important remedial features, and such a statute is not criminal or penal in an international sense, but civil rights founded upon it may be enforced in courts of another jurisdiction. Therefore a receiver of a railroad corporation in this Commonwealth appointed by a Federal District Court may be liable to actions of tort for personal injury arising from failure to give the statutory signals at a grade crossing to the same extent as a corporation owner would be liable if operating the railroad itself." Our court will enforce a death statute of a foreign State and assess damages under it on the theory that "in cases of other than penal actions, the foreign law, if not contrary to our public policy, or to abstract justice or pure morals, or calculated to injure the State or its citizens, shall be recognized and enforced here, if we have jurisdiction of all necessary parties, and if we can see that, consistently with our own forms of procedure and law of trials, we can do substantial justice between the parties," and otherwise the court is at liberty to decline jurisdiction." In considering the law of damages we should always keep in mind that our courts are not precision machines, but are and always have been tribunals striving as best they could, with often inadequate evidence, to work out rough rather than exact justice between the parties before them. It is obvious that there can be no certainty in fixing damages for personal injuries, and even in actions of contract in many cases the exact damages are often a matter of conjecture. Still, of course, the plaintiff is always bound to prove some damage. Therefore the amount of damages awarded should be fixed with reasonable certainty, but entire exactness is not required.¹ "The amount of damages seldom can be proved with the exactness of mathematical demonstration. Much must be left to estimate and judgment, sometimes upon meager evidence.” 2 Evidence is sufficient which affords the basis for an approximate determination of the plaintiff's damages. It is not

§ 22. Excluding Other Possibilities. It is not true that, if causes other than the defendant's negligence might have produced the injury, the plaintiff is bound to exclude the operation of such causes by a fair preponderance of the evidence. The plaintiff is not required to exclude all other possibilities as to the cause of the injury if by a preponderance of evidence he proves that it was caused by the defendant's negligence.5 

§ 23. Negligence of Attorney. Where action is brought against an attorney for negligence in prosecuting a claim for personal injuries and it appears that he failed to give a certain statutory notice, whereby the plaintiff was barred from recovery, the plaintiff's damages depend on what he lost. If independently of the notice he had no case on the merits, then he has suffered no loss except the expenses of preparing for trial. The question whether he had a case entitling him to go to the jury if the notice had been given and what he would probably have recovered was properly left to the jury." 

§ 24. Issue of Defective Execution. A justice of the peace is liable for issuing a defective execution, only for actual damage caused thereby and not for expense of attempting to levy it on property not belonging to the debtor. The rule in such case is well propounded by Bigelow, C.J., in the following language: 

4 Hill v. Winsor, 118 Mass. 251, where tug coming into pier shook piling on which plaintiff was working. 

5 Dunbar v. Ferrera Bros. Inc., 306 Mass. 90. 

See also 280, 639. 

7 McLellan v. Fuller, 226 Mass. 374. Negligence of attorney, see post, § 639.

"Through ignorance or carelessness, the defendant issued an execution which was irregular and invalid on its face, and as from such a violation of duty some damages are presumed to follow, the law will award a nominal sum, if no greater damages are proved. But beyond that, the plaintiff could recover only so much as was shown to have been the natural, necessary and proximate consequence of the negligent act of the defendant. He could not claim to recover speculative damages, or those which resulted from his own carelessness or negligence, or that of third persons.

If he could prove that, by reason of the defective execution, he was unable to arrest the body of the debtor, or lost an opportunity to make a valid seizure or levy on his property, whereby he was deprived of an opportunity to collect his debt, he would have been entitled to recover substantial damages to the extent of his loss. But if it appeared that, on a valid execution, the plaintiff could not have collected the amount of his judgment, or any part of it, for the reason that the debtor had no estate which could be taken on execution, and was so poor that the arrest of his body, if it could have been made in conformity with law, would have been ineffectual to enforce payment, then it is clear that the plaintiff would have sustained no actual damages, and could recover only a nominal sum as the damages which the law would imply from the technical injury sustained by the plaintiff in consequence of the defendant's breach of duty. 

In an action of tort in the nature of trespass on the case, the plaintiff can recover only such sums in damages as will be an indemnity to him for the loss or injury of which he complains. It was therefore competent for the defendant to show that the judgment debtor was not the owner of any property which could have been taken on execution in favor of the plaintiff, and that his condition and circumstances were such that the plaintiff could not have collected his debt on the execution, if it had been regular and valid.

1. IN GENERAL. 

§ 39. The General Rule. It is well settled that only those damages may be recovered which are the proximate rather than the remote consequences of the act complained of and flow from the wrong done without the intervention of any independent cause. What is a proximate and what a remote consequence is a peculiarly difficult question which permeates all the authorities, and a few examples which illustrate the rule will be found in the following sections. 

It may be said in brief that the old story of the king who lost his kingdom through loss of a horseshoe nail is not good law. Damages for a breach of contract can include only

$40 

losses on that contract, and damages for personal injury can include only pain and suffering and expenses of that accident, and not the loss arising from the fact that the accident prevented the plaintiff from meeting an heiress. If this were not the rule, every lawsuit would offer an entirely fantastic test of damages.¹ So in an action for malicious injury to machinery the plaintiff may recover only for the direct, consequential damages resulting, and not for remote, speculative or contingent consequences. Under a prayer for general relief in a bill in equity relief in damages may be had for such injury as is the immediate and consequential result of the wrongful conduct complained against and for loss inflicted intentionally or with reasonable ground for belief that it would follow almost necessarily from the action taken.³ 2 

§ 40. Independent Act Intervening. Damages cannot be increased by the independent intervening action of a third party. So if one sells the property of another to a third

Innocent Cause Concurring.

The question has arisen whether, if an innocent cause concurs with a cause negligently created to inflict loss upon an innocent third party, where does or should the law leave the matter? With each of the causes sufficient in itself to produce the result, has the negligent party's dereliction become an actionable wrong? This problem is well treated in a thoughtful article in 47 Harv. L.R. 1127, in which the author proposes the following solutions: "The propositions advanced herein as to these several situations may be stated as follows: (1) Where one cause is innocent and the two causes are strictly concurrent, the author of the wrongful cause is not liable. (2) 

Where an innocent cause is impending and a guilty one becomes operative,

23 

5 person, the seller is not responsible for the wrongful acts of the third person in injuring the property. This is a clear case of an intervening act by a third person which should not increase damages. So where a deputy sheriff is given a summons in supplementary process to serve and serves by error a blank summons, as a result of which the defendant is defaulted and a capias issued which the deputy serves by arrest, he will not be liable for the arrest on the capias but is liable for all damages proximately resulting from the false return. The plaintiff cannot recover for so much of the damages as were not the natural consequences of the arrest itself, but resulted from his resistance to arrest and would not have resulted if he had not resisted." 

§ 41. Bearing Child Not a Voluntary Act Breaking Causal 

Connection. The act of a woman in bringing a child into the world is not a voluntary act of the kind which will break causal connection in considering liability for damages. "The perpetuation of the human race cannot be termed a voluntary act, but it rests upon instincts and desires, which are fundamentally imperative." 

2. CONTRACTS. 

§ 42. In General. Where a contract is broken damages must be confined to the direct consequences of the breach and may not include the more remote results of the defendant's act unless these were in the contemplation of the parties at the imminence of the former is to be taken into account in ascertaining the extent of the damage caused by the latter. (3) In the case of two strictly concurrent wrongful causes there is joint and several liability for all the damage. (4) Where two wrongful causes are more or less successive, the same rule prevails, until a point is reached where the result created by each is so separable as to be no longer treated as a common product in fact." 

5 Jones v. Goodwillie, 143 Mass. 281. 

6 David v. Larochelle, 296 Mass. 302. 'Sullivan v. Old Colony Street Railway Co., 197 Mass. 512.

the time. This situation is more fully covered in the following chapter. 

§ 43. Damage from Leaky Roof. A contract to cover the roof of the plaintiff's building and warrant the same to be tight for five years entitles the owner only to have a satisfactory roof made or to recover the amount that such a roof would cost. Where the roof was composed of a newly invented substance that had not been thoroughly tested and was regarded by both parties as an experiment, this confirms the idea that the contractor did not intend to guarantee the owner against the more remote damages that he might be exposed to in the prosecution of his business and injury done to articles that might be stored in the building by reason of defects in the roof." 

§ 44. Remote Consequence of Breach of Contract. "A 

party who has failed to fulfil a contract cannot be held liable for remote, contingent and uncertain consequences, or for speculative or possible results which may have ensued on his breach of duty, although they may be traceable to that cause. The reason is, that damages of such a nature are not the natural or necessary incidents of a contract, and cannot be deemed to have been within the contemplation of parties when they agreed together. A rule of damages which should embrace within its scope all the consequences which might be shown to have resulted from a failure or omission to perform a stipulated duty or service would be a serious hindrance to the operations of commerce and to the transaction of the common business of life. The effect would often be to impose a liability wholly disproportionate to the nature of the act or service which a party had bound himself to perform and to the compensation paid and received therefor. 

The practical rule, founded on a wise policy, and at the same 

8 See also §§ 443, 808 et seq. 

9 Goddard v. Barnard, 16 Gray, 205.

§§ 45, 

25 

time consistent with good sense and sound equity, is that a party can be held liable for breach of a contract only for such damages as are the natural or necessary, and the immediate and direct results of the breach,-such as might properly be deemed to have been in contemplation of the parties when the contract was entered into, and that all remote, speculative and uncertain results, as well as possible profits and advantages and other like consequences which might have arisen from the fulfilment of the contract must be excluded, as forming no just or legitimate basis on which to determine the extent of the injury actually caused by a breach." 10 

3. TORTS. 

§ 45. Proximate Results of Personal Injury. How far the results of personal injuries can be traced in later illness or mishaps is a difficult medical and legal question on which the decisions seem somewhat inconsistent, though they are doubtless distinguishable. The question at issue is plain enough, whether the subsequent injury is due to the original injury or to an intervening cause. 

Damages for personal injuries cannot be affected by other intervening causes, 11 or from insanity resulting from other shocks.12 Still an attack of appendicitis may be found to be the result of a fall from a wagon,13 and the defendant may be liable for blood poisoning setting in.¹4

§ 47. Second Fall. Whether the consequences of a fall growing out of the original accident can be considered in damages is a question of fact largely, and it seems to be the more recent tendency of the court to allow such damages. 

The test seems to be whether the plaintiff at the time of the second fall was doing something unusual or not, that is, whether the plaintiff was negligent at the time of the second fall. In an action for injuries consequent on a defect in a highway the municipality is liable only for the direct and immediate results of the injury. Therefore, where the plaintiff received a weak ankle and due to this fell later while stepping from a chair to a settee, damages for this fall should not be included. This fall was in consequence of her voluntary conduct and a new and independent cause intervened between the original injury and this fall.16 Where there is evidence that an injury due to negligence resulted in persistent dizzy spells and about three years after the accident the plaintiff, while standing in a sink, became dizzy and fell and broke her wrist, this is too remote to be considered in damages for the original accident. The court denies the "but for" rule and holds that the "breaking of the wrist was due not to the collision but to her conduct in getting up into the pantry sink to look at the leak in the water pipe, and was the result of voluntary and independent action on her part.

It is not enough that the original injury caused conditions which contributed to the breaking of the wrist and but for whose existence it perhaps would not have happened." 17

The second injury caused by the slipping of the plaintiff's crutch could be found to have had a causal relation to the original injury for which the defendant would be liable.¹ Hence, where a plaintiff falls in walking on the floor in an ordinary manner and injures her wrist, damages in this fall may be included in the damages awarded for the original injury to her knee. § 50. Tuberculosis Following Personal Injury. Whether tuberculosis is caused by an injury to the hand may be a question of fact for the jury. "If the plaintiff's tuberculosis had been directly caused by this accident, it would of course have been an element of damages. So, if it were induced without any other intervening cause by her weakened condition or her loss of blood, itself directly caused by the accident, the same would be true. And if at the time of her injuries there were germs of tuberculosis in her system, and if the direct consequence of her injuries was to lessen her general health and cause weakness and reduce her power of resistance to the toxic effect of these germs, and if solely by reason thereof the tuberculosis which had been merely latent in her system became developed into an existing disease, as on the evidence the jury were warranted in finding, they would then have a right to find that the tuberculosis was a direct and immediate result of her injuries and to assess damages therefor. 

If, however, her tuberculosis came from germs introduced into her system after she had sustained these injuries, or by the operation of some other subsequent and independent cause, then, even though the disease would not have developed and manifested itself but for her physical condition having been weakened and her power of resistance diminished by those injuries, it well may be that she

Error of Identity by Surgeon. Such a mistake was not an act of negligence which could be found to flow legitimately as a natural and probable consequence of the original injury, but is a wholly wrongful, independent and intervening cause for which the original wrongdoer was in no way responsible. Here the surgeon did not intentionally operate upon the plaintiff for the injury received, but mistakenly understood and believed that he was operating upon another patient for a different injury.28

§ 59. The General Rule. The question whether damages in any proceeding should include future anticipated results of the wrong claimed depends entirely on the nature of the proceeding. Where the wrong done is of such a nature that only one action can be brought, it seems plain that all the plaintiff's damages, past, present and future, should be assessed in this action, as otherwise the plaintiff would not receive all he should justly have. In this class are actions for a positive, definite, final breach of a contract before its expiration when all future effects of the breach should be included in the assessment of damages. Furthermore, as only one action may be brought for negligence, it is obvious that all damages arising therefrom, past, present and future, must be assessed in this one action.

§ 61. Instalment Mortgage Note. Where a grantee of land assumes payment of a mortgage note signed by the plaintiff (the grantor), and the plaintiff fails to pay an instalment due on the note and the mortgagee thereupon forecloses and the property is sold for less than the face of the mortgage note, the grantee is liable in damages to the plaintiff for the whole amount of the unpaid balance on the note. "The defendant's contract was entire and was broken before the date of the writ. All the damages that the plaintiff ever is to recover he must recover now."

§ 64. Conditional Contract to Support. The rule as to assessment of subsequent damages is this: "If the damages subsequent to the date of the writ are merely incidental to the cause of action declared on, such damages are to be assessed if they are sustained up to the time of the verdict, and even in some cases indefinitely beyond; but if the damages sustained after the date of the writ are such as are not merely incidental to and growing out of the cause of action, but may be the damages arising from a new breach or a new cause of action, they cannot be so assessed. . . . “There is, however, another class of cases, to which these rules do not apply. They are cases of continuing contracts, in which there may be successive breaches out of which successive causes of action arise.”

So when the defendant agrees to support her husband "when he is sober and well-behaved," the damages are to be assessed to the date of the writ only. 15

§ 68. Personal Injuries. Probable rather than Possible 

Results.19 In an action for personal injuries the probable future results of the injury but not the possible results are to be considered in estimating damages,20 as in claims for personal injuries only one action can be brought, and therefore all the results of the tort, future as well as past, must be considered.21 Medical testimony may be admitted to the effect that the plaintiff probably will require future medical attention as the result of the accident,22 but it is error for a judge in an action for personal injuries to charge the jury that they may consider on the question of damages the possibility that an operation in the future might be necessary. 

Future damages should be limited to what is proved by a fair preponderance of the evidence as the damages which were reasonably to be expected to follow as distinguished from those that might follow.23 In an action for personal injuries a physician may state his opinion of the probable duration of the plaintiff's life if he had not received the injury and his probable length of life in view of the accident, as the probable length of life of the plaintiff as affected by the injury is relevant.24

Where a plaintiff in a tort case obtains large damages on a claim of permanent disability, a new trial may be granted after verdict on the ground of new evidence that after the verdict the plaintiff had been doing ordinary manual labor.² 25 § 69. The court, per Knowlton, J., lays down the following rule: "The practical difficulty in using annuity tables in cases of this kind, and in making computations upon the principle on which annuity tables are founded, is that there are too many elements which are uncertain, and which cannot be reduced to any close approximation to certainty. These tables are usually computed on the probabilities for sound lives, while in the cases on trial there are often many circumstances which make the probabilities as to length of life very different from those estimated in the tables. In estimating damages for personal injury, the amount to be allowed for loss of ability to earn money depends upon conditions which are not constant, but which vary from many causes. The physical condition of the plaintiff would very likely have changed from time to time from other causes if there had been no accident. His physical condition is usually likely to change as the years go on after the accident. The income to be obtained from labor or effort in any given calling is not a constant quantity from year to year as time goes on, but the ability to procure employment and the prices paid for services are likely to change. Future Profits. The former rule, rigidly applied, that anticipated profits cannot be included in damages for breach of contract has been largely submerged today, especially in cases where there is a definitely established profit, the amount of which is uncertain, as in the case of profits lost by the interruption of an established business where evidence of past earnings shows substantial damage. 

Damages may not be allowed, on the other hand, for the destruction of a new business without evidence that it was profitable. There is a third class of cases, embracing an opportunity to earn a profit not entailing any risk of loss, and in such cases substantial damages have been awarded in the English courts but refused in this country." § 75. Statement of Rule by Rugg, J. "The fundamental principle of law upon which damages for breach of contract are assessed is that the injured party shall be placed in the same position he would have been in, if the contract had been performed, so far as loss can be ascertained to have followed as a natural consequence and to have been within the contemplation of the parties as reasonable men as a probable result of the breach, and so far as compensation therefor in money can be computed by rational methods upon a firm basis of facts. When a claim for prospective profits is brought to the test of this principle, recovery can be had where loss of profits is the proximate result of the breach, and is such as in the common course of events reasonably might have been expected, at the time the contract was made, to ensue from a breach, and where it can be determined as a practical matter with a fair degree of certainty what the profits would have been. But profits cannot be recovered, when the contract interpreted in the light of all its surroundings does not appear to have been made in contemplation of such damages, or when they are remote, or so uncertain, contingent, or speculative as not to be susceptible of trustworthy proof. They must be capable of ascertainment by reference to some definite standard, either of market value, established experience or direct inference from known circumstances. This is simply a concrete 

13 Magnolia Metal Co. v. Gale, 189 Mass. 124.

§§ 76, 77  

application of the wider principle, which is frequently adverted to and which pervades the determination of all legal rights, to the effect that the complaining party must establish his claim upon a solid foundation in fact, and cannot recover when any essential element is left to conjecture, surmise or hypothesis. The difficulty is not so much in the statement of the general principle as in applying it. A comparatively insignificant incident may be in such combination with others as to lead to a conclusion in one decision apparently at variance with that reached in others. Each case must be decided on its own facts under this necessarily somewhat broad and comprehensive proposition." ¹4 

§ 76. Reasonable and Probable Consequences of Breach of 

Contract. Where the employer wrongfully breaks an agency contract the agent may recover loss of profits which appear to follow as a reasonable and probable consequence of the repudiation of the contract.15 So where a contract to run for a certain period is broken during the period, the measure of damages should include the profits which the plaintiff would have realized from the contract if it had been fully performed. So where the defendant agrees to buy milk from the plaintiff for a year and refuses to carry out the contract, the price for which the plaintiff sold the milk to another dealer, if the best price obtainable, is admissible for the purpose of showing the profits which the plaintiff would have realized and the loss which he sustained.¹ 16

§ 78. Where Profits Conjectural. Loss of profits in an undertaking cannot be recovered where the results of the enterprise are too conjectural,19 as in a bill in equity to enjoin the breaking of a contract the plaintiff cannot recover for loss of profits from the manufacturing which might have been done during that period in the shop where the master finds that this claim of damage was founded on conjecture.20 

Damages may be awarded for loss of prospective profits where the loss is such as might reasonably have been expected and where it can be determined as a practical matter with a fair degree of certainty what the profits would have been. They need not be susceptible of calculation with mathematical exactness provided there is a sufficient foundation for a rational conclusion. But such damages cannot be recovered when they are remote, speculative, hypothetical, and not within the realm of reasonable certainty. The nature of the business or venture upon which the anticipated profits are claimed must be such as to support an inference of definite profits grounded upon a reasonably sure basis of facts. Where Contract Entitles Plaintiff to Profits. Loss of profits may be allowed especially where there was a definite contract that the plaintiff should have a share in profits of the undertaking. "These constitute a valid claim for damages, because the parties have expressly stipulated that profits should be the basis on which a portion of the plaintiff's compensation for services should be reckoned. 

These earnings or profits were therefore within the direct contemplation of the parties, when the contract was entered into. They are undoubtedly in their nature contingent and speculative and difficult of estimation; but, being made by express agreement of the parties of the essence of the contract, we do not see how they can be excluded in ascertaining the compensation to which the plaintiff is entitled. 

Would it be a good bar to a claim for damages for breach of articles of copartnership, that the profits of the contemplated business were uncertain, contingent and difficult of proof, and could it be held for this reason that no recovery could be had in case of a breach of such a contract? Or in an action on a policy of insurance on profits, would it be a valid defence in the event of loss to say that no damages could be claimed or proved because the subject of insurance was merely speculative, and the data on which the profits must be calculated were necessarily inadequate and insufficient to constitute a safe basis on which to rest a claim for indemnity? The answer is, that in such cases the parties, having by their contract adopted a contingent, uncertain and speculative measure of damages, must abide by it, and

§ 83. Retailer's Profits Recovered from Wholesaler. § 87. Wrongful Classification of Product. Where an un derwriters' corporation maintained by insurance companies to classify devices and materials used in buildings with respect to fire and other damage resulting from their use improperly classifies a device competing with the plaintiff's electric switch and consequently permits competition in violation of its contract, while the plaintiff's switches were the only ones entitled to the highest classification, damages may be assessed for loss of profits on sales which the plaintiff would have made had the defendant not permitted competition by makers of substandard switches, and these damages should be assessed for the whole period of the competition. The fact that, if the defendant had withdrawn its label from competing switches, the manufacturers of them would have redesigned them within six months and the plaintiff's monopoly would have been short-lived is a mere speculation as to a condition which never arose, and should not be considered.30

It is the usual rule that a plaintiff cannot recover for breach of contract profits he would have made in other collateral contracts he made dependent upon it. Harding, 7 Cush. 516, 522, in which the subject is considered by Bigelow, J., in the following language: "The rule has not been uniform or very clearly settled as to the right of a party to claim a loss of profits as a part of the damages for breach of a special contract. But we think there is a distinction by which all questions of this sort can be easily tested. 

If the profits are such as would have accrued and grown out of the contract itself, as the direct and immediate results of its fulfilment, then they would form a just and proper item of damages to be recovered against the delinquent party upon a breach of the agreement. These are part and parcel of the contract itself, and must have been in the contemplation of the parties when the agreement was entered into. But if they are such as would have been realized by the party from other independent and collateral undertakings, although entered into in consequence and on the faith of the principal contract, then they are too uncertain and remote to be taken into consideration as a part of the damages occasioned by the breach of the contract in suit. 2. TORTS. 

§ 91. Complete Certainty Unnecessary. In assessing the damages against an outlaw bus line complete exactitude is not requisite, as it is difficult to assess in money the exact damages done by the defendant's act.43 In an action of tort for inducing a breach of a contract the damages recoverable are the loss of advantages either of property or of personal benefit which, but for such interference, the plaintiff would have been able to attain or enjoy. In such a case the damages assessed are not for breach of contract, but for tort, and include such loss of profits as the plaintiff can prove resulted directly and proximately from the wrongful acts of the defendant. There can be no recovery for speculative or conjectural profits, and if the amount could not with reasonable certainty be determined, only nominal damages can be recovered. The fact that there is an element of uncertainty in the assessment of damages is not a bar to their recovery. 44

§ 93. Wrongful Interference with Business. § 95. Wrongful Solicitation of Customers. § 96. Wrongful Use of Partnership Assets in New Busi ness. Where a partnership is wrongfully dissolved and the assets used in another business the owner of an interest in the partnership will be entitled to his share of the profits of the new business, but where it was not proved that this new business made any profits, he is entitled to interest only on the amount of his share from the date of the dissolution.53

1. IN CONTRACT. 

§ 102. General Rule.¹ Any expenses incurred by the plaintiff either in carrying out a contract or in reliance on performance of a contract may be recovered as damages for breach, but not expenses only remotely connected therewith. The question whether the expenses were within the contemplation of the parties is always important, and the application of these rules seems to depend largely on the facts in each particular case. The plaintiff, however, cannot have the same damages twice, and where he is awarded loss of profits he cannot at the same time be given expenses or losses already figured in the loss of profits. In an action for breach of contract the plaintiff's expense in fulfilling the contract must be considered in estimating damages.² 

1 See also § 621 et seq. 

2 Magnolia Metal Co. v. Gale, 189 Mass. 124.

$$ 103-105 

A careful study of the decisions seems to indicate that the earlier judges were not liberal in awarding damages, and many of the earlier decisions on losses and expenses as damages may be considered overruled by later cases. § 103. Failure to Advertise. In an action for failure to advertise in the plaintiff's publication as agreed upon, the measure of damages cannot be the full price of the contract, but the expense of inserting the advertisement which was saved must be deducted. Furthermore, if the plaintiff could have obtained other advertising matter for this space, this must be considered.³ 

§ 104. Expense of Putting Posters on Signboards. Under a contract by which the defendant was to pay for advertising space furnished by the plaintiff, the plaintiff has the burden of proving that it had available at all times the space contracted for which the defendant did not take. The contract further provided that the plaintiff was to put up the posters on signboards, but no deduction for this expense should be allowed where it appears that the plaintiff was under the necessity, as a matter of business for the purpose of keeping its billboards in respectable condition, of putting "fillers" on boards contracted for but for which no advertising matter had been provided. These "fillers" were advertising matter of other concerns which the plaintiff put up without compensation, to protect its own billboards.¹ 

§ 105. Expenses in Preparation for Arbitration Hearing. 

In an action for revocation of an agreement to arbitrate, the plaintiff's damages include the expenses to which he has been subjected by reason of his necessary preparation for a trial before the arbitrators, on account of his own loss of time and trouble, and in employing counsel and other dis-

He cannot recover them so long as these preparations and expenditures were available at the trial in court to which he had to resort. This result is attained although the verdict in court was for the defendant. § 106. Demurrage. Where the defendant contracted to deliver coal for shipment at stated periods and failed to do so the plaintiff may recover as damages demurrage paid for vessels waiting for coal." 

§ 107. Insurance Premiums. Where a builder defaults on his contract and the owner has to complete it and pay insurance premiums against liability in the work of completion, these premiums are properly chargeable against the surety on the contractor's bond as being necessary expenses of the work. So where a building contractor fully performs his contract except that he fails to take out compensation insurance, he may recover on his contract the amount due, less the cost of the insurance which the owner took out.

§ 137. Medical. times, an allowance of $40 is reasonable. "In a proper case, even unascertained future expenses may be allowed for." 54 § 138. Unnecessary Medical Expenses. In an action for personal injuries medical expenses are not confined to those which are necessary. The event may have shown them to be unnecessary and yet they may have been wise in the light of facts known at the time they were rendered. "The rule. . . is that where a person is injured by another's negligence, and uses reasonable care in selecting a physician to attend him and in following his directions, then the one guilty of negligence is liable for the resulting injuries even though a higher degree of medical skill might have minimized the injuries. If the appearance of the patient's body resulting from the defendant's wrong, together with an honest and fair statement of his feelings and sensations, are such as sometimes in common experience might cause an attending physician, selected in the exercise of reasonable prudence in view of the seriousness of the injury, to believe that a certain physical condition existed, and to give treatment in accordance with that belief, then the defendant will be responsible even though subsequent developments may demonstrate that the supposed physical condition in fact did not exist, and would not have been supposed to exist by a physician more skilful, experienced or highly trained, and even though the injury may be aggravated by the treatment in fact given. The causal connection is not broken under these circumstances, though one or even two surgical operations may have been performed."' 55

§§ 140-142  § 140. Future Expense of Cure. In an action for personal injuries where the plaintiff is threatened with consumption, evidence is admissible of the expense of a trip south and of a nurse to accompany him. "There could be but one action to recover damages for the injury, and therefore compensation for injury in the future, as well as in the past, must now be estimated and awarded. The question before us is not as to the rule to be applied when compensation for the future is to be made, but merely whether the evidence was competent. Elements of injury in the future which may be considered are the probable duration of life or of ill health, the diminished ability to labor, the loss of future income, and the increase of future necessary and reasonable expenses. The reasonable cost of employing physicians and nurses, when such assistance has been necessary, is not open to objection. One physician or one nurse may charge more than another, and a jury may have to determine whether actual expenses have been reasonable, or what future expenses may be reasonable. 

But we see no ground on which a jury can be shut off from considering reasonable expenses incidental to attempts to effect a cure or to lessen the amount of the injury." 57 The wife and not the husband may recover for future expenses for care of the wife.58

§ 143. Medical Expenses of Wife. In cases of personal in juries suffered by the wife it is usually presumed that the husband is liable to pay her medical expenses and he can therefore recover them, but where it appears that the expenses were incurred on the credit of the wife, she may recover them in her own action. An action by a husband for consequential damages for injuries to his wife accrues at the time of the injury although the medical expenses were not then paid or even incurred.62 A married woman living with her husband may bind herself for her own medical care, but in the absence of evidence that she has done So, her husband is solely responsible, as the husband is presumed to be liable for medical services rendered to the wife; but the wife may bind her own estate to pay for medical services rendered her and, when properly pleaded, she may recover for this expense in an action for personal injuries.64 

In an action by a husband for consequential damages for medical expenses in treating his wife it is a question of fact what injuries resulted from the accident and what if any diseases were set in motion by it as the direct and efficient cause, and then what medical and other attendance and treatment were reasonably necessary, and what was the fair value of the services and treatment so rendered.65 Damages

The rule is that neither spouse may recover for loss of consortium arising out of personal injuries to the other, although either spouse may recover for loss of consortium through alienation of the affections of the other. The husband may of course recover for expenses incurred in caring for his wife when she is injured through the negligence of a third party.75 Where a wife brings action for personal injuries and receives full compensation, the husband has no right to recover for loss of consortium,76 and his damages are limited to the expense to which he has been put for the care and attempted cure of his wife. This kind of case is to be distinguished from an action by a spouse for the alienation of the affections of his mate, as in that case and in that situation this is the only way in which any liability could be imposed; otherwise the defendant who has alienated the affections of the husband would have escaped all liability for the wrong done."

So a married woman cannot recover for loss of consortium arising out of physical injuries to her husband caused by the negligence of another person whose relations to the injured party are purely domestic and should not be permitted to share the compensation to which he is entitled for the impairment of his powers by the tort of another person, nor to receive an additional sum beyond the full compensation to which the injured person is entitled. 4. Loss or USE. 

§ 153. General Rule. It is the general rule that damages for detention of articles belonging to the plaintiff may include reasonable compensation for loss of use.85 In an action for injury to property the jury in their discretion and as incident to determining the amount of the original loss may consider the delay caused by the defendant. "The rule in substance adopted in these cases is that, while interest is not allowed as matter of right, the time for which the plaintiff has been kept out of the use of his property or the 

82 Croucher v. Oakman, 3 Allen, 185, 186. 

83 See also 861. 

84 Sherlag v. Kelley, 200 Mass. 232. 

85 Kittredge v. Peaslee, 3 Allen, 235.

$ 83 

damage occasioned by the wrong of the defendant may be considered and an amount not exceeding the legal rate of interest may be included therefor in the verdict if necessary in order to give adequate compensation. This principle is applicable to cases where there has been a definite injury to specific property. The reason is that stated by Chief Justice 

Shaw, in Parks v. Boston, 15 Pick. 198, in laying down the rule for the computation of interest where property is taken by eminent domain. The injury occurs and is finished in its results on a particular day, and can then best be ascertained, and exact justice would be done by a contemporaneous determination of the loss. An action for personal injuries is essentially different in its nature. The damages are not complete and ended on the day of the accident, but continue for a greater or less period thereafter. "The extent and magnitude of the injury are not infrequently unappreciated and incapable of reasonable ascertainment on the day it is received. Its degree of permanence is often deceptive at the first, and commonly the determination of conditions requisite for recovery is materially assisted by the perspective of time. The most helpful aids in learning the nature and degree of actual injury may be events occurring after the event complained of. There is no fixed standard by which the compensation to be awarded can be measured. Its general rules have been stated many times. The sum of money fixed upon must be such as fairly compensates the injured person for the loss of time, the physical pain and the mental suffering, both that undergone in the past and likely to occur in the future, and also money reasonably expended and to be expended in assuaging pain and in restoration to health. Elements that are past and also those which are to come must be considered. Most of them are not capable of mathematical computation. They can be settled only by the sound judgment and conscience of the tribunal by which they are assessed, and they are peculiarly within its province. The damages are to be deter-

§ 154 

mined, moreover, as of the day of the trial. It is apparent that interest or considerations akin to interest have no place in an inquiry of this sort. Interest is compensation for the use of money which is due. But the money which the wrongdoer is required by law to pay for the future suffering, expense or loss of time of one whom he has injured is not due until judgment is made up. It is not a debt and does not become a definite obligation until a verdict or finding has been finally entered. It is composed of divers elements, together making up a gross sum, many of which may not have sprung into being on the day when the tort was committed, although directly traceable to it as a cause. If interest were properly chargeable on that which has already accrued, discount should be allowed upon that which relates to the future. Such a method of computing damages would be wholly impracticable. The amount of damages recoverable in actions of this sort, as well as those under certain branches of the employers' liability act and under penal statutes for causing death, is limited to definite amounts. 

Plainly no interest can be allowed in instances of maximum injury.' 1986 § 154. Two Conflicting Theories. It is pointed out in a learned note in the Harvard Law Review 87 that there are two conflicting theories on the measure of damages for loss of use of a chattel, the first being the loss the owner has actually sustained and the second calculating the damage on the hest possible use which could be made of the chattel by its owner. The note traces these two theories in the English cases concerning loss of use of a vessel and concludes that the general American rule is to award damages based on the objective value of the plaintiff's right of use even though the article was used solely for pleasure or was only used occasionally. This objective value may be determined by 

86 Cochran v. City of Boston, 211 Mass. 171, 172. Cf. § 278. 

87 39 Harv. L.R. 760.

85 

the market rental value if the chattel had such a value, but, if not, evidence of the former average net earnings, provided they are sufficiently regular and constant, may be received, while, in the absence of other evidence of a vessel's earning capacity, interest on the value of the vessel is allowed as the best measure of value of its use. 

§ 155. Automobile. An allegation of damage to an auto mobile is sufficient to cover loss of use, and this is not special damage which must be specially alleged, and the plaintiff is entitled to recover as one element of damage the fair value of the use of his own automobile while it was being repaired, not the hire paid for a different car. Still an instruction that the plaintiff is entitled to recover as one element of damage the amount so paid for hire will not be ground for new trial where it has done the defendant no harm.89 

§ 156. Horse and Carriage. Damages for injury to a horse and carriage may include the time elapsed before the horse recovered so as to be fit for use and the time necessary for the repair of the carriage and the necessary expense of hiring another for use meanwhile if that was the most prudent course to adopt.⁹0 § 157.  § 161. Profits Gained in Wrongful Use." Damages are in most cases assessed at the amount of the plaintiff's loss, but there is at least one exception, as where one wrongfully uses the property of another. He may be liable to disgorge any profits obtained by such wrongful use. So, when one wrongfully used a play to produce moving pictures, an injunction against this unfair competition may be obtained and damages assessed at the profits which the defendants made from this wrongful use of the play.¹ 100

1. IN CONTRACT. 

§ 169. In General. There is a broad general principle, often applied, that the plaintiff in contract may only recover his unavoidable real loss and therefore has a duty in many cases to take reasonable steps to mitigate his loss, and cannot recover more where he fails to take such steps, as one must endeavor to put himself in as good a position as if the contract had not been broken." But in an action for breach of an agreement to pay plaintiff's debts he need not show that he tried to get others to pay his debts.³ 

§ 170. Duty to Stop Work on Notice. One cannot continue work under a contract after receiving notice from the other party of its repudiation, but the principle that one cannot increase damages by going on working after notice to stop does not apply to an employment of a committee to act for many manufacturers, as a notice by one to cease work does 

1 See also 601. 

2 Hall v. Paine, 224 Mass. 62. 

3 Banewur v. Levenson, 171 Mass. 1. 

* Martin v. Meles, 179 Mass. 114.

$171 

not stop the damages where there was a common interest in the performance and where what had been done and what remained to do were to a large extent interdependent.5 

§ 171. Duty of Discharged Employee to Seek Other Em ployment. Where an employee who has a contract for service is wrongfully discharged he has a duty to use reasonable diligence to secure other employment to lessen the loss, but where a plaintiff is engaged in a special service he is not obliged to engage in a business that is not of the same general character in order to mitigate the defendant's damages. In an action for breach of a contract to employ the plaintiff at a certain salary a ruling is proper that in order for the plaintiff to recover for the loss of wages the jury must find that the plaintiff was unable to procure, by the exercise of proper industry, other employment of some kind reasonably adapted to her abilities, and the plaintiff is not obliged to seek employment in another locality or of a substantially lower grade or character from that from which she was discharged. Here, where the plaintiff was employed in a special service, she is not obliged to engage in a business that is not of the same general character in order to mitigate the defendant's damages. It is for the jury to determine whether the plaintiff did exercise such reasonable diligence and whether she was justified in declining offers of employment out of town by reason of her mother's illness and whether the refusal of offers at a lower rate or of work in an inferior position was warranted by her expectation of early employment at her regular occupation and salary." 

Where a veteran entitled to priority in city work is wrongfully discharged and it becomes apparent that he will not be employed again short of a court order, he then is under an obligation to seek other employment, and if he does not do

On the question of mitigation of damages where an employee is discharged, he may show that he went to another man in the business and asked for work and then went into partnership with him. § 172. Duty where Work to be Done by Employees. Under a contract for hiring plaintiff's teams for trucking, broken by the defendant, damages are the loss of profits the plaintiff would have realized by completing the contract. § 174. Owner's Duty in Completing Building Contract.

§ 187. Marine Insurance. Return Duties. In computing a partial loss under a policy of marine insurance return duties are not to be deducted from the amount to which the underwriters are to contribute.33

§ 192. Profit on Later Contract Not Deductible.42 The damages of the subcontractor for breach of his contract are not affected by the fact that he later made another contract with the contractor on which he made a profit.43

But the fact that he has foreclosed and realized the full amount of his indebtedness and expenses should be received in mitigation of damages.45

 § 195. Attack on Foreclosure Sale to Reduce Amount Due on Note. In an action on a mortgage note to recover the balance due after a foreclosure sale where the mortgagors were not the owners of the equity at the time of the sale it is open to the makers of the note to show, as bearing upon the amount due, that the sale was not conducted as it should have been, as if the makers of the note cannot do this they would seem to be without a remedy.46 

§ 196. Removal of Building. For breach of a contract to remove old buildings only nominal damages may be recovered when the buildings might have been moved without expense.47

In an action of contract on a bond conditioned on removal by the defendant of a barn the defendant offered evidence that after the time when the barn should have been removed the plaintiff used and occupied it with the assent of the defendant free of rent, and it is held that this evidence should not be used in mitigation of damages. On this question 

Bigelow, C.J., remarks: "The evidence offered by the defendant was incompetent to show any ground for diminishing or abating the damages which the plaintiff was entitled to recover for a breach of the bond. It appears that the use of the building was a gratuity, for which no charge or claim was to be made by the defendant. It was on this understanding that the plaintiff made use of the premises. The defendant cannot convert that which was offered by him and received by the plaintiff as a favor or license without recompense into a debt or a claim, in the nature of a set-off against the damages which the plaintiff is entitled to recover. Such a defence is not only contrary to the original intent and agreement of the parties, but is a violation of good faith." 48

 2. IN TORT FOR OTHER THAN PERSONAL INJURIES. 

§ 197. Where Plaintiff Suffered No Loss. The defendant may always show in mitigation that the plaintiff in fact lost nothing by the wrong.49 

§ 198. Property Damage Preventable. The plaintiff can not recover for damages to property which he might have prevented.50 

§ 199. No Duty to Commit Trespass to Avoid Damage. 

In an action of tort for damages resulting from the discharge of sewage into a dock adjoining a wharf of the plaintiff it appears that it was impracticable to dredge the dock, as the Harbor and Land Commissioners refused to give the necessary permit and the neighboring owner objected to any trespass upon his dock, so that the work on the plaintiff's premises would be ineffectual unless the neighbor's dock also was dredged. The plaintiff's measure of damages is not necessarily the cost of such dredging and the damage occasioned by the incidental interference with her business. The plaintiff is not entitled to damages that were avoidable by the use of reasonable precautions, but was not called upon to take unreasonable steps or to commit a wrongful act or to trespass upon the property of another in order to abate the nuisance, and these are questions of fact for the jury.51

§ 202. Duty to Attempt Cure of Horse. Where a horse is injured by negligence "in such a way that proper care and attention reasonably may be expected to effect a cure, which will leave the damage from the injury much less than if he died, it is the duty of the owner to give it such care and attention, in order that the damages may not be augmented by neglect. . . The expense properly incurred for this purpose is a part of the damage to the owner, for which he is entitled to compensation, as well as for the diminution in value or other loss that may finally result directly from the injury notwithstanding these efforts." This is true although the effort is fruitless and the horse dies, provided the owner uses sound discretion and good faith so as not to make an unreasonable expenditure.57

Where one who hires a horse makes him sick by improper care and feeding he is liable for the value of the horse where the owner employs a competent veterinary whose treatment results in the death of the horse. The rule is stated by Merrick, J., as follows: "Thus in the present case, where the

This was all that the law required of him, because it was all that he could in fact do. There are no known means which can be resorted to with any absolute certainty that they will prove sufficient to eradicate disease and bring back health, or prolong the existence of animal life. Notwithstanding the utmost efforts of persons the most proper to be called on to render assistance in such exigencies, and most competent to afford it, fatal results may follow from their action or prescription, because there is no possibility of guarding effectually against injurious consequences which are the result of mere errors of opinion or mistakes in judgment. And therefore if the plaintiff did, on the return of the horse, employ suitable persons to take care of him, and they were faithful in the performance of the service in which they were employed, and the horse died notwithstanding their efforts to save and restore him, the death must be attributed to the disease caused by the culpable neglect of the defendant, even though the remedies applied in the course of the treatment, instead of having their intended effect, aggravated the disease and contributed in some degree to its fatal termination.", 58 § 203.  § 204. Excluded Members Forming Own Union. Where it was found that the plaintiffs had been wrongfully excluded from a labor union, the fact that the plaintiffs united in an organization of their own and held themselves out as a union did not bar them from money damages.60 

§ 205. Converted Goods Returned.61 In an action of trover damages may be mitigated by evidence that the defendant relinquishes all claim to the property.62 "If after the conversion the property is returned and accepted • " ac- ceptance mitigates and limits the damages to the difference between the value of the property when converted and the time when it is returned." 63

In case of conversion of goods the true owner is not bound to accept a return of the converted goods, but is entitled to the value of the goods at the time of the conversion, and also to interest upon that value to compensate him for the delay in obtaining redress. If the owner has retaken the goods, the damages are likewise based upon the value at the time of the conversion, but in mitigation of those damages the wrongdoer is entitled to credit for the value of the goods at the time of the return, though he is chargeable with the value of the use of which the owner has been deprived during the period of wrongful detention.4

§ 218. Payment by Joint Tortfeasor. It is a settled rule of law that payment by one joint tortfeasor bars action against other tortfeasors, and to avoid this result careful attorneys, where settling with one joint tortfeasor, give a covenant not to sue rather than a release. Even then payments made may be shown in diminution of liability of other tortfeasors, as the plaintiff can have but one satisfaction.

Strictly speaking a covenant not to sue is not in fact a release, although it is its equivalent with respect to the covenantee and is allowed so as to obviate circuity of action.8 88 Where an employee of a householder while walking on the grounds falls into an unguarded hole left by an independent contractor in sinking a gasoline tank, and receives money for a covenant not to sue her employer, in an action for personal injuries against the contractor the money she has already received in settlement with the employer must be deducted in mitigation of damages. The money paid was a partial satisfaction of her claim, and she cannot receive for the same wrong remuneration in excess of her actual damages.89

§ 219. Gift by Joint Tortfeasor. The question sometimes arises whether a payment made to the injured party by one not liable operates to reduce the damages, and it is the rule in this State that the party to whom the release is given and who makes the payment must be one against whom an action would or might lie, and that a claim has been made for or on account of the alleged tort, although it is not necessary that it should appear that he was in fact liable. So a gift from one of the joint tortfeasors will not operate to bar a recovery against the others. There must be something in the nature of a claim on the one hand and of possible liability under the rules of law applicable to the matter on the other, in order to render the release a bar to recovery against other joint tortfeasors.90 

§ 220. Settlement of Claim against Agent as Bar to Claim against Principal. Where the agent has taken from the injured person a covenant not to sue or press any claim growing out of the same accident, he may enjoin the prosecution by the injured person of an action against the agent's principal for damages growing out of the same injury. It is the general rule of law that a party may not receive anything more than one compensation for an injury, and where the injuries caused were the joint or concurrent negligence of two or more persons there can be but one full recovery. A cause of action of the principal against the agent for the latter's tort committed in the course of his employment does not arise until the principal has been required to pay the damages, so any payment to the injured person by one joint tortfeasor is admissible in evidence in reduction of damages in an action against a joint or concurrent tortfeasor.91

§ 225. Recoupment and Set-Off Distinguished.' There is in general no set-off or counterclaim allowed in actions of tort. The doctrine of recoupment exists only at common law and must arise out of the contract sued upon,2 while the right of set-off is created by statute and applies even where there are different contracts, or claims in contract not arising out of the same transaction.³

§ 231. Setting up Breach of Contract to Action on Quan tum Meruit. Where the plaintiff breaks a special contract with the defendant for advertising but continues to accept advertising from the defendant, the plaintiff may recover on a quantum meruit for work actually done, but the loss by breach of contract should be deducted to avoid circuity of action. The situation is well covered by Bigelow, C.J., as follows: 

"Instead of relying on his special contract, and, when it was broken by the acts of the plaintiffs, insisting on the breach and claiming damages for its non-performance, he subsequently accepted a part performance of the contract by the plaintiffs. This severed the entirety of the contract. 

By his own consent, with full knowledge of the breach, the defendant received and enjoyed the benefit of the services, labor and property of the plaintiffs. Although the plaintiffs, if they failed to perform the special contract on their part, are debarred from maintaining any action upon it, yet they have a legal claim for the actual value of the labor and services performed by them, which the defendant has accepted and enjoyed. From the act of the defendant in continuing to send his advertisements to the plaintiffs for publication, after he had notice of the alleged breach by them of the special contract, and thereby taking to himself the benefit of their subsequent labor, services and material, the law implies a severance of the original entire contract, and raises a promise to pay the amount, which the plaintiffs reasonably deserve to have. Bowker v. Hoyt, 18 Pick. 555. Snow v. 

Ware, 13 Met. 49. Oxendale v. Wetherell, 9 B. & C. 386.

Read v. Rann, 10 B. & C. 439. 2 Greenl. Ev. § 136 a. There 

13 Kenworthy v. Stevens, 132 Mass. 123.

§§ 232, 233  

is no allegation or proof in the present case, which tends to charge the plaintiffs with any want of good faith in the alleged failure to fulfil the special contract set up by the defendant. They are therefore well entitled to recover the fair value of their services. Snow v. Ware, ubi supra. "In estimating the amount which the plaintiffs were entitled to have for the beneficial enjoyment of their labor and services by the defendant, it was proper for the jury to deduct the loss or damage which he had sustained in consequence of the alleged breach of the special contract. This is allowed to avoid circuity of action, so that substantial justice may be done between the parties in one suit.”' ¹ª § 232. Defects in Work Done. It is a general rule that defects in work done may be shown in recoupment,15 as, for example, a contract to build a bicycle track provided for payment thirty-one days after completion unless some defect shall meanwhile have been discovered on said work, and the court holds that this clause allows a reasonable deduction from the contract price if a defect in the work is discovered.16

§ 244. Statutory Origin.¹ The allowance of interest in any case is a matter of statutory origin, there being great prejudice against interest at the time of the formation of the common law. Ordinary interest in this State is at the rate of six per cent,2 and the statutes contain many other provisions for interest in special cases,³ and even provide how interest may be pleaded.¹ 

§ 245. Interest as Incidental to Debt. Penalty against De linquent Attorney. The nature of interest as incident to the debt appears in a decision holding that the statute imposing a fivefold penalty of interest on an attorney withholding money of a client survives against the estate of a deceased attorney. The court, per Rugg, C.J., remarks as follows: 66 'Although the statute is not phrased with clearness, we think it more consonant with the nature of the relief afforded against the delinquent attorney, and the terms in which it is expressed, to hold that, although the word forfeit is used, an increase in the legal rate of interest as applied to a debt of this character is intended rather than a technical forfeiture. The meaning is that the rate of interest upon such a debt shall be five times that which otherwise would be the lawful rate. It substitutes a five fold increase for the rate

It is the general rule to allow simple interest in equity and law by way of damages, but this general rule is not always followed. result as to interest in tort actions. Keeping in mind the basic principle of the law of damages that it is an attempt to make the plaintiff whole of his injury, it seems that the court might have taken the position that interest should run from the date of a personal injury. After all, that is when the blow is struck, and the mere fact the consequences cannot be seen at once is no more an argument against figuring interest from the time when an occupant of an automobile is injured than against taking interest from the date of the injury to the automobile, although the full damage to the car cannot be seen until it is later repaired. 

On the other hand, the court might have started interest. from the date of recovery, as in case of a broken leg when, after six weeks, the plaintiff has a leg as strong as ever, although this would seem unfair in case of a slow convalescence. The court, however, has denied interest completely in actions for personal injury, notwithstanding the long delays in our courts in reaching these cases for trial. 

In actions for damage to property the court, however, has bent to manifest justice and reached a compromise, which seems defensible on no possible theory, that although interest in these cases cannot be figured as such, still the factfinding body may in its estimate of damages consider the lapse of time. In trover for wrongful detention of property, however, the court seems to allow interest as interest, and it might be argued that this creates a quite illogical exception to other actions of tort. 

§ 278. Distinction between Personal Injury and Property 

Damage. In an action for personal injuries arising from a defect in a way, interest for the delay in payment should not be added to the finding. The court distinguishes actions for personal injuries from actions for injury to property, and notes that adding such interest would be entirely impracticable, as the damages may be awarded in part on an estimate of future incapacity.

An action for personal injuries is essentially different in its nature. The damages are not complete and ended on the day of the accident, but continue for a greater or less period thereafter. Deceit.83 In the ordinary action of deceit where the plaintiff is seeking not to recover money paid out by him but an unliquidated sum equal to the difference between the value of the property received and its value if it had been as represented, damages do not become a definite obligation until the verdict or finding is recorded, and therefore interest cannot be added to the damages proved.84
