§ 286. The Massachusetts Rule.¹ Under the early common law no costs or expenses were awarded the successful party in litigation, but costs were provided by the Statute of 

Gloucester (6 Ed. I, c. 1), under the terms of which the court taxed as costs the moderate fees of counsel and attorneys who attended the cause." This statute seems to have been adopted with the balance of the common law in this State, but the legislature early fixed attorneys' fees which could be recovered at a nominal sum, whether due to the prejudice against lawyers at the time or for some other reason being a question for the historian rather than a textbook writer to solve. Our court early refused to allow counsel fees as such to be allowed as costs,³ although there was considerable doubt on the subject, for in 1821 the court were not agreed upon the subject * and as late as 1838 Chief Justice Shaw remarks that "Formerly a notion prevailed, that in trespass and other actions sounding in damages, a jury, being limited by no definite rule, might include in 

1 See also § 622. 4 

2 Per Grier, J., in Day v. Woodworth, 13 How. 363. 

3 Leffingwell v. Elliott, 10 Pick. 204. 

4 Rice v. Austin, 17 Mass. 197, 206, where the court advised the plaintiff that it was not agreed on counsel fees as damages and the plaintiff waived them.

their estimate of damages, the counsel fees, and other costs of litigation, not included in the taxable costs," but he con- Icludes that it was then well settled that this should not be done.5

It could hardly be claimed that counsel fees were not a natural and probable consequence of a wrong done or were not the proximate result of an injury, and the arguments against their allowance seem to have been practical rather than theoretical. Probably in view of the harsh poor debtor laws of the period there was a universal desire to open the courts to the poor as well as the rich, so that the loss of every case would not mean a period in jail for the losing party unless he had funds. Chief Justice Shaw hints at this situation when he remarks: "These are expenses incurred by the party for his own satisfaction, and they vary so much with the character and distinction of the counsel, that it would be dangerous to permit him to impose such a charge upon an opponent; and the law measures the expenses incurred in the management of a suit by the taxable costs." 

It is now well settled that in the ordinary case taxable costs are considered full compensation for the expense of conducting the litigation."

§ 287. Personal Injuries. A request for a ruling that the plaintiff in an action for personal injuries was entitled to reimbursement for all expenses incurred by her as a result of the accident is too broad and was rightly denied, as it would include counsel fees and other disbursements not recoverable under the law.8 § 288. Agreement for Indemnity. In an action to recover on an agreement for indemnity, damages may include costs, including reasonable counsel fees. Where the grantee assumes and agrees to pay certain mortgages outstanding on the property conveyed and the first mortgage is foreclosed, leaving a deficiency which the grantor has to pay, as this contract stipulated for full indemnity the grantor's damages are based on the loss actually sustained, which includes not only interest but legal costs and expenses.10 So in a bond of indemnity to cover expenses in a suit in equity brought to enjoin the foreclosure of a mortgage of real estate, this covers attorneys' fees, as the word "expenses" used in mortgages has been held to be broad enough to include reasonable counsel fees.¹¹ 

§ 289. Expenses of Action which Defendant should have 

Defended. One who is properly summoned in to defend another action which he has agreed to defend and does not do so is liable to pay the reasonable cost of defending it.12 

Thus where an insurance company fails in its agreement to defend the plaintiff against suits for injuries after notice, the company is liable for the principal sum paid in said action and also for all the expenses the plaintiff incurred in defending the action.¹ 13

Where a town is found liable for a defect in a highway caused by the negligence of a private citizen it may recover from him not only the damages paid but also counsel fees and expenses in defending the suit if it has notified this person to come in and defend it. The principle adopted is that, if a party is obliged to defend and defends solely and exclusively the act of such other party and is compelled to defend no misfeasance of his own, he may notify such party of the pendency of the suit and may call upon him to defend it, and if he fails to defend he is liable not only for the amount of damages recovered but for all reasonable and necessary expenses incurred in such defense.14 

An agreement to provide full indemnity against an action entitles the indemnified party to full protection, and the plaintiff's damages must be measured by the loss actually sustained, which includes interest and legal costs and expenses. Where the defendant was notified of the pendency of the action and was requested to assume the defense and made no reply, the plaintiff acted reasonably in going on and defending the suit, and the defendant is estopped from contesting the judgment and is liable for the amount which the plaintiff has been obliged to pay, with interest from the date of payment, and also for reasonable counsel fees necessarily incurred in the litigation.15 

§ 290. Expenses Caused by Plaintiff's Fault. § 291. Expense of Defending against Defendant's Wrong ful Act. If the wrongful act requires the employment of counsel to defend against the wrong, this expense may be recovered,18 as "It has been held that in certain actions of tort the plaintiff can recover expenses incurred in employing counsel as an element of damages arising out of the wrongful conduct of the defendant." 19 So in an action of tort for conversion of furniture the plaintiff may recover attorneys' fees paid in an effort to recover possession of the property, as such fees constituted no part of the expense of the present suit.20 And in an action by a constable against another constable for indemnity for taking insufficient surety on replevin bonds, evidence of the amount which the plaintiff had agreed to pay his counsel for services was competent although not conclusive.21

In a suit in equity for unlawful acts of interference with the plaintiff's business, including the bringing of vexatious and unwarranted actions, the actual cost of defending these proceedings, and not merely the statutory taxable costs, was properly assessed as damages. In an action for damages for exclusion from a union, fair and reasonable counsel fees should be included. As a general rule taxable costs are considered compensation for the expense of conducting litigation even though such costs are only nominal and wholly inadequate, but in actions based on the wrongful conduct of the defendant where the wrong is of such a character that the proper protection of the plaintiff's rights necessarily requires him to employ counsel to gain redress for the wrong, he may recover as an element of damage reasonable counsel fees, and this is true whether the services of counsel were rendered in a prior proceeding or in the action where the counsel fees were recovered.

In order to recover counsel fees it is not necessary to prove that they were actually paid to counsel. It is enough if the amount be reasonable and the plaintiffs were obligated to pay them.23

§ 293. Expenses of Reinstatement to Office. Where a city officer is wrongfully removed from office he may, in an action of tort against the officials removing him, have considered as an element of damages the amounts reasonably paid for counsel fees in procuring reinstatement in office where he was obliged to incur these expenses wholly by reason of the wrongdoing of the defendants. This situation is quite different from those cases where the taxable costs are held, so far as concerns a particular proceeding, to be full compensation for expenses in conducting litigation. 

Also his later inability to obtain a bond, which obliged him to resign, may be considered where this resulted from his removal. His mental suffering may also be considered.

cretion of the Probate Court.29 The Probate Court has full power, both in equity and in probate proceedings, to allow attorneys' fees and other expenses as costs, but it is held that this "is a power of great delicacy to be exercised with extreme caution. § 296. Contract to Pay Expenses. Where an agreement provides that bankers are to be covered for all outlay of every nature, including legal expenses, this includes reasonable and necessary expenses incurred by them in the employment of counsel.35 So in an action by a subcontractor against a contractor for building a sewer, where they had agreed to share in the fruits of an action against the city for not protecting the work, the plaintiff's damages are to be figured on the damages to that portion of the sewer which the plaintiff built, deducting the balance due on the contract and the excess per foot paid the subcontractor over the sum paid the contractor and deducting also the plaintiff's proportionate part of the amount paid for counsel fees and other expenses incurred by the defendant in the action against the city.36

However, where a banker advances money for the manufacture of leather goods under an agreement that it will be entitled to the "proceeds" of the leather, this means the gross proceeds without deduction of the cost of manufacture or legal expense in collecting the money due.37

§ 297. Liquidated Damages and Penalty Distinguished.¹ 

Contracts providing for payment of a sum of money on breach raise commonly the vital question whether this sum is intended as liquidated damages or a penalty. The question is crucial, as only if it is liquidated damages will the courts enforce it according to its terms. As pointed out in the leading cases noted in this section, this is a problem of the intention of the parties, keeping in mind whether the damages for breach are otherwise readily ascertainable, whether the sum named is reasonable, and whether the same payment is provided for important as for unimportant breaches.2

This is a question of the construction of the contract on which the surrounding circumstances may always be considered,³ and a payment to be made under a bond is commonly construed to be a penalty. Depending on the lan-

Contra: Hodges v. King, 7 Met. 583. See Chase v. Allen, 13 Gray, 42.

$153 

5 6 guage of the instrument the payment to be made may be construed a penalty or liquidated damages, and will be construed a penalty where it is based generally on a breach of any or all the stipulations of the contract.' Where the sum payable is expressly stated by the contract to be liquidated damages and not a penalty, it may be so treated. 

The sum agreed to be paid will be usually construed as liquidated damages where the actual damages are difficult to ascertain, but not where damages for the breach of some agreements are certain and easy to compute.10 It was formerly said that there is a presumption that a sum payable on breach of a contract is a penalty rather than liquidated damages, but this statement seems no longer true.¹¹

Where a contract for sale of a stock of goods and tools contains an agreement that in case either party breaks the contract he "shall forfeit to the other party the sum of three hundred dollars," this sum is liquidated damages and not a forfeiture. The rule is well explained by Bigelow, C.J., in the following language: "The true mode of arriving at a just interpretation of the stipulation for damages in such cases is, to take into view the subject matter of the contract, the nature of the agreements into which the parties have respectively entered and the surrounding circumstances, in order to ascertain whether the intention was to provide for a fixed measure of damages or only to stipulate for a penalty. Where the intention is clear that the entire sum should be paid, it is the duty of the court to enforce the agreement, however hard or inequitable the exaction may seem. If the parties go to the extent of making an agreement in clear and explicit terms to pay a certain sum on the non-performance of a covenant to pay a smaller sum, it is impossible to avoid giving effect to such a contract. Galsworthy v. Strutt, 1 Exch. 659.

It is only when the whole instrument is taken together and the intention is left doubtful that it becomes necessary to resort to the established rules of construction, in order to determine on which side of the line a particular stipulation falls. . . . There was only one object contemplated by the parties to the agreement declared on in this action. It was not a contract for the performance of divers acts of different degrees of importance, each of which could be easily estimated and measured in money. But it was a contract for the doing of a single specific act, and the sum named was in respect of a breach of this one stipulation only. The case therefore comes within the rule recognized in the adjudged cases, as being one in which there is only one event on the 

13 Edward G. Acker, Inc., v. Rittenberg, 255 Mass. 599.

$ 155 

happening of which the money is to become payable, and there is no adequate means furnished by the contract or otherwise of ascertaining the precise damage which may result to the plaintiffs from the failure of the defendant to fulfil his part of the agreement. If the contract had been to pay a certain sum of money, or to purchase certain specific articles of merchandise, the value of which as between vendor and vendee could have been ascertained without difficulty, the measure of damages arising from a breach would have been certain and readily fixed, and the intent of the parties to stipulate for a penalty only would have been fairly inferrible. But such is not the nature of the present contract. It is an agreement for the sale of an entire stock in trade, and all the tools used by the plaintiffs in carrying on the manufacturing business. A transaction of such a nature, involving the transfer and surrender of the business and good will connected with the trade and manufacture in which the plaintiffs had been engaged, differs essentially from an ordinary agreement for the sale of goods or the payment of money. It is impossible to estimate with accuracy, or to measure by any definite or precise rule, the extent of damage which either party might sustain by reason of the breach of the contract. The necessity of taking an account of stock, the consequent interruption of business, the preparation to relinquish an old occupation and to engage in a new one, and other similar elements, would necessarily enter into the contemplation of parties in making an agreement like that which is the subject of the present action. But the impossibility of placing any estimate in money on the damage which might result from such causes is obvious, and leads to the reasonable inference that the parties intended to fix the amount of compensation in the event of a breach by inserting a sum to be taken as liquidated damages in the literal sense of that term.'' 14 

14 Lynde v. Thompson, 2 Allen, 456, 459.

$298 

Where certain citizens subscribed sums to aid the defendant in building a hotel on his agreement to pay $20,000, “not as a penalty, but as fixed and liquidated damages," on failure to do so this was construed as an agreement for liquidated damages. Bigelow, J., in one of his lucid opinions, settles the question as follows: "The determination of the question, whether a sum named in a contract, to be paid for a breach, is to be regarded as a penalty, or as liquidated and ascertained damages, depends not so much on the form or language of the contract, as upon its subject matter, and the nature of the covenants or agreements, for a breach of which the damages are stipulated to be paid. Hodges v. King, 7 Met. 583. Mayne on 

Damages, 68. The rule of construction applicable to such stipulations is now well settled. Where a party agrees to pay a certain sum in case he fails to perform any one of divers acts which are of different degrees of importance, and which are capable of being estimated and measured in money, the sum named as damages is to be treated as a penalty; but if the contract consists of several stipulations, the damages for a breach of which cannot be well ascertained and valued, then the parties are deemed to have intended that the sum agreed on shall be treated as liquidated damages, from which there is to be no deduction. Green v. 

Price, 13 M. & W. 701, 702, and 16 M. & W. 346. Atkins v. 

Kinnier, 4 Exch. 783. Curtis v. Brewer, 17 Pick. 513. Heard v. Bowers, 23 Pick. 455. "The case at bar clearly falls within the latter branch of this rule. The subject matter of the contract is such as to render it quite impossible to form any estimate of the damages occasioned by a breach of its stipulations. No standard by which the damages can be measured is furnished by the contract itself, nor would extrinsic evidence afford any means by which they could be accurately or even approximately ascertained. The persons who subscribed to the fund to aid the defendant in erecting a hotel were prompted

$157 

to do so by the expected benefit which would thereby accrue to them respectively by enhancing the value of their real estate, and by increasing the business in that part of the city of Worcester. It is obvious that the damages which each would sustain by the loss of this anticipated benefit are peculiarly uncertain and difficult of estimation in money. 

This is therefore one of those cases where it must be presumed that the parties stipulated for the payment of a fixed sum of money absolutely, from the difficulty of ascertaining any exact amount of damage which would be sustained by a breach of the agreement." 15

A contract providing for the manufacture by the defendant of a certain quantity of a novel patented article provided that the defendant should deposit with the plaintiff the sum of $500, which should be forfeited to the plaintiff "as fixed, liquidated and ascertained damages" in case of breach of contract, and it was held that this was liquidated damages and not a penalty and that this limited the recovery which the plaintiff could have. Here it would be difficult to determine the damages for failure to manufacture this newly patented article, the success of which was problematical, and it is held that the rule that, where a sum is to be paid in case of a breach of any of several distinct stipulations of various importance, it will be construed as a penalty has no application. It is also somewhat indicative of the intention of the parties to make this $500 liquidated damages that it was a less sum than the defendants would otherwise be liable to pay on failure to make and pay for the patented article. Penalties usually provide for the payment of a larger sum on the failure of a party to pay a less amount.16

Where the defendant agrees not to sell a certain proprietary medicine below a certain price and it is agreed

The parties here fixed damages which are not capable of being ascertained by any satisfactory and known rule.18 

Under a contract by which the plaintiff was to pay $10 a month on account of certain building lots, with a provision that on the plaintiff's failure to complete the purchase the defendant might keep all payments made as liquidated damages, the plaintiff on repudiating the contract cannot recover money paid. This will be enforced as an agreement for liquidated damages and not a forfeiture.19 Where the defendant contracts to use the plaintiff's office for its telegraph business for ten years and the contract provides that on breach the party breaking it shall pay the other a cash payment of such a sum as would equal the amount of money that said party would have received if the contract had been carried out, this contract fixes the measure of damages. The action brought before the expiration of the ten years is not premature, and damages are to be a fair equivalent of what the plaintiff has lost in probable receipts."

§ 299. Cases where Payment is a Penalty. Where a con tract to convey binds the parties under a penalty of $1000, this may be found to be a penalty.23 So a contract by a dancer for performances containing a clause that for breach of the agreement the offending party shall pay "as damages" a large sum in excess of the total payments, although in other sections of the contract the words "liquidated damages" are used, shows merely an intent to fix a penalty.24

Where a contract for shipping goods provided a penalty for non-performance by either party of $2200, this is to be regarded as a penalty and not as liquidated damages, especially on breach of only one of the terms of the contract. "But further, and applying a rule which is among the most important in determining whether the sum named is to be treated as a penalty, or as liquidated damages, it appears very clearly by the contract that the penalty named would be alike incurred by the nonperformance by either party of any of its numerous stipulations; and that the actual damage caused by a failure to perform some of them might be very trifling in amount, and capable of very exact pecuniary estimation. If, for example, the plaintiffs had failed to furnish five or ten tons of the stipulated cargo, or if the defendants had failed in some trifling particular to keep the ship in proper order for the voyage, so that one or two packages of goods had been injured, can it be supposed that it was in the contemplation of either that so serious a consequence should follow? The penalty would be the whole sum to be paid for a breach of the whole contract; and it would be unjust and oppressive to require either party to pay it, for violating any one of the least important items.” 26

Where a lease provides that on breach of any of its covenants by the lessee the rent payments should be accelerated and all the rent for the balance of the term should immediately become due and payable, this is a penalty rather than liquidated damages. The court remarks as follows:

§ 300. Liquidated and Unliquidated Damages Distin guished. Where under a contract one of the parties agrees to give notes to the other, this agreement creates a debt, and damages for its breach are liquidated within the definition of liquidated damages.28

In a bill in equity to enforce a contract for oil which the defendants never delivered to the plaintiff, the question arose as to the payment of interest for breach of the con-

tract and it was held that this is a claim for liquidated damages and that interest runs from the date of the demand. "It has been stated to be the settled rule of this Commonwealth that in a claim for unliquidated damages interest runs from the date of the writ and not from the date of demand for payment. McGrimley v. Hill, 232 Mass. 462, 464. Childs v. Krey, 199 Mass. 352, 358. That principle in its broad aspect is not of universal application because there are numerous instances where interest may be added from the date when damages may be due, in order that reparation may be done for the full injury sustained. Frazer v. Bigelow 

Carpet Co. 141 Mass. 126. It is not necessary to consider the doctrine of this case because we are of opinion that the damages here in issue were liquidated and that interest ran from the date of the demand. Liquidated damages with reference to the facts here disclosed mean damages, agreed upon as to amount by the parties, or fixed by operation of law, or under the correct applicable principles of law made certain in amount by the terms of the contract, or susceptible of being made certain in amount by mathematical calculations from factors which are or ought to be in the possession or knowledge of the party to be charged. Unliquidated damages are those which cannot thus be made certain by one of the parties alone. "In our opinion the damages in the case at bar were liquidated within the principle thus stated. Ford v. Tirrell, 9 Gray, 401. The defendants must have known how much had been paid them by the plaintiffs for oil not delivered and also how much of the money so paid had been paid to the plaintiffs in way of profits. The several factors for determining the amount due to the plaintiffs were known to the defendants at the time the demand was made on them. 

The circumstance that, at the time of the demand by the plaintiffs upon the defendants, the principles of law governing the rights of the parties in view of the somewhat complicated facts had not been declared, does not prevent the

Where a contract required the plaintiff to repair certain houses and have them fit for occupancy by a certain date and that for every day's delay the plaintiff should "forfeit $5," this is an agreement for liquidated damages. The rule is well discussed in the following language by Bigelow, C.J.: "The principles on which courts of law proceed in determining whether a sum named in a contract, to be paid in case of a failure to perform its stipulations, is to be treated as a penalty, or as liquidated damages from which no deduction is to be made, have been very fully discussed and applied by this court in recent cases. Chase v. Allen, 13 Gray, 42. Lynde v. Thompson, 2 Allen, 456. According to those principles, there can be no doubt that the sum named in the contract declared on is to be treated as liquidated, and as fixing the exact measure of compensation to which the defendant should be entitled in case the plaintiff did not complete his contract within the stipulated time. Such seems to us to have been the intention of the parties. The language

Where defendant hired a chronometer and failed to return it the court remarks: "The contract was an agreement to hire at a certain fixed rent for a period which was to end, at the option of the hirer, at the end of the contemplated voyage, or at the expiration of fourteen months. The chronometer was then to be returned to the plaintiffs. The article was not returned as stipulated; and, if this were all, it is plain that the plaintiffs would be entitled to recover the rent agreed for the whole period of fourteen months, and whatever the jury might find the value to be at the expiration of that time. 

That value would of course be affected by the consideration that its original value had been diminished by the period of its use, or on the other hand increased by the enhanced market value of such articles. Under the peculiar terms of this contract, it is claimed that this rule cannot prevail, because the contract states the value of the article to be $240 and requires that it shall be returned in the same good order as received. Upon the whole, we do not regard these provisions as intended by the parties to be conclusive between them upon the value of the article. In a subsequent clause, the right of the master to purchase within six months at that price is given. And the value seems to be named either in reference to that right of purchase or as mere matter of description. The agreement that it shall be returned in the same good order does not provide against that deterioration which comes from ordinary use and wear. In order to give the recital of value the conclusive character contended for, it must appear from the whole contract that the parties intended to liquidate the damages. evicted before the end of the term of the lease of the sublessee, and the lessee is evicted, the court holds that this bond is for liquidated damages. The court, per Holmes, C.J., admits that there may be cases where an undertaking may be treated as a penalty although it is called liquidated damages in the contract, and cites as a typical case where it secures several promises of varying importance, one or more of which are for the payment of a much smaller sum of money. Still, so far as precedent permits, the proper course is to enforce contracts according to their plain meaning and not to undertake to be wiser than the parties, and therefore in general, when parties say that a sum is payable as liquidated damages, they will be taken to mean what they say and will be held to their word.53 So a provision in a lease to indemnify the lessor by paying a lump sum of $34,000 on termination is not void as calling for a penalty where this sum named bore a reasonable relation to expenses reasonably to be anticipated.54

Still, where a lease provided that the lessor might terminate it on payment of $2500 and the tenant is evicted by a grantee of the lessor, the lessee cannot bring action to recover the $2500. This is not a covenant to pay $2500 as liquidated damages, but is a clause giving the lessor the option to terminate. The only right the lessee has is to sue for the eviction.55 § 309. Bond to Arbitrate. Where the defendant gave a bond in the sum of $500 to abide by the decision of arbitrators, but instead of doing so brought a suit in equity to set aside their award, the bond is a penalty bond and not for liquidated damages where not so stated. The plaintiff cannot recover the expense of the successful defense of the defendant's bill in equity, as his costs are considered full 

53 Guerin v. Stacy, 175 Mass. 595. 

54 International Paper Co. v. Priscilla Co., 281 Mass. 22. 

55 Harrison v. Jordan, 194 Mass. 496.

$ 310 

compensation for that and the plaintiff is therefore entitled only to nominal damages.56

So where two parties submit their differences to arbitration under an agreement providing a payment of $1500 for breach, the court holds this to be a penalty rather than liquidated damages, using the following language: "The court are of opinion that the plaintiff is not entitled to recover more than the amount of the award, even as against Reuben Carpenter. In his agreement the sum of fifteen hundred dollars is mentioned as liquidated damages. 

But in Shute v. Taylor, 5 Met. 61, the court say, 'It is not always the calling of a sum, to be paid for the breach of contract, liquidated damages, which makes it so. In general, it is the tendency and preference of the law to regard a sum, stated to be payable if a contract is not fulfilled, as a penalty, and not as liquidated damages; because then it may be apportioned to the loss actually sustained.' See also Fisk v. Gray, 11 Allen, 132. In this case the contract of Simon

Carpenter calls it 'the penalty of fifteen hundred dollars;' so that as to him there is no ground to call it liquidated damages; and in Reuben Carpenter's contract it is stipulated that the party neglecting or refusing to perform the award 'shall forfeit to the other party' that sum. Forfeiture is in the nature of penalty; and, looking at both contracts and the object to be secured by them, we think a penalty was intended. It would be extremely harsh to regard it as liquidated damages, because there are a variety of things to be done under the award, especially by the defendants; and it would be difficult to perform all of them without such delay as might be held to amount to negligence.' 1957 § 310. § 312. General Rule. Statutory Exceptions. The rule of punitive or exemplary damages which prevails in many States has never found favor with our court in this State and it has been repeatedly laid down that the recovery of vindictive, exemplary or punitive damages has never been permitted in this Commonwealth.¹ This rule of confining damages to compensatory recovery seems reasonable in ordinary actions of contract or for negligence, but where the tort or the breach of contract takes on a quasi-criminal form, the compensatory-damage rule appears in many cases entirely inadequate.

It is in such cases entirely contrary to public sentiment as expressed by the legislature, and the situation is that the rule expressed by the court is today quite contrary to the result of legislative action, which has created innumerable cases of punitive damages to be recovered, as appears in the note below.2

Where in a bill in equity to enjoin flowing water on the plaintiff's land the amount of damages need not be determined, the plaintiffs are entitled to nominal damages. So where a plaintiff, a riparian owner, had a right to the reasonable use of the water in common with other riparian owners and the defendant diverts water, a finding that the plaintiff suffered no actual damages but had all the water he needed is conclusive, and he can recover only nominal damages for the invasion of his right to undisturbed possession.10

Where the owner of an easement seasonably asserts his rights he should not be compelled to surrender the easement in part at a valuation because the pecuniary benefit of the defendant may outweigh any disadvantage suffered by the plaintiff, and therefore a decree with costs should be entered awarding nominal damages and permanently enjoining the defendant from obstructing the passageway." So in a bill in equity to enforce the rights of an adjoining owner against the construction of a cellar and bay windows where it appears that the plaintiff has a technical right only and has proved no damages, a decree awarding nominal damages and costs may be entered.12

2. CONTRACT. 

§ 334. Agreement to Pay Void Assessment. In an action on an agreement to pay a betterment assessment no damages can be awarded where it appears that the lien of the assessment had been lost so that the plaintiff has suffered no damage by breach of the agreement.¹¹ 

§ 335. Failure to Finish Building on Time. Where there is a plain breach of a penal bond by not finishing a building on time there must be judgment for the plaintiff at least for nominal damages although the plaintiff's estate was benefited by the defendant's extra work above the terms of the contract.15 

§ 336. Where Plaintiff could Not Carry out Contract. If a manufacturer repudiates a contract with a dealer appointing the dealer his exclusive agent and at that time the dealer was in such financial condition that it would have been impossible for him to make certain payments which the contract required, the dealer cannot recover substantial damages.10 

§ 337. Contract to Purchase. Where the buyer refused to carry out a contract to purchase real estate and it was not questioned at the trial that the contract price was a fair price, it is difficult to see how the plaintiff can recover more than nominal damages.¹ So where the defendant broke a contract to purchase lamps and the plaintiff wrote the defendant: "If you cannot use the lamps at these prices, I will dispose of them elsewhere, as I can easily do so at better prices," this is not a waiver of the right to nominal dam-

On the other hand, where the buyer refuses to accept goods sold under contract and there is evidence that they have no market value, substantial damages may be awarded of the difference between the contract price and the market value, and the jury should not be instructed that only nominal damages may be awarded.19 

§ 338. Failure to Notify Indorsers of Note. The measure of damages for failure to give notice to indorsers of a note would be prima facie the amount of the note and interest thereon, but if the defendant could show that the loss to the plaintiff was merely nominal and that it suffered no actual loss on account of the negligence of the defendant, the amount recoverable would be limited to nominal damages. 

Whether the plaintiff suffered a loss by reason of the failure to give notice to the indorsers depended upon their financial responsibility, and presented a question of fact. The measure of damages recoverable was the loss shown to have been the natural and proximate consequence of the negligence of the defendant.20 

§ 339. Contract to Loan Money. Where a defendant agreed to loan a corporation $25,000 for its new unit and broke his agreement by loaning the corporation more than that for working capital in running the business, still no damages should be awarded where it appears that the corporation suffered no damages, that if the money had been loaned for the new unit as agreed upon the corporation would have had to close down for lack of working capital.21

NOMINAL DAMAGES § 340. Disclosing Libellous Statements to Person Libelled. 

It seems to be the English rule that only nominal damages can be awarded for breach of an agreement not to disclose libellous statements to the person libelled, even though the information is given pursuant to an agreement to indemnify for any breach of the agreement.22 

§ 341. Agreement to Pay Mortgages. Where a grantee assumes and agrees to pay mortgages and there is a foreclosure sale for a price sufficient to pay the mortgage debt and expenses, there can be no recovery of even nominal damages on the agreement to pay the mortgages, as the plaintiff has suffered no harm.23 

§ 342. Tax Lien Paid. Where a covenant against incum brances is broken by the existence of a tax lien but the taxes are paid by the procurement of the defendant, the plaintiff cannot have a claim for more than nominal damages.24 

§ 343. Right to Subscribe to Stock. Where a plan for re organization of three corporations providing for forfeiture of rights in failing to pay a subscription for common shares referred only to the right of the shareholder in respect to his common shares, therefore he may be entitled to a decree for the transfer to him of a certificate of deposit representing preferred shares, but it is held that he was not entitled to damages.25 

§ 344. Stockbroker Selling Stock. Highest Intermediate 

Value Denied. The rule of nominal damages is often applied where a stockbroker wrongfully sells his customer's stock but, due to a falling market or other causes, no actual loss 

22 Bradstreets British Ltd. v. Mitchell &c. Co., [1933] 1 Ch. 190. This de cision is criticized in a note in 46 Harv. L.R. 1336. 

28 Warneke v. Wyczatycki, 269 Mass. 179.

results. Thus in an action of contract against stockbrokers to recover a deposit made where the brokers sold out the stock held on margin, the plaintiff can recover only nominal damages without evidence of the price at which the stock could have been bought after he first learned of its sale.26 

In an action for rescission of a sale of stock by a stockbroker on account of his breach of duty in selling his own stock to the plaintiff, the damages would be measured by the difference between what the plaintiff paid and what on the day of the purchase he could have purchased the stock for in the market. If unable to prove actual damage, he would be entitled to nominal damages for this breach of duty.27 

Where a stockbroker holding securities on a margin account wrongfully sold them, the customer's sole remedy was for actual damages, and where the customer is given prompt notice of a sale and could have replaced the stock by buying other stock at prices below those at which the wrongful sales wére made, he is entitled to nominal damages only.28 The theory of damage for a breach of contract calls for the determination of the amount of money necessary to put a plaintiff in the same position he would be in if the contract had been fulfilled. If the position of such a party has not been altered, he has suffered no actual damage; so where a stockbroker broke his contract to keep in his possession securities left with him as collateral but the customer never demanded the securities and suffered no loss on account of the conduct of the stockbroker, the customer would be entitled only to nominal damages, but where he seeks equitable relief it is proper to dismiss the bill without reference to nominal damages.29

Where the plaintiff, a customer of a stockbroker who is carrying stocks for him on margin, sues to recover for losses 

26 Papadopulos v. Bright, 264 Mass. 42. 

27 McNulty v. Whitney, 273 Mass. 494. 

28 Dennett v. Wilmerding, 291 Mass. 264. 

29 Cragin v. Jones, 283 Mass. 474.

NOMINAL DAMAGES 

caused by sales made by the stockbroker, the rule of damages in the ordinary case is the difference between the market value of the stocks sold at the time of the sale and that at the time when the plaintiff was notified of the sale. Hence the plaintiff can recover only nominal damages where he might have purchased the stock at substantially the prices at which they were sold by buying them back on receiving notice of each sale.

The plaintiff in this case relied on the highest intermediate value rule, that the customer can recover the highest value at which the stock sold between the date of a sale and the date of the trial, but the court finds that this rule has never been adopted in Massachusetts. 

Chief Justice Rugg in his able opinion relies on the fixed rule that the plaintiff is entitled to compensation for loss sustained and to nothing more; that actions as to stocks stand on no other basis than any other commodity, and that the rule of fair market value as the test for damages is the prevailing rule in this Commonwealth. The court finds that exceptional circumstances might require the application of some other than the ordinary rule, as if the sales were made in panic periods or timed to work oppression to the plaintiff. 

Here immediate notice was given to the plaintiff in every instance and ample opportunity was afforded to repossess himself of a like amount of the stock sold at the same time if he had so desired.

Stockbrokers may be liable for sales of stock on margin to themselves, and the correct rule of damages to be applied in that case is that the plaintiff may recover the difference between the value of the stocks when sold and the value when their sales were made known to and repudiated by him, together with interest from that date.³ 30 30 Hall v. Paine, 224 Mass. 62. The court finds that the rule of highest intermediate value was repudiated in this Commonwealth in the following cases among others: Gray v. § 360. General and Special Damages. General Rule.* The rule is well settled and clear that general damages need not be specially alleged in the declaration, but special damages must be so stated; but the application of this rule is often difficult. "Under that requirement the general allegation of damages is sufficient to enable a plaintiff to recover all damages which are the natural or necessary consequences of the cause of action so stated. Damages such as the law will imply from the facts set forth in the declaration may be recovered. But when special or peculiar damages are claimed, it is necessary to aver them specifically. The salutary rule of 

1 See also 317. 

2 Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153. 

3 Booras v. Logan, 266 Mass. 172; Brockton Olympia Realty Co. v. Lee, 562. 

266 Mass. 550, 4 See also 4.

§§ 361, 362 

195 

PLEADING 

the common law requiring the plaintiff to allege in his declaration particular or unusual damages remains unchanged. 

The underlying and sound justification for that rule is that the defendant ought to be guarded against surprise at the trial by evidence tending to prove damages of which he had no previous notice. The statement of the rule is simple. It sometimes may be difficult to determine what are the natural consequences, actually but not necessarily flowing from that tortious conduct." 5

It is not necessary to set out in detail the elements of damage, but a general claim of damage will cover all damages that naturally flow from the cause of action. Special or peculiar damages must be specially pleaded if claimed, and any particular damage must be set forth in the declaration, at common law and under the practice act. 

Special or peculiar damages which are not the usual or natural consequences of the act done should be set forth specifically in the declaration." Special damages not implied by law as a necessary consequence of a breach of an agreement to convey real estate must be specially alleged.10

Although the statute provides for the assessment of damages in a petition for mandamus,¹³ still this right seems quite limited. Thus in a petition for a writ of mandamus addressed to city officers demanding them to recognize the petitioner as an employee and to place his name upon the payroll, the petitioner cannot recover sub-

§ 397. Scope of This Chapter. The rules of evidence are not within the possible limits of this book, but a few decisions bearing particularly on damages are here inserted for convenience.¹

In an action for damages for death, evidence is admissible that the defendant had pleaded guilty of operating so as to endanger the lives and safety of the public on the occasion on which the death occurred, and this bears on the degree of culpability of the defendant." § 400. Length of Disability. In an action for assault and battery the plaintiff may show that his eyes were injured and how long it was after the injury before he was able to use his eyes and how long it was before his nose got well.¹

The insult and indignity inflicted upon him may well have occasioned distress of mind and injury to his feelings more serious than the physical damage, and the plaintiff was entitled to recover reasonable compensation therefor." § 403. § 408. General Rule. Damages for breach of contract are the natural and proximate consequence of the breach which was within the contemplation of the parties. 1 

§ 409. Damages for Breach Entire at Time of Breach. The damages for a repudiation of a contract are entire and accrued on the date of the breach.2

§ 411. Amount Due under Contract. In an action on a con tract the measure of damages is the difference between the amount actually received by the plaintiff and that to which it is entitled upon a true accounting in accordance with the contract.¹ 

§ 412. Damages on Rescission Different from on Perform ance. The damages recoverable for a rescission of a contract are not the same as those to which the plaintiff would be entitled on proving a full performance, and therefore it is error for the judge to give the jury an instruction under which they could award the plaintiff the amount to be paid him on his performance of all the things required by the contract if the plaintiff proved that the defendant repudiated the contract and thus excused him from further performance.5 

§ 413. Expense of Completing Contract. It is the general rule that in figuring damages for breach of contract the expense of completing the contract must be considered. So the damage for failure to put fixtures in a building is the cost of putting them in. Also where defendants agreed to procure for a railroad a right of way and failed to do so the railroad was entitled to recover expense of taking the right of way and land damages, costs and legal expenses in land-damage suits and fees paid to attorneys.' § 414. Deduction for being Relieved from Performance. 

Where the plaintiff had a contract to keep signs painted for which the defendant was to make monthly payments which the defendant failed to make, the plaintiff may be entitled to recover as damages the difference between what he would actually have received if the contracts had been fully performed by him and what he did in truth receive after taking into account as a deduction from the difference thus ascertained whatever benefit came to him by reason of being relieved from fully performing the contract.10

Arbitration Agreement. It is settled that the mutual promises of the parties in an agreement for arbitration are sufficient consideration each for the other, and that whichever party without right prevents arbitrators from acting is liable to an action. "It is argued that, as it is found by the auditor's report and by the jury that there was nothing due upon these claims, the plaintiff is entitled to no damages, or at most to but nominal damages, on account of the revocation, and that it must be deemed that the arbitrators would have

The expenses to which he has been subjected by reason of his necessary preparation for a trial before the arbitrators, on account of his own loss of time and trouble, and in employing counsel, taking depositions, payments to witnesses, arbitrators, and expenditures of a similar nature, are proper matters of claim. He is entitled to recover these so far only as he has lost the benefit of them by the act of the defendant. So far as these preparations and expenditures were available for the trial of his cause before the ordinary legal tribunals to which the revocation of the defendant compelled him to resort, he is not entitled to recover, as he has had or might have had the benefit of them. Ordinarily, it is true, as the defendant argues, counsel fees are not recoverable; but if the plaintiff has been deprived, by the wrongful act of the defendant, of the benefit of those services of counsel for which he had incurred expense, upon the former agreement for arbitration, inasmuch as they were expenditures he might properly incur, so far as they were suitable, there is no reason why he should not recover them in this action. § 426. Breach of Promise to Pay School Tuition. Where a contract of a correspondence school provides that the defendant shall pay certain sums in instalments and the defendant stopped studying and refused to make any further payments, the agreement of the defendant subscriber to pay the stipulated price for a scholarship was an independent promise, and therefore the proprietor of the school was entitled to recover the amount of all unpaid instalments and was not limited to a recovery merely of the damages sustained by reason of the subscriber's breach of contract.38

§ 429. Error in Telegram. Compensatory Damages. In an action of tort against a telegraph company for failure to transmit a message accepting an offer to sell certain goods at a certain price, the measure of damages is "The sum therefore which would compensate the plaintiffs for the loss and injury sustained by them would be the difference, if any, in the price which they agreed to pay for the merchandise by the message which the defendants undertook to transmit, if it had been duly and seasonably delivered in fulfilment of their contract, and the sum which the plaintiffs would have been compelled to pay at the same place in order by the use of due diligence to have purchased the like quantity and quality of the same species of merchandise." 42 

Where the telegraph company makes a mistake in quoting the price and the seller refuses to return the goods or to pay a higher price than that named in the telegram and the seller to avoid litigation accepted payment of the lower price and where the buyer is in another State and it might be expensive and difficult to collect, this does not estop the plaintiff from enforcing his rights against the telegraph company for breach of its contract by failing to deliver the message. Damages to the plaintiff might have been inferred.48

 § 430. Error in Telegram. Where Company has No Notice of Danger of Error. Failure of a telegraph company to deliver a code message whereby the plaintiff lost the freight for a ship gives rise to an action, but the measure of damages can be only the cost of the tolls and not the loss of the freight, as there was no notice to the telegraph company of the general nature of the transaction.44 

Damages for mistake in a telegram are the natural and proximate result of the error, and where there is nothing in the transaction to bring home to the company knowledge of any particular damage which will be likely to result from a mistake in sending a message or a failure to deliver it, the damages that can be recovered are only the expenses of sending it.¹ 45 

§ 431. Error in Telegram. Limitation of Liability. In an action against a telegraph company for failure to send a message correctly, damages are limited by the terms of an agreement stated on the blank.46 Where a telegraph company takes a message under a stipulation that it will not be responsible for failure to deliver it beyond the amount paid for the message, the only recovery which can be had for negligence in delivering is the cost of the message, although the negligence may be claimed as gross negligence. 47

§ 432. Difference between Value Called for and that Built. 

In an action on a building contract the rule of damages will

"Generally the loss of the use of a building by reason of the failure of a contractor to complete it in accordance with the terms of an agreement may be considered as an element of damages, but in the case at bar it does not appear that any loss of rent was incurred as it was found that no tenants were available. The rule as to damages in case of a breach of an agreement to erect a building where the agreement is with the mortgagee and not with the owner is the same except that, as the mortgagee holds the property for security only, he cannot recover more than the difference between the value of the property in the condition in which it is left and the amount due on his mortgage." 49 

In a building contract where there were some omissions or defects in the construction of a house called for by the contract the rule of damages is that there should be deducted from the contract price the amount by which the value of the house as left by the builder fell short of what that value would have been if the contract had been exactly performed. This rule is to be applied to a petition for the enforcement of a mechanic's lien as well as to an action upon a quantum meruit against the landowner, but if the contractor has abandoned his work while yet unfinished, or

It was proper for the plaintiff to make such repairs as should supply all such deficiencies as could be supplied without disproportionate or unreasonable expense. If, after this was done, there should still remain deficiencies and injuries which could not be repaired except at a cost greatly disproportionate to the value of the building, he would be entitled to have the effect of those deficiencies in diminishing its value estimated by the jury.51 52 In an action on a building contract where floors are not constructed in accordance with the contract the owner may recoup as damages the difference between the value of the floors if they had been built as designed and their value as built and left by the plaintiff. If resurfacing the floors is practical, the jury may consider the cost of resurfacing as the measure of damages. Where a contract to build a house calls for a roof to remain tight for two years, if the roof is not of that character the owner may "recoup from the contract price, as damages, the difference between the value of the building as constructed and what it would have been if the house had been built according to the contract; or, if the building had been paid for before the defect was discovered, they might bring an action to recover back that difference. § 433. Rights of Mortgagee. Where the owner of land agrees with the mortgagee to construct well-built houses on the property and fails to build them properly, the damages are the difference between the value of the houses as they were in fact built and the value they would have had if built in conformity to the agreement, or so much of this difference as would have been necessary, with the value of the houses as built, to pay the mortgage debt and interest then due; and the time for determining these values was the time when the defendant left the houses as finished or as soon afterwards as the plaintiff had notice of the defects or might have had such notice by the exercise of reasonable diligence. So if the houses later deteriorated in value, the defendant is not chargeable with this loss.54 § 434. Construction Bond. In an action on a construction bond guaranteeing construction of a building according to contract the measure of damages is the difference between

The loss of use of a building may usually be considered in an action by the owner, but as the mortgagee holds the property for security only, he cannot recover more than the difference between the value of the property in which it is left and the amount due on his mortgage. Therefore it was error to make the test the difference between the value at the time of the foreclosure and the value as it would have been if the building had been completed as agreed upon, as the value at the date of foreclosure may be different from that at the time of the breach by the contractor when he abandons work on the property.55 

§ 435. Substantial Performance. Value Added to Land. 

There is in this State an anomalous doctrine to the effect that a builder who has substantially but not fully performed his contract may recover in quantum meruit the amount by which his efforts have increased the value of the owner's property. Such a doctrine seems to deprive the owner of the benefits of his contract and runs counter to the usual rule that damages should be based on the difference between the value called for by the contract and that built. 

This doctrine goes by the name of the Rule of Hayward v. Leonard,56 and is based on language used by Chief Justice Parker in that early decision. This decision, however, adopted no such rule and flatly held that the jury "should have been instructed to deduct so much from the contract price as the house was worth less on account of these departures. 

55 Province Securities Corp. v. Maryland Casualty Co., 269 Mass. 75, 94. 

56 7 Pick. 181, reported post, note 62.

$ 435 

The doctrine received a new lease of life in Gillis v. Cobe 57 notwithstanding a powerful dissent by Chief Justice Knowlton, and seems now to be firmly planted in our jurisprudence although when one rule is to be used and when the other is not perhaps clearly settled yet. 

The doctrine has been recently described as follows: "Again, a builder who, in an honest attempt to perform a contract, has performed it substantially though not sufficiently to enable him to recover upon it, may recover upon a quantum meruit for the benefit conferred." 58 This statement is, however, a mere dictum, and in the recent case of Glazer v. Schwartz 59 the court did not follow this rule at all. All the decisions cited in section 432 seem inconsistent with this doctrine.

In an action on an account annexed where the plaintiff seeks to recover payment for building a house according to a special contract and proves that he has substantially performed it, the measure of damages is the contract price deducting what the house was worth less to the defendant by reason of deviations from the contract.60 "One who in good faith substantially performs his contract may recover on a quantum meruit, . . the sum recovered being the contract price, less 'the amount by which the value of the house as left by the . . . [builder] fell short of what that value would have been if the contract had been exactly performed.' .. But where the default is wilful there can be no recovery either on the contract or on a quantum meruit." Therefore the builder cannot enforce his lien either upon the contract or upon a quantum meruit. The principle applicable where the builder acts in good

Where a contract to build a building is carried out substantially but not exactly, the builder may bring an action for quantum meruit, but is not entitled to recover what the house as built was worth to the defendant; but the rule is that there should be deducted so much from the contract price as the house was worth less on account of these departures. This rule is confined to "cases in which there is an honest intention to go by the contract, and a substantive execution of it, but some comparatively slight deviations as to some particulars provided for." If there is a gross violation of contract, as if a man who had contracted to build a brick house had built a wooden one, or instead had built a barn, he "could recover nothing without showing an assent or acceptance, express or implied, by the party with whom he had contracted." 62

 § 437. Owner Completing Building. "Where a contractor in violation of his contract has abandoned his work, the owner may complete it and charge the reasonable and necessary cost to the delinquent contractor. Lawton v. Fitchburg Railroad, 8 Cush. 230, 233. Gleason v. Smith, 9 Cush. 

484, 486. Hebb v. Welsh, 185 Mass. 335, 337. Pelatowski v. 

Black, 213 Mass. 428, 431. "In the case at bar the contractor employed its own workmen to do this work. This necessitated withdrawing them from other work which they would have been able to perform and for which the contractor would have been entitled to a profit. In these circumstances it was entitled to a reasonable profit, in addition to the amount required to pay its workmen as the reasonable and necessary cost of doing the work. To hold otherwise not only would the contractor be required to do the work at an actual loss, but the subcontractor would be required to pay for its default a less amount than if the contractor had employed others to complete the contract. Although there are no cases in this 

Commonwealth in which the precise point under discussion has been decided, we see no sound reason for holding that a reasonable profit may not be included as an element of damage. The contractor was bound by its contract with the owner to do this work, but it was not obliged to do it with its own men who might have been otherwise employed at a profit. In other words a reasonable profit, such as the contractor ordinarily would have been required to pay if it had employed others, was a necessary part of the reasonable expense incurred by reason of the default of the subcontractor.'' 65

§ 440. Breach of Contract by Owner. 71 Snelling v. Lynch, 5 Allen, 443.

The ordinary rule undoubtedly is, that the plaintiff must repair or rebuild the defective wall within a reasonable time, and that the expense of such repair or reconstruction, and the loss of the use of the land for such reasonable time would be the measure of damages. What was a reasonable time was to be determined in view of all the facts in the case. One material fact was that the defendants, admitting their failure to fulfil their contract, promised to rebuild, and the plaintiff relying, as he well might, upon such promises, delayed himself the rebuilding of the wall. The question was, whether the delay caused by the promises of the defendants, and their failure to keep them, could enter into the consideration of what was reasonable time. The presiding judge in the court below instructed the jury that they might take them into consideration. We think he was clearly right. Upon notice to the defendants of the defects in the structure of the wall, and the promise of the defendants to rebuild, the plaintiff might well wait and give the defendants the opportunity to perform their promise; and the delay so caused was as truly reasonable as that occasioned by the state of the season or other physical cause. Damages for the loss of the use of the land during such time are not remote, speculative or contingent, but the direct and immediate consequence of the defendants' failure to perform their contract and duty. The instructions to the jury were good law and good sense, clearly and accurately stated." 76

Indemnity and Mental Suffering. In an action for breach of promise of marriage damages may include the money value or worldly advantage of a marriage which would have given the plaintiff a permanent home, the wound and injury to her affections, mortification and distress of mind, but the jury cannot assume that the defendant by associating with the plaintiff prevented her from forming any other marriage alliance. 4. CONTRACT FOR SUPPORT. 

§ 451. Damages for Total Breach.88 Damages for breach of a contract to support another for life are the whole value of the contract.89 So where one conveys land in consideration of an agreement to support the grantor for life he may recover damages for the breach and is not obliged to declare for the value of the land.⁹0 90 Where the defendant in consideration of the conveyance to him of certain real estate promised to support the plaintiff for the rest of his life and the defendant breaks the contract in such a way that the plaintiff has the right to treat the contract as absolutely and finally broken by the defendant and he elects so to treat it, the damages are assessed as of a total breach of an entire contract. "Such damages are not special or prospective damages, but are the damages naturally resulting from a total breach of the contract, and are suffered when the contract is broken, and are assessed as of that time. From the nature of the contract they include damages for not performing the contract in the future as well as in the past. The value of the contract to the plaintiff at the time it is broken may be somewhat indefinite because the duration of the life of the plaintiff is uncertain, but uncertainty in the duration

judge, based wholly or partly on replacement cost, less depreciation. Consequently, the facts reported support the conclusion that, so far as the propriety of the payments of premiums depends upon the amount which would be recoverable under the policies, the trustees exercised sound discretion.'' 102

This decision is certainly more in consonance with insurance practice, as insurance companies are wont to set up an insurance value based on the cost of reconstruction of buildings insured far in excess of any possible market value of the structures. For example, the author recently passed papers in a sale of land in Boston with an old building upon it valued by the insurance company at $112,000 on which a policy of $88,000 was written and the land and building together sold for $12,500. The extraordinary recession in land and buildings in certain parts of Boston and other cities during the depression years has brought about a situation where the rule laid down by the court by 

Chief Justice Rugg in the King case would leave insurance policies as very small protection to the owners. 

It may also be said that the companies are insuring on the basis of reconstruction value, possibly for the reason that in that way they collect higher premiums; but whatever the reason, it is a universal practice which it seems the courts are likely to recognize in one form or another.

§ 462. Partial Loss of Freight. In a case of a partial loss of freight, half of which is covered by a policy of insurance, the underwriters were responsible only for the proportion of the amount of the valuation of freight in the policy which the freight actually lost by the peril insured against bore to the actual value of the entire freight. The valuation in the policy should be applicable to any part lost in like proportion as it would be to the true value of the whole.106 

§ 463. Marine Insurance. In an open policy of marine insurance the rule of damages is the market value of the goods, with certain costs and charges, at the beginning of the risk, rather than the invoice price.107

§ 468. Damage by Bailee to Machine. So where the defendant leased a machine and damaged it by his own negligence and continued to use it although he knew it was unfit by reason of insufficient repairs made by him and where because of such use it was incapable of being made fit for use, the lessor may recover the rent of the machine as stated in the lease as well as for loss of its value.

§ 470. Recovery under Wagering Law for Loss of Securities 

Pledged. In an action to recover under the wagering statute the liability of the defendant can only be for the value of what the customer delivered to the broker to be used on a margin account, and where the customer's stock was already pledged to another, the recovery must be limited to the value of the securities subject to the pledge.13

In an action against a stockbroker for loss in a margin account where the securities pledged were sold and the proceeds applied towards the extinguishment of the stockbroker's lien, the plaintiff is not entitled to recover the value of the securities in an action under the wagering contract law, but only the net money received by the defendant from their sales made on the express order of the plaintiff's intestate. This decision was said to be limited to the peculiar facts here presented and does not extend to nor affect a case where the initial deposit with the broker is not subject to a valid pledge or lien.¹4

§ 473. Property Attached and Taken on Execution.¹ 

an action for attaching property of the plaintiff where it remained in his possession until it was taken on execution, the measure of damages is its value when taken on execution. The court gives the reason for this rule as follows: "The general principle is, that in actions of trover and trespass for the unlawful conversion of personal property, the owner shall recover the value of it as it was at the time of the first wrongful taking, with interest afterwards from that date. If this rule were here to be applied, the plaintiffs would be entitled to claim the value of the property as it was on the day of the attachment thereof on mesne process, with interest afterwards. But under the particular circumstances of the present case we think that rule is inapplicable; and that it would be unjust to allow it to be enforced. The plaintiffs did in fact have the full and entire use of the engines, cars and other articles until they were seized by the sheriff on the execution. They are therefore to recover whatever the value of the property shall be

§ 474. Place of Conversion Immaterial. "The rule is per fectly well established, that in actions of tort for the seizure and conversion of personal property, the measure of damages is its value at the time of the conversion. This was so stated by the court in its directions to the jury, which were therefore in that particular entirely correct. The additional qualification, asked for by the defendant, that the market value of the property at the place where it was converted should be taken into consideration, was properly refused. 'Place,' as used in this connection, was indefinite and uncertain. If adopted, it might have misled the jury by its being supposed to limit them in ascertaining the value of the property to inquiries as to sales made on the precise spot where the conversion took place, or its immediate vicinity. Within such a circumscribed range, it may have been impossible to find that the property had there acquired any marketable value. It is sufficient that the true and established rule of law upon the subject was distinctly stated as the basis upon which the verdict ought to be rendered.", 3

3. PARTIAL INTERESTS. 

§ 485. Special Interest. "Where one has a special property in a chattel, or a lien thereon, he may in some instances recover its full value against a wrongdoer who appropriates it; but as in such case he recovers all that exceeds his own special property or interest therein, for the benefit of the general owner, when the wrongdoer is not a third person, but the general owner himself, his rights are fully maintained, and circuity of action is avoided, by permitting him to recover the value or amount of his special property or interest alone."

So where hides were delivered to the plaintiff's intestate to be tanned and sold and he dies and the owner takes them back and completes the operation and sells the hides, the administrator is entitled to recover only the difference between the amount at which the hides were charged to the intestate and the amount realized from the sale by the owner, 21

CONVERSION § 494. Goods Subject to Lien for Freight. "As a general rule, the measure of the damages in trover is the market value of the goods converted, with interest from the date of the conversion. This rule is, however, subject to modification when the plaintiff has only a special interest or property in the goods, and is not answerable over to any person for the balance of the value. . .. The object of the law is to give the plaintiff compensation or indemnity for the injury he sustains by the conversion." So where the goods converted were subject to a lien for freight and the only interest which the plaintiff had in them was their market value less the freight that is all he can recover. 36 In an action of trover by a pledgee "The amount of freight and storage, having been paid not in good faith nor in accordance with the terms of the defendants' contract, could not be demanded by them of the plaintiff, as a condition precedent to the delivery of his property to him, and could be deducted from the value of the goods in the assessment of his damages, only because the payment enured to his benefit, by discharging the goods from a lien to which they were subject, and without payment of which he could not have obtained his property." 37 

§ 495. Bill to Redeem Pledged Stock Wrongfully Sold. In a bill in equity to redeem certain stock pledged it appeared that the pledgee had sold the stock wrongfully, and the court holds that the damages are not fixed by the market value as of the date of the sale as in an action of trover, but rather by the market value at the date of bringing the bill. 

The plaintiff here is entitled to be placed substantially in the same position as if the sale had not taken place and has the right to judge for himself whether to sell them or not.

He should recover as damages such sum as would enable him to purchase new shares to replace those which have

been taken from him, with such additional sum as would indemnify him for the dividends which he has lost since the sale, and also an equitable allowance for interest.38

§ 496. Conversion of Bond. Interest at six per cent. In an action for conversion of a four per cent bond, interest will be allowed at six per cent from the date of the writ.³ 39 

§ 497. Retaining Note till Maker Becomes Insolvent. 

Where the defendant wrongfully took and retained a promissory note for a period of two years until after the maker had become insolvent, the defendant became thereby chargeable for the value of the note at the time of the conversion and interest thereafter.40 So in an action for conversion of a promissory note the measure of damages is the value of the note at the time of the conversion, and evidence of the financial condition of the maker at the maturity of the note several months later is inadmissible.* 

§ 498. Savings-Bank Book. The measure of damages for the conversion of a savings-bank book is the value of the account it represents.¹2

The value of property converted may be at least the highest price that a normal purchaser not under peculiar compulsion would have paid in order to get the property, and the master may also consider the time during which the articles had been in use and their condition and the cost of replacing them. Stereotype Plates. In an action for conversion of stereotype plates containing labels and advertising matter pertaining to the plaintiff, which plates had no value to anyone except the plaintiff, the court laid down the true rule of damages as follows: "The proper rule of damages was prescribed by the judge, namely, the fair value of the plates to the plaintiffs. 

And he allowed the jury to take into consideration, in estimating that value, the cost of replacing the plates. The defendant insists that the market value was the true rule of damages. And this is doubtless the general rule in trover. 

But this rule presupposes the conversion of marketable property. Whereas, in this case, it was admitted by the defendant's counsel, in argument, that the plates in question were made for the printing of labels or advertisements in the plaintiffs' names, which were to be used by them only, in their special business; and the exceptions show that it was in evidence that they were of very trifling value, except to the plaintiffs. Such things cannot with any propriety be said to have a market value. And the actual value to him who owns and uses them is the just rule of damages in an action against him who converts them to his own use.

2. ORDINARY DAMAGES. 

§ 538. Warranty under Sales Act. The rights of the buyer in case of a breach of warranty are set forth in detail in the Sales Act, G.L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 106, § 58, and the decisions noted below should be read in view of this statute. The usual rule of damages for breach of warranty under the statute is "the loss directly and naturally resulting, in the ordinary course of events, from such breach," and the usual test will be "the difference between the value of the goods at the time of delivery to the buyer and the value they would have had if answering to the warranty."

Express or implied warranties on sales of goods are cov ered in G.L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 106, §§ 14-18. 

Where a contract for sale of dress goods contained no express warranty there is no implied warranty entitling the defendants to damages in recoupment on a claim that the colors ran.3 § 539. Warranty at Common Law. "In an action for breach of warranty on a sale of chattels, the rule of damages is the difference between their actual value and the value which they would have borne if they had conformed to the warranty. Reggio v. Braggiotti, 7 Cush. 166. Mayne on Damages, 88. The rule is the same in an action for a deceit in the sale. Stiles v. White, 11 Met. 356. And the same principle is applied in a suit (like this) by the seller for the price of chattels warranted, but which do not conform to the warranty, and in a suit on a note given for the chattels. The plaintiff, in such case, can recover no more than the actual value of the chattels in their condition at

On the question of a breach of warranty in the sale of chattels the rule of damages is the difference between the actual value of the article sold and the value of the same article if it had been such as the vendor warranted it to be. 

On this issue evidence is incompetent as to the price the buyer sold the property for and what was his total loss.5 

§ 540. Delivery of Defective Goods. The difference be tween the contract price and the actual value of goods delivered is the correct measure of damages. So in an action for failure to deliver coal as called for by the contract the damages are the difference between the value of the coal received and the value of that called for by the contract.' 

Under an entire contract for a stipulated amount of sugar where some of it is damaged the rule of damages is the one ordinarily applicable in actions by a buyer for breach of warranty in a contract for purchase of goods delivered to and accepted by him. That rule is the difference between the market value of the property contracted to be sold in the condition required by the contract at the time and place stipulated and its actual market value. In defense of a note given on exchange of horses the defendant might put in evidence the actual value of the plaintiff's horse at the time of the exchange, and the jury might deduct the difference between this and his alleged value at that time from the amount of the note and give a verdict to the plaintiff for the balance.⁹
