 § 541. Course Open to Buyer. "Where there is a breach of warranty, express or implied, of the quality of goods delivered in instalments the buyer may elect to accept and receive them as conforming to the contract, or he may receive them and set up the breach of warranty as a defence in whole or in part to the seller's claim for compensation; or he may return or offer to return the goods to the seller in substantially as good condition as they were at the time they were transferred to the buyer; or he may accept or keep the goods and maintain an action against the seller for such breach.'' 10 "The precise question in this case is, whether a purchaser of personal property, sold to him with an express warranty, and taken into possession by him, can rescind the contract and return the property, for breach of the warranty, when there is no fraud, and no express agreement that he may do so. It appears from the cases cited for the plaintiff that in the English courts, and in some of the courts in this country, he cannot; and that his only remedy is on the warranty. See also 2 Steph. N. P. 1296; Addison on 

Con. (2d Amer. ed.) 272; Oliphant's Law of Horses, 88; 

Cripps v. Smith, 3 Irish Law R. 277. But we are of opinion (notwithstanding a dictum of Parsons, C. J. in Kimball v. 

Cunningham, 4 Mass. 505) that, by the law of this commonwealth, as understood and practised upon for more than forty years, there is no such difference between the effect of an implied and an express warranty as deprives a purchaser of any legal right of rescission under the latter, which he has under the former; and that he to whom property is sold with express warranty, as well as he to whom it is sold with an implied warranty, may rescind the contract for breach of warranty, by a seasonable return of the property, and thus entitle himself to a full defence to a suit

§ 542. Buyer Retaining Goods. The buyer who has re ceived goods and retained their benefit cannot avoid payment altogether on the ground that they did not conform to the contract, but should pay their actual value if they did not satisfy the contract.12 So in an action of contract for goods sold and delivered the defense was that the goods were not of the kind ordered, and Shaw, C.J., lays down the rule as follows: 

"Whether, when goods are ordered for a special use, there is an implied warranty on the part of the seller that they are fit for that use, was wholly immaterial, because no such order was stated or relied on; of course, no such warranty could arise. The action is for goods sold and delivered. It is conceded that the defendant received the goods and retained them. The law implies an obligation to pay their value, quantum valebant. If they were ordered for a special purpose, and were not fit for such purpose, the defendant's remedy was to return them or decline receiving them. Such a refusal to accept would enable the party ordering them to recover back the price, if paid; or afford him a good defence to an action for the price. But he may prefer to keep them, and apply them to some other use, or sell them; and if he does, he must pay their actual value, that is, what they were worth at the time and place of delivery, for any purpose.' 13

§ 545. Recovery of Money Paid for Defective Parts. Where the plaintiff has paid money to the defendant for working parts for a machine and the parts are improperly made and the work is delayed, an action for money had and received is not the proper remedy for recovery of damages, as there was no promise, express or implied, to pay any definite sum or one capable of ascertainment by a computation.16 

§ 546. Where Some Goods Sold are Defective. Where the buyer refuses to carry out a contract to purchase tanned skins the measure of damages where title passed is the purchase price less an allowance because some of the leather was below the grade contracted for. As to the residue which the defendant refused to take and which therefore the buyer was excused from preparing for delivery, the measure of damages is the difference between the price agreed upon in the contract and the market price at the date of repudiation of the contract by the defendant.¹7

"The ordinary rule of damages for refusal to perform an executory contract for the future delivery of property when the title, from the nature of the property or the terms of the contract, is not changed until delivery, is the difference between the price agreed to be paid and the value of it, and not the full price of the goods. A party to an executory contract may stop its performance by an explicit order, and will subject himself only to such damages as will compensate the other party for being deprived of its benefits." But where the seller offers the buyer goods not up to the specifications of the contract, this may be shown in mitigation of damages. The plaintiff should not be allowed to recover for unsound and defective lumber, for example, the price of sound lumber.19

In suits to recover the price of personal property sold, it is well settled that a partial want or failure of the consideration, or a breach of the warranty of title or quality, may be shown in defense, in reduction of damages. This rule is adopted to avoid circuity of action. But when the consideration consists of real estate conveyed by deed with covenants of title, the grantee, in the absence of fraud, cannot show, in defense of an action for the consideration, a breach of the covenants of the deed, but he is remitted to his action upon his covenants.20 

§ 548. Defects Set Up in Recoupment or Cross-Action. 

Where the buyer of goods claims damages for defects he may set up these defects both in his answer and in a crossaction, but he cannot have damages assessed in both actions for the same breach of contract. If he desires to recover full damages in the cross-action, he must submit to a verdict in the first suit for the whole amount due under the contract of sale. In an action by the buyer for breach of contract of sale of goods the plaintiff is entitled to recover the difference between the contract price and the market value at the time of the breach even if the plaintiff made no purchase of similar goods then or thereafter.26 § 551. Premature Rescission. So damages for failure to perform a contract of sale and delivery of goods should be assessed as of the date of non-performance and not as they were as of the day of the renunciation of the contract.27 

In an action for breach of a contract to sell and deliver certain metals where the defendant, about a week before the time of performance, notified the plaintiff that he would not carry it out, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market value on the day of performance and not on the date of the notice. The promisee, if he pleases, may treat the notice of intention as inoperative and await the time when the contract is to be executed, and then hold the other party responsible for all the consequences of non-performance.28 

The premature repudiation of a contract before the date of performance does not ordinarily give an immediate right of action, and the damages are to be determined as of a day when there should be performance and not as of the date of the repudiation.29

In an action to recover the price of certain timber sold by the plaintiff to the defendants the answer set up that the timber was delayed in delivery, resulting in loss and increased cost in building a ship with this timber, but the claim was denied. The court remarks: “The ordinary measure of damages for breach of a contract to sell and deliver goods is the value of the goods at the time at which it was agreed that they should be delivered, deducting whatever may not have been paid of the contract price. This is the established rule in this commonwealth. Shaw v. Nudd, 8 Pick. 9. To support any further claim for damages, it must appear that some other element of damage was included in the nature or terms of the contract. Batchelder v. Sturgis, 3 Cush. 204. All the cases upon which the defendants' counsel relies are cases where the particular purpose for which the goods were to be furnished appeared by the contract, and constituted a part of the intention of the parties in making it. But by the exceptions, or the pleadings, in this case, it does not appear that the contract was to deliver the timber at any specific place, or for any specific purpose. It does not even appear that it was agreed to be delivered from vessels, or from wagons. There is nothing to show that any peculiar use to which the defendants might wish to apply it was ever in the contemplation of the plaintiff. The defendants could make such use of the timber when they had it, as they pleased. There is nothing to show that it was expedient for them to build the vessel with it when it was delivered.

§ 557. Partial Delivery. Where the seller of goods did deliver in quantity the goods he contracted to sell, and the buyers accepted them until they cancelled the contract, and there was no acceptance by the buyers with knowledge that the seller would not perform his contract in full, it is manifest that title passed, and the case is not the case of delivery of a smaller quantity of goods than the amount bargained for under G.L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 106, § 33 (1). Therefore the seller may recover the contract price of goods shipped before a certain date and the buyers cannot recover as an element of damage the cost of insuring or storage of their own goods.44

§ 571. Portion of Drove of Pigs Diseased. In a claim on a warranty that a drove of pigs sold were free from disease, the fact that some of the pigs had an infectious disease is evidence of the value of the whole on the question of damages. "If the breach of warranty or fraudulent misrepresentation on which the defendants rely relates to the existence of a contagious or infectious disease in any of the pigs sold, the evidence offered that other pigs in the same drove had the disease, and that the plaintiff knew it, would be competent. It would obviously be admissible to show, upon the question of how much the pigs sold were reasonably worth at the time of the sale, that they came from a drove in which they had been exposed to the disease; as this would affect their market value. And if they were sold in one lot, the value of the whole lot when sold would be the subject of inquiry, and they might be found to be collectively of no value, or of very little value, from their liability to communicate the infection, though some of them may not have died from the disease. "It has been held in a recent English case that, in an action for fraudulently misrepresenting that a cow sold to the plaintiff was free from infectious disease, if the plaintiff placed the cow with others which thereby caught the disease and died, he can recover as damages the value of all the cows.

Mullet v. Mason, Law Rep. 1 C. P. 559. The nature of the subject matter of the warranty or deceit is such, that when animals are sold in one lot together, the warranty or representation as to the whole being single, we can have no doubt that the same principle should apply to the extent of a recoupment; and that the right to recoup in damages should not be confined to the diminished value of those which are proved to have the disease at the time of the sale. In determining the damages caused to the defendants by the breach of warranty or deceit, the defen-

$299 

dants were therefore entitled to have the jury consider in recoupment of damages the whole loss to them occasioned by the presence of the disease among the animals purchased, as well among those which took the infection after the sale as those which had it when the sale was made.'' 60 

§ 572. Fire from Inflammable Goods.61 Where the defen dant sells the plaintiff material of an inflammable character under a warranty that it will be safe to manufacture in the usual way, and it ignites when so manufactured and sets fire to the plaintiff's factory, the usual rule of damages of the difference in value between the goods contracted for and the goods delivered will not apply.

The defendant is liable for whatever damages follow as a natural consequence and the proximate result of his conduct or which may reasonably be supposed to have been within the contemplation of the parties at the time the contract was made as a probable result of the breach of it, and in this case it is a question of fact for the jury whether the fire was a natural result of the breach of warranty. 

The following rule of damages was laid down by Rugg, J.: "When there is no fraud or deceit, the ordinary rule of damages is that the plaintiff is entitled to recover the difference in value between the article which he bargained for and that which he received. Bartlett v. Blanchard, 13 Gray, 429. Wiley v. Athol, 150 Mass. 426. But it may be found that the delivery of an article having different qualities from that ordered, which were not discoverable by inspection, reasonably justified the plaintiff in using it as he would have used the article ordered, and that thereby injury in excess of the value of the property bought ensued as a proximate result, and that such injury ought to have been apprehended by a prudent manufacturer and seller. If this be 

60 Bradley v. Rea, 14 Allen, 20, 23. 

61 See also § 748 et seq.

§§ 573, 574 

found to be so, the vendor may be compelled to indemnify the purchaser against whatever loss might have been anticipated to arise in the ordinary course of events from a failure to supply the goods ordered. For such a breach, whether it be described as of contract to deliver or of implied warranty of merchantability, the rule of damage is the same as that heretofore stated in discussing the principles applicable to a breach of an express warranty, but with the limitations and qualifications there set forth. Whatever may be said as to the weight of evidence in the case now before us, it cannot be ruled as matter of law that it is impossible for a jury to find that a natural consequence or a result, which may be found to have been within the contemplation of the parties as likely to follow from failure to deliver such fiberloid as was ordered, was a fire in the plaintiff's factory. 99 62 

§ 573. Consequential Damages from Using Cement Relying on Warranty. In an action for the price of cement sold where the defense was breach of warranty, it is proper to charge the jury that, if there was a breach of warranty, the defendant was entitled to have deducted the difference in value between what he bought and what he got. If, relying on the warranty, defendant put the cement into his work and suffered loss thereby, then whatever loss was the natural result of using it for that purpose he would be entitled to recoup as damages.

"The loss of prospective profits may be allowed as an element of damages in an action for breach of contract where it appears that the loss was the natural, primary and probable consequence of the breach, that the profits arising from the performance of the contract or the loss likely to result from its non-performance were within the contemplation of the parties, and that the profits are not so uncertain or contingent as to be incapable of reasonable proof.'

In view of this evidence the court holds that the anticipated profits were not too conjectural or contingent, but that the question of the amount might be submitted to the jury where the plaintiff had no increased overhead expense in his business while using the stamps. § 579. Effect of Resale by Purchaser. In an action of contract to recover damages for a breach of warranty of a horse the following rule is laid down by

§ 583. Portion of Boxes Defective. § 595. Value in Fact where No Market Value. In an ac tion of contract on an agreement to exchange certain bonds the trial judge found that the plaintiff's bonds had no market value, and the court, per Wells, J., comments as follows: "From the manner in which this latter conclusion was reached, we cannot regard the finding, 'that said bonds had no market value,' as equivalent to a finding that they had no value in fact.. If it was so intended, we think the judge erred in holding that there was 'no evidence deemed competent to show such a market value anywhere.' A market value, as signifying a price established by public sales, or sales in the way of ordinary business, as of merchandise, is not necessary to the assessment of damages, or the appraisal of property that is the subject of a judicial valuation. 

Property is often the subject of such legal valuation, for which no proof of value in the market could be given, because it is not brought into the course of trade, and is not known in the market, and therefore is incapable of any estimate in that mode. In such cases the real value is to be ascertained from such elements of value as are attainable. 

The promissory note of an individual may have no market value. But proof of the solvency of the maker, or that the note is secured on real estate, in whole or in part, would require that some value, according to the fair estimate of its probable proceeds, should be put upon it. Reverse the present case, and suppose the defendants to have delivered the indorsed bonds according to their contract, and that the plaintiff had withheld the other bonds, can it be maintained that their right to recover anything would depend upon their ability to prove a market value? The competency of 

99 F. W. Stock & Sons v. Snell, 213 Mass. 449.

§§ 596, 597  

the proof offered in this case is the same as it would be in the case supposed. When there is 'a market value,' it shows the price at which either party may have relief from the consequences of the default of the other; and therefore it properly measures his damages. But when there is no such standard, the damages must be estimated from other means of valuation. Without discussing the evidence which related to market value strictly, or evidence of facts occurring long since the breach of the contract, we are satisfied that the testimony of the defendants that the bonds, ($250,- 000 in all,) were secured by a mortgage on the road to trustees; that about forty miles of the road had been graded, and 'was worth about the amount of the bonds,' was competent to prove value in the bonds. Whatever that value was should have been estimated and allowed to the defendants in reduction of the plaintiff's demand." 100

§ 600. Cost of Goods. In an action to recover the price of 

105 Snelling v. Dine, 270 Mass. 501, 506.

The court discusses the problem as follows: 

"It is an elementary principle in the law of damages that, where a contract is broken, the promisee is entitled to be placed in as good position as he would be in had the promisor fulfilled his contract. Garfield & Proctor Coal Co. v. New York, New Haven & Hartford Railroad, 248 Mass. 

502, 507. It was said in John Hetherington & Sons, Ltd. v. William 

Firth Co., 210 Mass. 8, at page 21: "The fundamental principle of law upon which damages for breach of contract are assessed is that the injured party shall be placed in the same position he would have been in, if the contract had been performed, so far as loss can be ascertained to have followed as a natural consequence and to have been within the contemplation of the parties as reasonable men as a probable result of the breach, and so far as compensation therefor in money can be computed by rational methods upon a firm basis of facts.' Having this principle in mind, we consider first the measure of damages applicable to the forty refrigerators that were never completed. "If the defendant had performed his agreement to accept and pay for the refrigerators, the plaintiff would have realized a profit amounting to the difference between the contract price and the cost of the component parts, plus the cost of assembling them into the completed refrigerators. 

Because of the defendant's breach, these refrigerators were not assembled, and the plaintiff never received for them the market price of completed Socold refrigerators. The plaintiff was under no obligation to continue, for the benefit of the defendant, to manufacture the refrigerators, expend money in their assembling, and take the risk attendant on finding a market for them. Besides, the plaintiff could not enhance damages by assembling parts and completing the refrigerators after notice that the defendant refused to receive them. Cumberland Glass Manuf. Co. v. Wheaton, 208

Mass. 425. Roehm v. Horst, 178 U. S. 1. Meyer Brothers Drug Co. v. 

McKinney, 137 App. Div. (N. Y.) 541, affirmed 203 N. Y. 553. The rule stated in Daniels v. Newton, 114 Mass. 530, is not applicable to the facts in the present case. If the difference between the contract price and the market price is taken as the measure of damages, it must be on the assumption that the plaintiff at the time of the breach, or subsequently, had in his possession the goods contracted for and that these goods could be sold in the open market. Garfield & Proctor Coal Co. v. New York, New 

Haven & Hartford Railroad, supra. Williston on Sales (2d ed.) § 582.

To apply the rule of damages as stated by the trial judge in respect to the forty uncompleted refrigerators, is to ignore the fact that they never came into existence and that the plaintiff never received their market value. The application of this rule would not place the plaintiff in the position he would be in had the defendant fully performed his obligations under the contract."

§ 601. Seller's Duty to Minimize Damages.108 In an action to recover damages for failure to accept goods manufactured under a contract, the buyer is chargeable with the contract price less the cost of articles not manufactured, the cash payment made, the amount received from the articles sold and the value of the unused sets. The plaintiff is entitled to recover such damages as were fairly within the contemplation of the parties after the defendants had refused to accept and pay for the sets manufactured. The plaintiff was entitled to sell them for the best price obtainable and credit the proceeds to the defendant. It was his duty to exercise reasonable diligence to minimize damages, and he can recover only for the direct consequences of the breach of contract and not for damages that could have been avoided by the exercise of reasonable precautions on his part.100

In an action by a seller for failure to carry out a contract to purchase goods, the correct rule for damages is the difference between the contract price and the fair market price at the time and place agreed upon for performance, and the seller is not limited to the difference between the contract price and what the seller later sold it for.116

Where the buyer of goods repudiates the contract the measure of damages is the difference between the market price of the goods at the time and place of delivery and the contract price. Here, however, the plaintiff introduced no evidence of this, relying on his claim that the measure of damages was the contract price, and therefore the only thing the court could do was to award nominal damages.118 

§ 604. Refusal to Repurchase Stock. Where the defendant agrees that he will after a year buy back stock he sells the plaintiff and refuses to carry out his agreement, the measure of damages is the amount the plaintiff paid for the stock with interest as agreed upon. 119 § 605. Exchange. In an action for breach of an agreement to exchange property the measure of damages is the difference between the market value of the plaintiff's property and the amount which he would have received for it if the defendant had carried out his bargain.120

118 Tufts v. Bennett, 163 Mass. 398. 

119 Thorndike v. Locke, 98 Mass. 340. 

120 Brigham v. Evans, 113 Mass. 538.

 § 606. Instalment Contract. Where the defendants con tracted to take books in instalments and repudiated the contract on delivery of the first instalment of books, this is a repudiation of the entire contract, and the plaintiff could not insist on proceeding under it by tendering later instalments and compel them to pay the contract price for goods sold and delivered. The measure of recovery is the difference between the market price and the contract price at the place of delivery.121

Under a contract for sale of iron to be delivered in instalments, which the buyer repudiates, the contract was entire, even if payments were to be made by instalments, and, as no part of the purchase had ever been delivered, the measure of damages was the difference between the market price of the entire amount at the time of repudiation and the price at which the iron had been sold.¹ 122 Where the defendant gives notice that it will not carry out a contract to purchase goods at intervals during a stated period, the seller has a right of action from that date for breach, and the measure of its damages must be determined from that date. So when the goods could have been sold on that date without loss, only nominal damages can be awarded to the seller. 123

1. RECOVERY FOR SERVICES RENDERED. 

§ 607. Fair Value of Services. In an action on a quantum meruit for services in taking care of the testator, the question is what the services were worth and not what the plaintiffs expected to receive.¹ So in an action of quantum meruit for services rendered another upon his express request, the value of the services is not to be determined by the amount of benefit which the party requesting them receives, but rather is the compensation determined by the value of the services.2

However, in an action to enforce a mechanic's lien, it is error to allow as damages the fair value of the work and 

1 Chandler v. Baker, 191 Mass. 579. 

2 Stowe v. Buttrick, 125 Mass. 449.

$$ 608 321 

AGENCY 

materials even though it should exceed the contract price less the work not done, but he can recover under the statute only "reasonable compensation for as much as he has performed, in proportion to the price stipulated for the whole. '' 3 

§ 608. Deduction of Damages for Breach of Contract. 

Where the plaintiff contracted to keep certain roads in good repair the defendant may put in evidence the amount he necessarily expended to keep the roads up as tending to prove that the contract had not been substantially performed, and also to show the extent of the damage caused by the non-performance. So in a petition to enforce a mechanic's lien for work on a house built under a contract, the lien may be enforced for what the labor was reasonably worth, not exceeding the entire price agreed upon in the contract, after deducting from that price any damages suffered by the respondent from the non-completion of the contract.5 

§ 609. Set-Off of Liability Imposed by Plaintiff's Neglect. 

In an action to recover for work done on a contract with the town for digging trenches where the plaintiff under his contract was bound to guard the trenches and failed to do so and the town was held liable for a defect in the highway, the damages which the town had to pay in this action should be set off by way of defense to the contract declared on, to prevent circuity of action." 

§ 610. Recovery where Contract Abrogated on Account of 

Mistake. Where a contract for sewers is set aside on account of mutual mistake of the parties, the plaintiff may

§ 611. Agreement on Value of Services Not Binding. The jury is not bound by an agreement of parties as to the value of plaintiffs' services as architects, but in an action of contract for these services it may bring in a verdict for one-half of the sum agreed upon. 8

On the value of a doctor's services, it seems that the financial standing and ability of the patient should be considered where it is a common practice to charge wealthy patients more than poor people, as this would seem to determine the market value of the service to a wealthy person."

4. INTERFERENCE WITH EMPLOYMENT. 

§ 633. Loss of Advantages. In an action for unlawful interference with a contract the damages are limited to the loss of advantages, either of property or of personal benefit, which, but for such interference, the plaintiff would have been able to attain or enjoy. The damages must be limited to the actual value of the contract viewed in the light of the attendant circumstances of which the jury could find that the defendants had knowledge. It is what the plaintiff would have received if he had not been deprived of its performance through the acts of the defendants, and the evidence introduced relating to events occurring after that date and to some extent tending to show that even if the contract had remained in force he could have derived no benefit therefrom is properly admitted.45 In an action of tort for inducing a breach of contract the damages are the loss of advantages, either of property or of personal benefit, which but for such interference the plaintiff would be able to attain or enjoy. The plaintiff cannot recover speculative or conjectural profits or losses of any description. The measure of recovery is limited to what the plaintiff would have received if he had not been deprived of the performance of the contract through the acts of the defendant.46

Mental Suffering and Other Losses.48 For wilful interference with the plaintiff's contract of employment he is entitled to recover for his mental distress and anxiety.49 

In an action for wrongful interference by the defendant with a contract of employment of the plaintiff, evidence as to the plaintiff's mental suffering was admissible on the measure of damages, which were the natural and necessary result of the discharge from the employment.50 

In an action for loss of employment where the defendant without justification served on the plaintiff's employer a mistaken notice of assignment of wages, the plaintiff's damages may include his loss of employment, loss of wages and his inability to obtain other work, although he was employed by the piece and could be discharged at any time.

§ 636. Forcing Plaintiff to Pay Bill. Loss of Wages. In a suit alleging that the defendants have conspired to interfere with the plaintiff's contract of employment and that they coerced him to pay a bill which he had denied was due, he can recover as damages the sum paid by an action of contract. The measure of damages is not based upon the breach of contract, but upon the direct and proximate results of the wrongful act of the defendants. Here the payment of the insurance claim was the very object which the defendants are endeavoring to accomplish, and the loss of employment was the natural consequence of their efforts to compel the plaintiff to pay, and therefore the payment of the claim and the loss of wages were the direct results of the defendants' wrongdoing." 53 

5. ATTORNEYS. 

§ 637. Compensation. In an action by an attorney for compensation the only standard is the fair and reasonable compensation regardless of what is paid by the State for similar work. This standard applies to work done by an assistant although what the plaintiff paid him was more or less than what was reasonable. The court remarks: "As to the fifth and sixth requests, the court instructed the jury that, in the absence of any agreement as to the price or value of the plaintiffs' services, they were entitled only to a fair and reasonable compensation. It could not have gone further. It could not set up the salaries paid by the State as a standard or a limit. Free competition prevails at the bar as well as elsewhere, and different men command different rates of compensation,-some of them

§ 638. Breach of Contract to Employ Title Examiner. 

Where an attorney is employed by a co-operative bank to examine titles for a year and he is to be paid by the borrowers, the bank is not entitled to all his time and he is more in the position of a subcontractor than an employee. 

Evidence was admitted as to what money was paid to another attorney who did this work after the plaintiff's wrongful discharge, and a verdict returned for the plaintiff on that basis. An instruction that the plaintiff is entitled to have assessed as damages the loss to him by the failure on the part of the bank to give him such work as might be reasonably expected by him during the year is sustained.55 

§ 639. Negligence of Attorney Resulting in Loss of Prop erty.56 Where an attorney negligently brought an action which placed the title to an engine in a third party, the measure of damages was the market value of the engine at the time of bringing the action.57

§ 643. Broker's Rights on Buying Stock for Customer. 

Where stockbrokers bought stock for the defendant they could hold it for his account and recover from the customer the full cost, or they could sell the stock within a reasonable time after his failure to pay for it and recover from him the difference between the purchase price and the sale price.  § 644. Broker Repudiating Contract to Carry Stock. 

Where the plaintiff claims that the broker repudiated a contract to carry stock, the repudiator can be liable only for the actual loss at the time of the breach, but damages are not determined by the value of the stock when it was ordered to be sold.62 

§ 645. Customer's Failure to Pay for Stock. Where a broker obeys an order to buy stock for a customer and pays for it and the customer then refuses to pay for it, the measure of damages is what the broker paid for the stock and not merely the difference between the price paid for it and its market value on the day of the broker's demand. 

Here the plaintiff bought the stock as agent for the customer and had no order to sell it.63 

§ 646. Failure to Deliver Stock. Where an order is given to deliver a certain amount of stock and the order is accepted and states no time for performance, "The true measure of damages was the value of the stock at the time when, under the contract, it should have been delivered. 

No time being specified in the order for the delivery, the time when the demand was made must be the point at which the value is to be fixed." 64

§ 650. Stockbroker Selling to Irresponsible Person. Where a stockbroker sold shares of stock for the customer's account and risk to an apparently responsible purchaser, but failed to make a valid and enforceable contract with him, and the purchaser became financially irresponsible before the time came for delivery of the stock sold, the stockbrokers are liable for the damages caused by their failure to make the contract of sale a valid and enforceable one. 

The measure of damages, however, is not the whole loss caused by the depreciation of the stock, but the amount which the plaintiffs could have collected by way of dividend or otherwise from the purchasers, who had become financially irresponsible. 69 

§ 651. Sale by Factor against Orders. Where the plain tiff delivered goods to a factor with orders not to sell it at less than forty cents a pound and the factor sold it for less and refused the plaintiff's demand to return it, the damages will include the loss sustained by the failure to obey orders, or the market value when the return was demanded. "We do not find it necessary to decide what rule of damages is absolutely correct. It has sometimes been said that the highest market price before action brought is the standard; at others that the highest value before the trial may be awarded. It is safe to say that the factor is at least liable for the highest market value of the goods within a reasonable time after a sale in violation of in-

And in the present case there can be no doubt that the time when the plaintiff demanded the return of the goods was soon enough after the defendants' disobedience of instructions to make the highest market price previous to that date a limit sufficiently favorable to the defendants." 70 

§ 652. Failure of Foreign Factor to Transmit Funds. 

Where a factor in a foreign country breaks his agreement to receive goods and sell them and transmit the proceeds, the measure of damages is stated as follows by Bigelow, C.J.: "The question then arises as to the measure of damages. 

It is to be borne in mind that this is not a suit on a debt for a sum of money, but is an action brought to recover damages for the breach of duty and of contract by the defendants as agents towards the plaintiffs as principals. The question is, not what sum shall the plaintiffs recover for a sum of money due and owing as a debt by the defendants, but what sum will indemnify the former for the neglect and omission of the latter to regard their instructions and fulfil their duty under a contract of agency. The general rule on this point is perfectly well settled. The agent is bound to make full indemnity to his principal for all loss or injury caused by his neglect, misconduct or other violation of duty. Story on Agency, §§ 217-220. Suydam v. Jenkins, 

3 Sandf. 614. According to this rule, for the refusal of the defendants to surrender to the plaintiffs' agent the money, notes, goods and evidences of debt, on demand duly made therefor in Surinam, the plaintiffs have a right to recover a full indemnity. They had a right to demand and receive them then and there; and for the failure of the defendants to fulfil their duty they are entitled to such 

70 Maynard v. Pease, 99 Mass. 555, 556. As to highest intermediate value rule cf. ante, §§ 344, 484.

§§ 653, 654 

sum as will put them in the same situation as they would have been in if the property had been then given up and received by them at Surinam. Clearly such indemnity would not be had, if the plaintiffs could recover only such sum in the currency of this country as is nominally equivalent to the sum which they would have been entitled to recover in the currency of Surinam. It would fall just so far short of full compensation for the injury sustained as that sum in the current money of the United States is worth less than the same sum estimated in the currency of Surinam. The only just rule is, that in such cases the party who has suffered a loss or injury through the fault of another shall be allowed such sum in the currency of the place where a suit is brought as most nearly approximates to that which he would be entitled to recover in the country where the injury or loss happened and the damage was sustained. The cases in which actions have been brought on a contract to pay a certain sum of money in a foreign country depend on different principles and are not applicable to transactions like that out of which the present action has arisen.'' 71

§ 658. Liability for Escape. In an action against an officer for an escape by a debtor the rule of damages is such damage as the plaintiff has suffered by the escape as should appear on all the evidence. It is not the rule that the plaintiff is entitled to recover the whole amount of his execution, unless the defendant proved the debtor's inability to pay the same.79 In an action against an officer for suffering the escape of an arrested debtor the measure of damages is the loss sustained rather than the amount of the debt. On this issue the defendant may show that the debtor had no funds and was unable to pay the debt.80

§ 659. Agent's Commission on Orders Not Accepted. The plaintiff was an agent on commission to sell the defendants' goods by samples which the defendants were to send on order and the plaintiff was to receive a commission on all goods so sold if the orders were not rejected. The court holds that the defendants are not liable for orders which were not accepted, as they had a right to reject all orders, and whether such orders for goods would have been obtained if the samples had been sent and, if so, to what amount is too much a matter of conjecture to afford a basis for more than nominal damages." 81 § 660. AGENCY § 661. Agent's Breach of Contract. Where a manufacturer agrees to make a certain guaranteed amount of its product daily, which the selling agent agrees to sell at a certain guaranteed profit, and the selling agent breaks its contract, the loss of prospective guaranteed profits is plainly within the contemplation of the parties as the probable result of a breach, and was the natural and probable consequence of the breach and was susceptible of reasonably certain and satisfactory proof.83 Where a selling agent for a manufacturer wrongfully breaks his contract of employment, recovery for loss of profits may be denied where too speculative, but substantial damages may be awarded for the expense incurred by the manufacturer in setting up another agency to market its products and in regaining the position acquired by it under its contract. This is the direct result of the defendant's breach of the contract and no doubt is capable of approximately accurate proof.84

The assessment of any damages for breach of an agency contract may be improper if the damages are too speculative in view of the newness of the venture, its dependence upon the temperament, energy and perseverance of the defendant, the absence of any evidence as to prospective customers and the inability of the manufacturer to fill orders promptly.85

§ 666. Agreement to Indemnify for Loss in Stock. Where the defendants agreed to indemnify the plaintiff for all loss at the end of three years that he might sustain by reason of the purchase of certain stock, damages should be assessed at the difference between the price paid, with interest, and the market value of the stock at the end of the three years. A sale of the stock at the end of the three years, fairly conducted, might have furnished a convenient measure of its value at that time, but was not required. 

If, since the expiration of the agreed time, the stock has risen in value, the defendant may perhaps be entitled to the benefit of such rise, but where there was no such rise and the stock is now worthless, the damages should be assessed at the price paid, with interest.8 § 667. § 684. Evicting Diseased Passenger.¹ In an action for evicting a passenger from a steamer on the ground that she suffered from a dangerous disease, evidence is compe-

tent that the plaintiff was left by the eviction at a long distance from her friends and that she sailed on another liner the next day after her eviction.2 

§ 685. Failure to Furnish Drawing-Room. Where the plaintiff has a ticket for a drawing-room in a Pullman car for an overnight journey and it appears that there is no drawing-room on that train, whereupon the plaintiff makes the journey sitting up all night in an ordinary passenger coach although suffering from heart trouble and is made ill, he can recover only nominal damages where it appears that he was offered equal accommodations in another train leaving three hours later. Here the injury to the plaintiff's health was not the direct and proximate result of the breach by the defendant of its contract, but there was an intervening cause, the plaintiff's refusal to accept the accommodations tendered to him and sitting up all night. He should do what he reasonably could, taking all the circumstances into account, to lessen the injury and not to aggravate it.3 

§ 686. Notice that Passenger Sensitive. Damages to a passenger on a public conveyance cannot be increased by the fact that the conductor has notice that the passenger was a particularly sensitive person.* § 687. Loss of Money in Luggage. A carrier of passengers is not liable for loss of money contained in his luggage beyond travelling expenses of which the carrier had no notice. The rule is well expounded by Bigelow, C.J., as follows: "In regard to carriers of passengers, there can be no doubt that persons who enter into contracts with them to transport themselves and their luggage, nothing being said 

2 Mountford v. Cunard Steamship Co., Ltd., 202 Mass. 345.

as to the contents of the parcels which are delivered for carriage, and these being in the form of trunks or valises such as are commonly used for clothing and other personal effects, represent by implication to the carriers that they contain no articles or property not properly included within this class or description, and such as a traveller may carry with him as part of his luggage, and for which he can hold the carrier responsible under his contract. If other and different articles of greater value are contained in such trunks or valises, it is a disguise of their true nature and value, and operates as an unfair and fraudulent concealment of them which absolves the carriers from liability therefor in case of loss. Nor is this all. In such a case, the owner can prove no contract for the transportation of any articles other than wearing apparel and other ordinary personal effects and an amount of money reasonably sufficient for the payment of travelling expenses. What is the contract into which the carrier enters when he receives a passenger? 

It is only to transport him safely, together with such articles and money as are properly contained in the luggage which he brings with him; but he does not contract to transport anything which he may bring with him in the shape of luggage, when in fact it is not properly such, but merchandise or money which he cannot ask the carrier to receive in that form. Therefore it is that he cannot be held liable at all, not even for gross negligence, for the loss of any articles not embraced within the contract. He did not agree to receive or transport money beyond a certain amount, or merchandise of any kind; and he cannot be held liable for any, even the smallest degree of care of that which he did not agree to take into his possession and keeping. 

And that is the exact difference between the class of cases where a carrier has by special contract given notice that he will not be responsible for loss of property beyond a certain amount, and those cases where a concealment or deceit as to the nature and value of the property has been

$ 688 

practised on the carrier. As to the former, it has been held that the effect of such a notice is only to exempt the carrier from his extreme liability for property intrusted to him, but that he is still liable for a certain degree of care for property which he receives into his custody and undertakes to transport, although of greater value than that named in the notice which he has made public. But in the latter class of cases there is present the element of fraud or deceit, by reason of which the carrier has not entered into any contract for the care of property the knowledge of which has been concealed from him by the owner." 995 

2. FREIGHT. 

§ 688. Market Value at Time and Place of Delivery. In an action of contract against a carrier for loss of coal, the damages are to be computed at the time and place of delivery and not at the time and place of shipment. So when a carrier receives goods for transportation, and fails to deliver them, the owner is entitled to recover the market value of the goods at the time and place at which they should have been delivered. And where the carrier negligently delays the delivery of goods, he is liable for loss in their market value during the delay. A larger liability can be imposed upon him only when it is in the contemplation of the parties that the carrier is to respond, in case of breach, for special and exceptional damages. In such a case the extent and character of the obligation he assumes should be known to the carrier, and the mere knowledge on the part of the carrier that the shipper intended to sell the freight to be transported cannot impose a liability upon the carrier for loss of profits on such contracts.

"In an action against a carrier to whom goods have been intrusted, for not delivering them according to contract, the measure of damages is the value of the goods at the place of delivery and at the time when they should have been delivered; with interest from that time. "The defendants contend that the rule should be the prime cost of the goods and interest. § 691. Loss of Building Plans. When a carrier loses plans for the plaintiff's new house it is liable in damages for the reasonable cost of the new plans and for other expenses in procuring the new plans, but is not liable for the delay in constructing the house caused by the loss of the plans. 

The plans had no market value and were useful only to the plaintiff, and therefore the rule of damages is their value to the plaintiff. Here the defendant had no notice of the contents of the package or that the plaintiff needed the plans for the construction of a house which he planned to build. The damages caused by the delay are not such as usually and naturally arise solely from a breach of the contract to carry the package safely, nor were they within the reasonable contemplation of both parties to this contract as likely to arise from such a breach.13 § 692. The fact that a railroad delays transportation of goods so they are damaged by flood and if the goods had been carried seasonably they would have been delivered before the flood does not create liability. It is an ancient rule that the wrongdoer shall be liable only for the proximate and not for the remote consequences of his actions, and here the negligence of the defendant was remote and the flood was the proximate cause of the damage.28 

§ 699. Loss in Market Value during Delay. "The ordinary measure of damages, in an action against a common carrier, for a failure to deliver in time goods intrusted to him for carriage, is the difference between the market value at the time when and place where they ought to have been delivered, and their market value at that place on the day when they were in fact delivered." The rule is no different where the consignee had sold the goods "to arrive" where the carrier on receiving the goods had no notice of these sales and the profits to be made by these sales could not have been in the contemplation of the parties to the contract of transportation as an element of damage. Here the plaintiff can always protect himself from loss, where the property has an established market value, by supplying the commodity from other sources at the market price.24 "The true rule and measure of damages, in our opinion, whenever by reason of inexcusable delay of the carrier the goods are not delivered until after they have diminished in market value, is the amount of the diminution. This allows to the person injured the value, as exactly as it can be estimated in money, of that of which he has been finally deprived by the wrongful act of the defendant; and is the most simple 

22 Weston v. Boston & Maine Railroad, 190 Mass. 298. 

23 Denny v. New York Central Railroad Co., 13 Gray, 481. 

24 Scott v. Boston & New Orleans Steamship Co., 106 Mass. 468.

$700 

and just rule, as well as the easiest to be applied; for it depends on the general market value of the goods, and involves no question of contingent or speculative profits, and no consideration of any other contracts made or omitted to be made by the plaintiff in view of his contract with the defendant. To refer to such other contracts, or the profits which might have resulted from them, not within the knowledge or contemplation of the defendant, would be to hold him liable for the consequences, or allow him the benefit, not of his own contract with the plaintiff, but of dealings between the latter and third persons, with which the defendant had nothing to do.", 25 "The rule of damages was accurately stated. If, as we understand from the exceptions, the defendants received the cattle knowing that they were designed to reach New York in season for a particular market day, the loss sustained by wrongful delay in transportation is the difference in market value between the time when they ought to have arrived and when they actually did arrive at the terminus of the road. Whether without such knowledge, in a case of unreasonable detention or delay, the rule would not be the same, we need not now decide.'' 26

Where a carrier failed to deliver goods at the date agreed upon and the consignee then cancelled the order and the carrier then unreasonably delayed to return the goods and in the meantime there had been a diminution in their value, such diminution in value was the correct measure of damages and was not special damages of a peculiar or unusual nature not to be anticipated by a carrier.27

The court reasons as follows: 

"The proposition stated by the counsel for the plaintiff, that a common carrier is liable for all the damages which are the consequences of his negligence, is a sound proposition, rightly understood. He is liable for all damages which the law sees to be the consequences. But the law looks to and regards the proximate, and not the remote consequences the direct proximate consequence of the negligence, and not remote results that may be traced to it by a chain of causes, however sound may be each successive link. 

It may not always be easy to draw the line, and say what is proximate and what remote; but this renders it none the less obligatory to adhere to it when it can be discerned. In cases of this kind, the rule of damages seems to be the diminution in value of the goods, as articles of merchandise, at the time of their arrival, by reason of the delay. What were the goods worth the less, at the time of their arrival, than they would have been if they had come without delay, or in the usual course of transportation? The difference, in some cases, may be very slight, scarcely appreciable; in others, as the case of fruit or other perishable articles on their way to market, it may cover the entire value; and this

§ 701. Closing Factory Due to Delay. Where the plain tiff orders new special boilers for its plant sent by railroad and through the negligence of the railroad delivery is delayed eight days, damages cannot include the loss caused by closing the plaintiff's plant to install them during that period, and other losses from the delay, where there was no evidence that the carrier had notice of the use to which the boilers would be put or that the plaintiff's plant would be shut down for the purpose of making the change in boilers. 

Such damages were not within the contemplation of the parties and were not the proximate result of the delay. 

However, cash items of expense in looking for the boilers and sending a team to get them are recoverable.30 

§ 702. Theatrical Scenery Delayed. Where a railroad de layed in transporting scenery and other theatrical property used by the plaintiff in his show business, the damages may include ordinary damage from a delay in the transportation of that kind of freight. To get those ordinary damages notice that the freight to be transported is that kind of freight and that it is to be used at its destination must be given to the carrier, and the damages recoverable are the ordinary earnings of the property in question. The plaintiff can recover, not the ordinary net earnings, but the ordinary gross earnings less such expenses, if any, as the deprivation of the use of the property saved him from.³¹

§ 706. Shipper's Liability for Failure to Keep Contract with Carrier. Where the defendant agreed to ship certain freight on a certain voyage of a certain ship and failed to do so, the measure of damages is full indemnity for all the carrier has lost through the default of the shippers. "It seems therefore proper that all the attendant circumstances be brought before the jury in each particular case, to enable them to estimate the proper sum to be awarded as damages for a breach of contract of this nature. The carrier is to receive full indemnity for the breach of contract on the part of the shipper. He is to be made as good, in a pecuniary point of view, as if the shipper had furnished the goods according to his contract, if the carrier has been guilty of no laches as to substituting other freight, or adopting other available arrangements to mitigate the loss, or avoid the expenditure incident to the proposed voyage. But if by proper and reasonable efforts he can substitute other goods, he is bound to do so, and, to the extent of the freight thus received, this should go in reduction of the damages. Nor is the reduction necessarily confined to his receipts from goods actually substituted. 

The carrier may have been remiss in his attempts to fill up his ship, or have neglected to avail himself of opportunities presented by other offers of goods, and if guilty of negligence in these respects, this may be a ground for a deduc-

1. TRESPASS. 

§ 713. The Rule Stated.' The assessment of damages for a trespass on real property must depend in large measure on the circumstances of each case, as appears by the decisions noted in this subdivision. In a simple case the cost of repairs may be the proper measure, and where the owner has lost substantial rights to use the property, his loss of use and even his loss of profits from use might be considered, but where the cost of restoration is excessive, the rule of damage to the property as a whole will govern. 

§ 714. Plaintiff's Title Qualified. In an action of trespass the defendants may show, to limit the damages, that the plaintiff's right in the property was only a qualified right.2 

§ 715. Recovery for Trespass by Life Tenant. A life tenant with a power may recover full damages for trespass to the property, and the court does not decide whether the remainderman may intervene for his protection.³ 

§ 716. Mortgagee's Recovery for Fixtures Removed. A 

mortgagee can recover full damages for the value of fixtures removed by the defendant from the mortgaged premises, and his right to recover does not depend upon the sufficiency or insufficiency of his security. Until his whole debt is paid he cannot be deprived of any substantial part of his entire security without full redress therefor.*

§ 717. Rights of Owner against Wrongful Foreclosure. In a bill in equity by the owner to have a foreclosure of a second mortgage set aside where the property has been sold to a bona-fide purchaser, the court may award as damages the fair market value of the property subject to the first mortgage, although it was sold for more than this amount." 

Where the defendant has a mortgage as trustee to protect the interest of the plaintiff, the owner, and wrongfully permits a prior mortgage to be foreclosed, the defendant may be assessed with damages the amount of the loss of the plaintiff's equity in the property less what the plaintiff owed the defendant." § 718. Injunction against Trespass. In a bill in equity to enjoin trespasses the plaintiff may be entitled to recover damages for trespasses already committed, and a permanent injunction against future trespasses. In a petition in equity to remove trespassing structures and assess damages, the damages should be assessed only on the theory of a temporary trespass where the buildings are ordered removed.⁹

3. NEGLIGENT INJURY. 

§ 740. Time as of which Damages Assessed. Damage to property may be fixed at its loss of value at the time of the injury.40 

§ 741. Defective Wall. A subcontractor is liable in tort where he negligently builds a cellar wall on the plaintiff's property which falls. The right of action is not for breach of a contract, but is for an injury to the plaintiff's property resulting from the neglect of the defendant properly to perform acts which he had undertaken to perform upon the property of the plaintiff. The measure of damages is the cost of restoring the wall.41 § 742. Causing Wall to Settle. Damage for causing a wall to settle may be the difference in the fair market value before and after injury rather than the cost of restoration.42 § 743. Loss of Support. At common law every landowner has a right of support for his land from the abutting owner, but this right does not apply to buildings, as it is presumed that he should not place his buildings too near the line, and such claim would limit the right of adjoining owners to use land; and therefore no damages can be awarded for damage to buildings caused by taking away the support from the adjoining land.43 Therefore, where an adjoining owner excavates near the boundary, causing the plaintiff's land and building to slip, the damages are confined to injury to the

§ 750. Statute Not Retroactive. In an action of tort for damage from a fire set by a locomotive the measure of damages is the fair value of the property upon the day of the fire, and a statute enacted later will not be construed to act retrospectively.59 

§ 751. Building Destroyed to Stop Spread of Fire. In an action of tort to recover damages for the destruction of the plaintiff's dwelling which was destroyed illegally to stop a large fire, the court lays down the rule of damages as follows: "But we are of opinion that the rule of damages was erroneously stated, and that upon this point the exceptions must be sustained. The jury were instructed that the fact that the house and furniture in it were in imminent peril of destruction by fire would not diminish the damages to which the plaintiff was entitled. This instruction was afterward qualified in its application to the building, by stating that if it was so far on fire at the time it was blown up as to make its destruction inevitable, it might be considered as already destroyed, and the defendants would not be answerable; and that if it was partially burned, but not to such an extent, the amount of injury which it had received should be deducted from its value. But it was still held that unless the house or furniture was actually on fire at the time nothing was to be deducted from their full value on account of any peril to which they were exposed. This ruling would include the case of a building or furniture so surrounded by fire as to make their preservation, or even access to them for more than a moment, impossible, while they were yet not actually burning. The defendants asked that the jury should be instructed that they were 'liable for the destruction of such personal property of the plaintiff, if any, as might have been saved if they had not interfered, and for no more.' This was in substance the true rule. As the de-

§ 752. Effect of Insurance. In an action for damages for burning the plaintiff's building damages are not affected by the fact that the plaintiff has recovered insurance for the loss.61 But in an action against a railroad company for damages from fire started by one of its engines, although by statute the damages are to be reduced by the insurance received, the damages sustained are not determined by the amount of insurance or the sum received. The railroad company is not bound by the award of the referees in insurance as to the amount of the plaintiff's damages or the value of the property destroyed.62

§ 754. Flooding. Whether Damage Permanent or Tempo rary. In an action for flooding the plaintiff's land, damages should be measured by the depreciation in the market value of the property injured if the injury caused by the nuisance was of a permanent nature, or by the difference in the rental value of the premises before and after the injury if the nuisance was of an occasional or temporary character. But there is no warrant in assessing in addition loss of profits from year to year due to inability to use the land. In an action of tort to recover damages caused by the negligent overflowing of land it is error to permit the plaintiff to testify as to the difference between the value of the land before the opening of the drain into the brook and its value thereafter, as such testimony is based on the theory that the wrong done to the plaintiff was permanent. It is not to be assumed that the defendant will continue its tortious acts.66 

Where land was damaged through the backing up of water on it on account of an insufficient culvert and the cause is not permanent but is one that can be remedied at the option of the defendant, then damages should not be awarded once and for all time upon the theory that the injury to the land is permanent, but should be limited to the actual injury sustained to the date of the writ, and the diminution in the value of the use of the land is the correct measure of damages where there is no evidence that the land had been permanently damaged or that the owners had incurred expense in repairing actual injury to their properties.67

"The measure of the damages recoverable where real estate is flooded differs with circumstances. Wrongfully Closing Sewer. Where a city wrongfully closes a sewer and builds a new one, it is error to rule that the owners can recover as damage only the expense of connecting with the new sewer. "If the plaintiffs were entitled to recover at all, they were entitled to recover all the damages to their estate that were the natural and proximate results of the act complained of, and such as reasonably might be supposed to have been within the contemplation of the parties, if, at the time of the doing of the act, they had taken thought of the consequences likely to ensue.

 7. COVENANT OF TITLE. 

§ 776. Recovery of Consideration Paid. In an action on a covenant of seisin the grantee may hold the grantor to the extent of what the grantor actually received, and otherwise his liability is the actual value of the land at the time of the conveyance.109 The general rule is well settled that the measure of damages for breach of a covenant of seisin is the consideration paid or price agreed upon for the conveyance. The actual consideration may be proved for this purpose by parol evidence, even in contradiction to the recital thereof in the deed itself. It does not modify the rule if the actual consideration is paid in other commodities than money or even in other real estate, or if the consideration is in fact paid or delivered to another person than the grantor or if it is itself, before delivery, the property of another than the grantee; provided it is agreed upon between the grantor and the grantee as the consideration upon which the deed is given.110

The usual rule for damages for a breach of a covenant of seisin and good title is "the amount of the consideration actually paid by the grantee to the grantor, with interest from the time of the payment." But there may be anomalous cases, as where, in a negotiation between two, there is a stipulation by one with the other to execute a deed to a third person, in which case the value of the land title to which fails will be the measure of damages. 

The rule was set forth by Shaw, C.J., as follows: "The case is very similar in principle, and considerably so in its facts, to that of Smith v. Strong, 14 Pick. 128. It was there laid down that, in such case, the measure of damages is the consideration paid, with interest from the date of the deed; but if the consideration cannot be ascertained, the value of the land, at the time of the intended 

109 Staples v. Dean, 114 Mass. 125. 

110 Hodges v. Thayer, 110 Mass. 286.

$401 

REAL PROPERTY 

conveyance, with interest from the date of the deed, will be the measure of damages. "It appears to us, that this rule will afford indemnity in the present case. If the failure of title extended to the whole of the land, then the entire value of the land is to be the measure; if to a part only, and the plaintiff does not tender a reconveyance, of the part upon which the conveyance operated to give title to the grantee, then the value of the part, the title to which failed, with interest, will be taken as the measure of damages."' 111

In an action by the assignee of a claim against the United States against his assignor, which claim the plaintiff could not collect, on account of a prior authority given by the assignor, the rule of damages is set forth by Bigelow, J., as follows: 

"In regard to the extent of the defendants' liability, it seems to us that the breach of the contract is analogous to that of a covenant of good right to sell and convey land, where the measure of damage is the price paid. There being no fraud on the part of the defendants, the amount paid by the plaintiff, with interest, is the true measure of the defendants' liability. The evidence tends to show that the value of the claim at the time of its purchase by the plaintiff was less than par. He ought not therefore to recover the full amount of the certificate, but only the consideration paid by him therefor. It having been a sale, the vendee taking all risks, except the wrongful act of the assignors in defeating the collection of the claim, this seems to be an equitable rule of damages, which does exact justice between the parties. 112

REAL PROPERTY 8. COVENANT AGAINST INCUMBRANCES. 

§ 779. Damages Assessed as of Date of Deed. A covenant against incumbrances is broken when made and the damages must be assessed as of that time without regard to the later rise or fall in the value of the property, and interest from the date of the deed to the verdict should be added 116 § 780. Rule of Just Compensation. In an action for breach of a covenant against incumbrances the true rule of damages is "a just compensation to the plaintiff for the real injury resulting from the incumbrance." This rule may be stated as being "the real injury resulting to the estate in its market value from the incumbrance.' § 781. Eviction or Extinguishment Prerequisite to Damages. The general rule of damages for breach of a covenant against incumbrances is that, "if the covenantee has extinguished the incumbrance, he may recover the reasonable expenses incurred in doing so; if he lies by without doing so, and has not been disturbed in the enjoyment of the estate conveyed, he can recover only nominal damages. If he cannot remove the incumbrance, the measure of damages is a just compensation for the direct injury resulting from it." Where the plaintiff had sold the property at auction and the purchaser refused to complete the purchase on discovering the incumbrance, the court did not allow the assessment of damages for the fees of the auctioneer at the sale, on the ground that this was not "the immediate consequence of the breach of the covenant. It is too remote and indirect to be an element of damages." In this case the plaintiff has not been disturbed in the enjoyment of the estate and has not paid anything to extinguish the 

116 Bailey v. Agawam National Bank, 190 Mass. 20. 

117 Wetherbee v. Bennett, 2 Allen, 428.

$ 782 

incumbrance, and therefore cannot recover the auctioneer's fee.118 66 § 782. Expense of Extinguishment. In an action on a covenant against incumbrances, if the incumbrance has been removed the damages are the fair and reasonable amount expended in good faith in removing them.119 In an action to recover damages for a breach of the covenant in a deed against incumbrances, where the incumbrance is one which can be removed by the grantee, he may recover the amount fairly and justly paid by him for the removal of such incumbrance, not exceeding the value of the estate, although he pays it after the action is commenced.'' 120 

In an action for breach of a covenant against incumbrances in a deed, on the question of damages, if it was reasonable for the plaintiff to buy off the incumbrance and if the sum paid was reasonable, the plaintiff can recover such reasonable sum in the present suit with interest from the time of payment. If it was a question reasonably doubtful whether the third parties were right in their claims, the present plaintiff had the right to defend those suits and it may be that he had the right to ask the present defendant to defend them and that any expenses reasonably incurred in defending those suits he can recover of the present defendant.

If it was the duty of the present defendant to defend these suits and she had an opportunity to defend them and declined to do so, then reasonable counsel fees should be recovered. If no opportunity was given the present defendant to defend the former suits, the law is more doubtful.121

§ 789. General Rule. In an action for failure to perform a contract to convey land the plaintiff is entitled to recover as damages the difference between the value of the property at the time when he was to have a conveyance and the price which he was then to pay.¹ 130 

§ 790. Partial Performance. Where the defendant is un able to convey all the land he agreed to convey and the plaintiff agrees to take what the defendant can convey, the plaintiff can recover only damages based on the fair value of the part of the estate which is not conveyed to him.131 § 791. Failure to Convey Property as Represented. In an action by the buyer for breach of a contract to convey property as represented, the rule of damage is the excess of the value of the property as it was represented to be over its value as it actually was. The defendant could not relieve himself from the consequences of this rule by showing that the plaintiff had conveyed the property to some one else. It could not have been ruled that the damage was merely nominal, as there is a difference between a house filled with tenants and a house only one-third filled, and that may be so even if the tenants are merely tenants at will. On this question all reasonable probabilities as to the time when the house may be wholly occupied and the probable loss of rents during that time may be properly considered. 182

§ 799. Breach of Contract to Convey to Trustee. The comprehensive rule is that a party injured by a breach of contract is entitled to be compensated for the loss sustained as the natural and probable consequence arising from the failure to perform by the other party. There are two ways of looking at the question of damages. The first commonly prevails in breach of a contract to convey, where the rule is the difference between the price named in the contract and the fair market value at the time when, by the terms of the contract, the conveyance is to be made. 

In another aspect the damages may be viewed as limited by the special terms of the contract. A situation may arise where the injured party may recover whatever sum he has fairly expended to extinguish the incumbrance. 

So where the plaintiff obtains an option to purchase land, not for himself but as a public-spirited citizen to induce a new enterprise to come into town, he may recover full damages as a trustee for this concern.140

§ 801. Action by Two Tenants in Common against a Third. 

In an action by two tenants in common against a third, the plaintiffs may recover for mesne profits and rents, while the tenant may recover compensation for improvements.³

In actions by two tenants in common against a third for their share of the profits earned by the defendant while he carried on a farm held in co-tenancy by all, the defendant is entitled to be allowed for his services and board and the use of his farm animals and utensils, and the claim for contribution for taxes can be set off. It would not be just to lay down an absolute rule of law that the expenditures should be marshalled so that the taxes should be paid first out of gross profits and the balance only applied to the defendant's labor and expenses. It seems unfair to say that one who tries to make a gain in which all will share if he succeeds shall necessarily be in a worse position unless he succeeds.* 

1 See also §§ 189, 773. 2 G.L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 231, § 3. 4 

3 Backus v. Chapman, 111 Mass. 386. 

4 Dewing v. Dewing, 165 Mass. 230.

§§ 802, 803 

§ 802. Owners in Severalty. Where petitioners did not own property jointly, they are entitled to damages in severalty, for a taking of the property by eminent domain.5 

§ 803. Action by One Co-Owner for Injury by Third Party. 

In an action of tort for injury to a well on leased property where it appears that the plaintiff lessee had a partner who was not joined, the plaintiff cannot recover full damages, but only that proportion of the whole damage that his share in the property and interest of the firm bore to the whole property and interest of the firm." On the other hand, the mere fact that there was evidence that a damaged automobile was owned jointly by a husband and wife does not limit the amount of recovery by the husband, and a ruling requested that the plaintiff is only entitled to recover half the value of the car is properly refused as phrased as not being a correct statement of law."

§ 804. Claim for Use and Occupation. Damages for use and occupation of real estate cannot be awarded in an action of contract in the absence of evidence of a landlordand-tenant relationship, as a contract, express or implied, is necessary in order to sustain assumpsit for use and occupation.¹

Where the plaintiff gives the defendant a license to run a music department in its department store and the parties. agree that this license is not to be assigned, but the defendant does withdraw and attempts to assign the license to another, "the measure of damages was the difference between what the plaintiff would have received if the contract had been fully performed, and what the plaintiff actually did receive, taking into account any benefit the 

1 Stevenson v. Donnelly, 221 Mass. 161.

§§ 805, 806  

plaintiff may have derived from the defendant's non-performance of the contract or from the plaintiff's use of the space occupied by the defendant's music department." 2 

§ 805. Lessee Holding Over Not Using Power. Where a tenant wrongfully remains in occupation of premises which he uses for storage only but which premises are furnished with power for a machine-shop and foundry, the defendant is liable for the fair rental value of the premises as a machine-shop and foundry, whether the defendant used the power or not when the owner notified the tenant that he should hold him so liable if he continued his occupation. "The defendant claimed not to be liable for compensation for the occupation of the premises as a machine-shop and foundry; and offered to prove what they were fairly worth, without power, for storage purposes. The presiding judge ruled that the defendant was liable for the fair rental value of the premises as a machine-shop and foundry, whether the defendant used the power or not. To this ruling the defendant has no valid ground of exception. The power formed a part of the premises which he occupied, and by his possession thereof he deprived the plaintiff of its use as much as of the use of the buildings. If he saw fit to continue to use for storage purposes premises equipped and adapted for other purposes also, by reason of which their rentable value was enhanced, he must compensate the plaintiff. To make the sum for which the defendant is liable depend upon the value of the occupation to him would be unjust to the plaintiff, who is entitled to a fair rental for all the premises of which the defendant's occupation necessarily deprived him." 3
