§ 807. Landlord's Covenant to Heat.5 Damages for the failure of a landlord to heat on certain days a building leased for a schoolhouse under an agreement to heat it are the increase in expenses or diminution in receipts caused by this failure. Evidence of the plaintiff's ordinary daily expense in running the school is not competent on this question. In an action for breach of a covenant in a lease to heat certain leased premises the measure of damages is the difference in value of the leased premises heated as stipulated and the value heated as they were in fact heated, and this difference could not exceed the reasonable cost of supplying that heat which the defendant had agreed and failed to supply."

However, where a lease contained a covenant to furnish steam for drying the lessee's lumber, which covenant the lessor broke, and the lessee had its lumber dried elsewhere, this additional expense was a consequence of the breach of covenant which may reasonably be supposed to have been within the contemplation of the parties, and may be assessed as damages.

Lessee's Covenant to Leave Premises in Condition. 

For a breach of a covenant by a lessee to leave premises in as good order and condition as they were in at the beginning of the term, the measure of damages would be such a sum of money as at the end of the term would put the premises in the condition in which the tenant was bound to leave them.16 In an action for failure to leave a leased house in the condition in which it was at the beginning of a lease as provided by a covenant in the lease the measure of damages is what it would cost to repair it and put it in the condition it ought to be in, and therefore plaintiff cannot testify what he paid to do this, as this question raises a different test.17 As a general rule the measure of damages for the breach of a lessee's covenant to keep in repair and to surrender the demised premises at the end of the term in as good order and condition as they are in at the beginning of it is the sum it would cost to repair the premises, and put them in the condition they ought to be in. When the lessor sues on the covenant to repair pending the lease, and so before he is entitled to possession of the premises, the damages may perhaps be limited to the diminution in the market value of his estate.

Where the breach consists in removal of fixtures and action is brought after the termination of the lease, the measure of damages must be the sum which will put the premises in the condition in which the defendant was bound to leave them, allowing for reasonable use and wear, even though this exceeds the injury to the market value of the premises. Otherwise a tenant who altered the nature or the arrangement of the buildings demised without the consent of the landlord might escape all liability for more than nominal damages by proving that his alterations had increased the market value of the estate.18 "A lessee who breaches a provision of the lease requiring him to make certain repairs or to deliver up the premises at the termination of the lease in a certain condition is liable in damages for the reasonable cost of making such repairs or of putting the premises in the condition prescribed by the lease. But the plaintiff is not to be put in a better position than it would have been if the defendant had performed the terms of the lease," and therefore, where the cost of repairs is in excess of the damage to the land, the award should be limited to the damage to the land. LANDLORD AND TENANT § 813. Lessee Holding Over after Term Expires. A tenant who holds over after the expiration of his term is liable only for the fair rental value of the premises in their condition at the time, and the landlord cannot recover increased returns he expected from improving the property, in the absence of notice to the tenant of his intention to improve the premises.20 

§ 814. Payment to Tenant Conditioned on his Quitting. 

Where a lease contains a provision that the lessor may terminate it on payment of $400, when the tenant shall quit, and the lessor tenders the $400, which the tenant refuses, and the tenant refuses to quit and has to be evicted by summary process, then the tenant is not entitled to the $400. Payment was conditional on the tenant's concurrent surrender of the premises, and his refusal to accept the tender and vacate the premises prevents any recovery." 21 

§ 815. Overpayment by Lessee for Electric Current. Where an electric company made with a lessee of a building a contract to supply him with current for his use at the wholesale rate, and by a mistake of the company a separate meter designed to measure current to a sub-tenant was connected for a time on the wire on which was the lessee's meter so that current used by the sub-tenant during that period registered on both meters, it is held that the company is in equity and good conscience obliged to pay back as damages what the lessee had paid for the current intended to be sold at the wholesale rate. The lessee cannot recover money paid by the sub-tenant.22

 § 816. Eviction. Lessor's Covenant of Quiet Enjoyment.23 

In an action by a lessee for a breach of a covenant of quiet enjoyment where special damages are claimed, damages may include the lessee's expense of removal, and the evidence that the fair rental of the property was more than the rent he paid should be considered.24 The tenant's damages for eviction are the difference between the agreed rental and the actual value if no rent had been paid; but where a lessee has been excluded from possession and nevertheless has been compelled to pay rent during the period of such exclusion, the amount so paid is to be added, otherwise his actual loss by reason of the breach of the implied covenant will not be made good.25 

§ 817. Eviction. Damages Entire. Where the defendant lets his farm for a year to the plaintiff on shares and after a few months evicts the plaintiff, the damages like the contract were entire and all accrued on the day when the contract was repudiated. They were measured by the value of the contract of which the plaintiff was deprived, and did not consist of a series of items, although, for the purpose of estimating the value, the items on each side of the account during the year, as well after as before the breach, were properly admissible.26 

§ 818. Eviction. Value of Property for Any Use. Where a lessor has prevented a lessee from enjoying the leased premises the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the leasehold and the rent agreed upon. This value means the value for any and all uses to which the property is adapted and can readily be applied. If it is capable of being used in some particular

§ 821. Eviction. Injury to Health. Damages for a wrong ful, wilful eviction, even when done with gross negligence, properly include payment for injury to property and for the wound inflicted on the feelings of the plaintiff, but not for any injury to health arising out of exposure in travelling from the premises or from attending his family when ill, nor from grief that they were ill. So evidence of subsequent illness of the members of the plaintiff's family was incompetent.30 

§ 822. Eviction. Building Erected by Lessee. Where a lease provides that the lessee may be allowed the value of buildings he erects on the premises and the lessee holds over after the termination of the lease under a tenancy for years until the lessor wrongfully evicts him, the lessee is entitled as damages to the value of the buildings on the termination of the lease less the rent from that time to the eviction.31 § 823. The limits of this book do not permit of any adequate treatment of the intricacies of the involved subject of eminent domain, and the reader will find here only a few of the most recent decisions noted which may bring out some of the general outlines of the subject and which bear on the general subject of damages.

§§ 825-828  1. INTEREST OF OWNER. 

§ 825. Tenants in Common. In estimating damages for landowners holding land as tenants in common for a taking by eminent domain the jury should first find the total amount of damages sustained by the owners as an entire estate and then apportion such damages among the several parties in proportion to their several interests and to the damages sustained. Where only one of two tenants in common brings a petition it is error to award to him the whole of the damage and to oblige him to account to the other co-tenant for one-half the amount, but judgment is to be entered for the co-tenant who petitioned on a verdict of one-half the total damage found by the jury.¹ § 826. Lessee under Lease Terminated. A lessee in possession under a lease which has terminated and has not been renewed is at most a tenant at will and as such has no right to damages for a taking by eminent domain.² § 827. Fee in Private Way. In the assessment of damages for a taking for railroad purposes the plaintiff owning the fee in a private way need not obtain the consent of all abuttors to the laying of a railroad crossing across this way, and an instruction to that effect is error.3 

§ 828. Value of Agreement Respecting Property. In a petition for assessment of damages for taking land and water rights the value of an agreement the landowner had that he might remove pending water easements on payment of a certain sum of money should be considered in assessing damages.¹

2. WHERE PORTION OF PROPERTY TAKEN. 

§ 829. Taking of Portion of Land. Damage to Remaining 

Land. Damages to remaining land should be assessed where a taking left the plaintiff with the title in fee to one-half the land adjoining the lot taken where this land could not be used except in connection with the land taken, but with that land could have been found to have had a substantial value. It is proper to instruct a jury in case of a taking by eminent domain of a portion of a lot that they should compare the fair market value of the whole lot just before the taking with the fair market value of the whole lot right after the taking and consider what in fact was the fair value of the land actually taken and what the result or damage was to the land remaining even where a small strip is taken." 

§ 830. Damage to Remaining Land from Taking Strip. 

Rental Value if Land Improved. In a petition for damages caused by taking a strip from vacant land of the petitioner for widening a street, the petitioner could show as an element of damage that the rental value of the unimproved land as it was at the time of the taking had been diminished or destroyed, but evidence of the rental value if the land were improved by the erection of buildings for business purposes was inadmissible. It is too prospective and indefinite in its nature to be competent evidence of the present value of land not built upon."

§ 832. Fact that Land Already Graded for Street Railway. 

Where land is taken by eminent domain it is the detriment to the owner that is to be considered and not to the party exercising the right. Recovery should not be measured by the adaptability of the property for the use for which it was taken unless that adaptability added to its market value generally. So where land taken had already been cut and filled for a street railway it is error to admit evidence of the price per cubic yard of the fills, as this testimony was likely to confuse the jury as being evidence that the respondent might be saved the cost of making these fills in using the land for highway purposes." 

§ 833. Demand for Bath Houses. Loss of Business. Where a part of a beach used for bath houses is taken, the owner may recover damages for the property taken and damages for the land not taken, because its value was impaired, and the jury cannot award damages for the loss of business. 

The petitioner should be allowed to show the demand for bath houses already on the remaining land and could show that the use of the remaining land as a bathing establishment was a reasonable and proper use.' 10 § 834. 4. SPECIAL USES OF PROPERTY. 

§ 836. Value of Land for Special Purpose. In a petition for assessment of damages for a taking of land by eminent domain the petitioner may prove its value as a piece of real estate, but cannot introduce evidence of the value of the property as a gravel pit alone,13 although evidence of all possible uses of the land may always be shown as bearing on its value as real estate. Evidence of the uses to which property may be practically put is admissible, but evidence of the special line of development proposed by the owner may be too speculative and indefinite to be competent evidence of the present value of the land.¹4

Where land is taken for a water supply the landowner is not entitled to have included in damages his proportionate part of the land and waters considered as an indispen-

Damages are not to be measured by the value of the property for special or possible purposes, but by its market value in view of all purposes to which it was naturally adapted.15 

§ 837. Special Value to Taker Alone. Reproduction Cost. 

In case of a taking by eminent domain the special utility of the property to the taker alone cannot be stated or described. In the Cape Cod Canal case it was held that evidence of reconstruction cost would not be admitted unless the jury was satisfied that a reasonably prudent man would purchase or undertake the construction of the property at such a figure. The actual cost within a reasonable time of the property taken is always regarded as evidence, but the reproduction cost does not include costs of financing the company. 16 § 838. Loss of View. 5. EFFECT OF USE BY TAKER. 

§ 840. Benefits from Building State Highway. In a pe tition for damages for taking for a State highway, the benefits to the petitioner's remaining land accruing from the building of the highway must be considered even though they are shared by other neighboring abutting owners. 

These are direct and special benefits which should be set off. Thus, if the petitioner's property is actually worth as much or more after the taking as before, no damages can be awarded for the taking.20 § 841. Damage by Abutting on Side Track rather than

Main Line of Railroad. On a petition for taking by eminent domain it may be found that the petitioner suffered no damage from having his land abut on the side track rather than on the main line of a railroad.21

6. PROCEEDINGS. 

§ 843. Value at Date of Taking. In a petition for the assessment of damages for a taking by eminent domain the value of the property at the date of the taking was the measure of damages and evidence of its condition a year before the taking is incompetent.23 

§ 844. Jury's Verdict Supersedes Award. Where land is taken by eminent domain and an award made and a petition is subsequently filed for assessment of damages by the jury, who assess damages at less than the award, the plaintiff must then rely on the jury verdict and cannot then claim under the award. The petition for a trial by jury is in the nature of an appeal from the initial award and vacates the action from which appeal is taken. The right of appeal for a trial by jury is given both to the landowner and to the body politic in whose behalf the land has been taken, and if the landowner has the right to elect between the verdict and the award, the respondent would have the same right, which would lead to a ridiculous result.24 

§ 845. Evidence of Sales with Mortgage Back. Where land is cut up into house lots in a development scheme and some are sold, these sales may be admitted in evidence as to the value of parts of the tract taken by eminent domain, although the sales were made with a small cash payment and the balance by mortgage. 25

§ 846. Scope of This Chapter. The subject of damages for personal injuries so permeates the whole law of damages that it can hardly be treated in one chapter alone, and this chapter includes only those topics which do not logically belong under some other classification. The subject of personal injuries is also treated elsewhere in this book, as appears by the note hereto appended.¹

§§ 847-849  § 847. Amount Based on Common Knowledge. Auditor's 

Report. In an action for personal injuries a finding of damages cannot be made according to any arithmetical calculation. A proper estimate depends upon sound judgment, based largely upon common knowledge. So where a case is presented to the jury on an auditor's report without further evidence and the auditor finds for the plaintiff in the sum of $448, the amount of the damages may still be fixed by the jury and their verdict in the sum of $2000 may be sustained. An auditor's report awarding damages for personal injuries is not binding on the court where his findings of fact were not final and his description of the injuries warrants the finding by the jury of a different amount.2 3 

§ 848. Nominal Damages Sustained. Where the jury bring in a verdict for one dollar in an action for personal injuries and damage to an automobile arising out of a collision and the court declines to set aside the verdict, exceptions are overruled on the ground that no abuse of discretion was shown. The degree of credibility to be attached to the statements of anybody cannot be ruled as matter of law.*

An action by a married woman against the proprietor of a barroom for personal injuries resulting in a miscarriage from an assault upon the plaintiff by her husband in consequence of intoxication caused by liquor sold by the defendant may be maintained and the labor pains of the plaintiff in giving birth to a dead child may be considered. § 866. Liquor Dealer. Intoxication Causing Crime and 

Conviction. In an action of tort to recover damages sustained by the plaintiff by reason of the sale of intoxicating liquor by the defendant to the plaintiff's minor son, whereby the son became intoxicated and was arrested for crime committed, there is no causal connection between the sale of the liquor and the damage that the plaintiff sustained in disgrace and shame and expenditure of money for the defense of the son, and the imprisonment of the son with the loss of his services to the plaintiff. The perpetration of a crime is not the natural and probable consequence of furnishing intoxicating liquor to the criminal. 

Here the plaintiff is pursuing a common-law remedy to recover damages for expenses incurred and loss of services sustained on account of a wrong suffered by his son, but the son could not recover damages that were directly attributable to the criminal assault which he committed. "The plaintiff's right to recover consequential damages on account of an injury sustained by his minor son is derivative and, if the son had no cause of action, the plaintiff has none."

The court distinguishes the cases of Colburn v. Spencer, 177 Mass. 473, and McNary v. Blackburn, 180 Mass. 141, as arising under a statute and not being authority for the proposition that the seller of the liquor is liable at common law to one who has sustained damage by the sentence and

"The determination of damages for the impairment of earning capacity is not susceptible to arithmetical calculation; its ascertainment must to a large degree depend upon the practical sagacity, common knowledge and good sense of the jury in considering the age, skill, training, experience and industry of the plaintiff, the extent of his physical injury, the wages commonly received by one pursuing a similar occupation in the vicinity of the plaintiff's employment, and whatever other evidence is introduced to aid them in arriving at a just conclusion." 5

13 § 873. Earnings before and after Injury. One of the grounds of damages for personal injuries is the loss or any lessening of the ability to work, and this loss of ability to earn money can be measured by a fact-finding tribunal. 

The plaintiff is not entitled to recover as such the wages lost, but the difference between the amounts which one has earned and received before and after an injury generally affords some indication of the economic value of his loss through the impairment of his working capacity. Hence the wages that the plaintiff was receiving at the time of the accident may properly be shown as bearing on the question of damages for personal injury,¹ and evidence is admissible of the plaintiff's average monthly earnings to ascertain the economic value of his loss; 15 and where the earning capacity of the injured person is in question, it is proper to receive evidence of additional wages for overtime work.16 So the loss of earning capacity of a cripple in selling lead pencils and in appraising automobiles may appear from his testimony as to his average weekly earnings before and after the accident, and this evidence is not too speculative.¹7

In an action for personal injuries evidence as to the wages earned by the plaintiff at the time of the injury is competent on the issue of damages without special averment in the declaration. It is an element to be considered in determining the amount of compensation to which the plaintiff is entitled. The circumstance that the plaintiff is a married woman made no difference in this particular.¹ 18 § 874. Ability before and after Injury. In an action for personal injuries evidence may be received of the business activities of the plaintiff before and after the injury, simply as bearing on his physical condition and not to show loss of business income. It does not follow that superior education, experience or ability in the management of business insures pecuniary success. The uncertainty of the continuance of health and life, with the taste and disposition for such pursuits, and especially the proverbial uncertainty of trade, preclude the making of any estimate which can have weight beyond the merest conjecture. If this evidence had been offered by the plaintiff with a view of increasing the damages on account of his wealth or peculiar skill as a manufacturer, or the large profits he would be able to realize in his future business, and it had been admitted for that purpose, the argument of the defendant would be entitled to further consideration. § 875. Evidence of Headaches, Dizziness, Nervousness, Etc. 

It is always competent to show by the plaintiff's physical condition his inability to earn, and an impairment of the plaintiff's future capacity to work may be shown by showing there was a permanent impairment of the vision of the left eye, headaches, dizziness and drowsiness, nervousness and a progressive thickening of the skull.22

§ 878. Plaintiff Not Working. A tailor who conducts a tailoring business consisting of both making and repairing clothes and who works at the business himself and also has working for him at least two people, and where part of the work was done by outside tailors, and he is prevented from doing this work for a considerable time as the result of an accident by which he claims damages, cannot put in evidence the fact that the profits of his business for the six months before the accident were $1200 and for the corresponding period after the accident were $500. Here the profits must in the nature of things have been derived to a substantial extent from a gain on the sale of goods and employment of labor, and this partakes more of the nature of business than of personal service. "The principles upon which damages for personal injury caused by tort are to be assessed are settled. In general the plaintiff is entitled to such sum of money as will compensate him for the loss actually sustained by the injury to his person. It is personal and not property damage which may be recovered. As bearing upon the question of compensation, disability and impaired capacity are to be considered. If one receives wages or salary, the amount lost in this regard from the enforced inability to work is a proper element to be considered in assessing damages, but it is not strictly recoverable as wages or salary. The loss of time and the diminution of earning power in the past and in the future are to be considered in estimating the damages. Sibley v. Nason, 196 Mass. 125, 131. Profits hoped to be derived in the future from a business are too remote and uncertain to be regarded as an element in estimating damages. Ballou v. Farnum, 11 

Allen, 73, 76. That is not a personal injury, but a property damage. Decrease in income is an element to be weighed, when it arises from inability to exercise personal effort or especial efficiency directly producing the income; but not when it is interwoven with profits derived from a busi-

$ 882

ness in which capital is employed and to the success of which the service, skill and zeal of others contribute. Personal earnings may be considered, but the more or less uncertain profits from a business venture arising from an investment and from ability in employing and managing labor cannot be taken into account. Where the element of personal expertness is the essential and dominant factor and the capital invested is insignificant as compared with the earnings and merely incidental to the individual capacity which is the fundamental cause of the income, then the income stands on the same basis as wages or salary and may be shown. On this ground the income of the physician or other professional man or author may be shown, although there may be some money invested in a library, instruments and similar collateral necessaries. 

Conklin v. Consolidated Railway, 196 Mass. 302, 307. 

Nebraska v. Campbell, 2 Black, 590. Gray v. Boston Elevated Railway, 215 Mass. 143. One is not precluded from recovering loss of earning capacity because he happens to be engaged in business for himself; but he cannot prove what is in substance profits from a business under the semblance of earnings. The business man may show the nature and extent of the business conducted by him, the part actually performed by him, and the compensation usually paid to those performing a like service for others. 

These are circumstances which may be helpful in determining the value of the time he has lost, in order to reach the ultimate result of just compensation for the injury sustained. But the uncertain profits of a commercial undertaking dependent for its success upon other essential factors beside his personal service are too remote to be of assistance in this respect. These principles are generally recognized. They are the same whether the commercial venture involved is on a large or a small scale."' 38

The § 887. Measure of Damages for Mental Suffering. 

difficulties of measuring damages for mental suffering and physical injuries is well stated as follows: "In a variety of actions founded on personal torts, and in many where no positive bodily harm has been inflicted, the plaintiff is permitted to recover for injury to the feelings and affections, for mental anxiety, personal insult, and that wounded sensibility which follows the invasion of a large class of personal rights. The impossibility, in all such cases, of precisely appreciating in money mental suffering of this description is certainly as great as is suggested where the question is what shall be allowed for a permanent injury to mental capacity. The compensation for personal injury occasioned by the negligence or misconduct of others, which the law promises, is indemnity, so far as it may be afforded in money, for the loss and damage which the man has suffered as a man. Some of its elements may be bodily pain, mutilation, loss of time and outlay of money; but of more important consideration oftentimes is the mental suffering and loss of capacity which ensues. Of these several items of injury, if compensation is to be confined to those capable of accurate estimate, it will include but a small part, and must exclude all those injuries commonly regarded as purely physical; for the difficulty in ascertaining a pecuniary equivalent for the last named is precisely the same and quite as great as any that have been suggested. In fact, it will be found impossible to fix a limit to injuries of a physical nature so as to exclude from consideration their effect on the mental organization of the sufferer.” " § 888. Where a plaintiff in an action for personal injuries had suffered a general breakdown in health, accompanied by heart trouble, about two years before an automobile accident, it may be found that the accident aggravated his condition and caused reasonable fears that the accident would hasten his death, and this mental suffering may be considered on the question of damages.¹¹

 § 891. Sorrow from Loss of Child. Physical injuries may cause a nervous condition resulting in a premature birth and death of a child after the accident, but damages awarded cannot include the mental suffering of the plaintiff on this account. "She was thus permitted to recover money compensation for the sorrow and anguish endured as a result of the contemplation of the death of her child conceived nearly seven months and born fourteen months after the injury. This is extending the rule of damages beyond any limits heretofore recognized. It is an expansion which finds no support in any principle of law. Mental suffering connected with and growing out of physical injury is a legitimate element to be considered in determining damages against a person wrongfully causing an injury. Such suffering is to a greater or less extent inseparably connected with physical harm, and flows from it as a natural result. 

Canning v. Williamstown, 1 Cush. 451. The rule of damages is a practical instrumentality for the administration of justice. The principle on which it is founded is compensation. Its object is to afford the equivalent in money for the actual loss caused by the wrong of another. Recurrence to this fundamental conception tests the soundness of claims for the inclusion of new elements of damage. 

The landowner, whose home, rendered dear by ties of ancestry and personal attachment, is seized under the power of eminent domain, has a right to receive no larger sum, on account of the mental distress he endures in leaving it, than a mere stranger, holding it purely for speculative purposes. The parent, who sues for the loss of services of his minor child, cannot recover for his own sympathetic sorrow in witnessing the sufferings, which cause his loss of service. In an action for deprivation of consortium, the anguish of mind of the husband, in observing the bodily pain of a sensitive wife, forms no element in the damages he may recover. These considerations apply peculiarly to a case like the present. Wealth brings no consolation to

$ 461 

MENTAL SUFFERING 

those who mourn. The grief occasioned by the death of loved ones touches chords in the human soul which lie outside the compass of pecuniary relief. The solace, which stills the voice of lamentation, comes from sources which cannot be found through the medium of money. The mental suffering, for which damages can be recovered, therefore, is limited to that which results to the person injured as the necessary or natural consequence of the physical injury. But sentiments of grief, sorrow and mourning, which are aroused by extraneous causes, thoughts or reflections, are excluded. The contemplation of the suffering and death of a child, begotten long after the event complained of, is too remote from the original physical injury to the parent and too intangible and ethereal to be connected with the original wrong of the defendant as a result to be reasonably apprehended from such a cause. The law cannot enter the realm of pure sentiment in this class of case, and award pecuniary compensation for those injured feelings which spring from sympathy and the severance of ties of love and affection. It follows that there can be no recovery for the mental suffering which ensues from the contemplation of the pain, deformity, imperfections or characteristics of any other person or thing." 14

Under such circumstances, the natural injury to the feelings of the plaintiff may be taken into consideration in trespasses to real estate as well as in other actions of tort. Where a plaintiff is thrown and receives certain bruises and also a nervous shock which later was followed by paralysis, the plaintiff need not prove that the nervous shock was the result of the battery, but it is enough if the shock resulted from a jar to her nervous system which accompanied the blow to her person.24 There can be no recovery for personal injuries where the only result of the injury is fright or mental distress unaccompanied by some physical injury to the person from without. § 896. Mental Suffering with No Physical Injury. In the first case on the subject in this State 27 the court laid down

The decision in the Spade case (168 Mass. 285) "is an arbitrary exception, based upon a notion of what is practicable, that prevents a recovery for visible illness resulting from nervous shock alone." Per Holmes, C.J., in Homans v. Boston Elevated Railway Co., 180 Mass. 456.

the rule that there can be no recovery for such physical injuries as may be caused solely by fright, terror or anxiety where there is no injury to the person from without, and this view is supported on the basis that this would open a wide door for unjust claims which could not successfully be met. The decision is not extended to cases where an intention to cause mental distress or to hurt the feelings is shown, as in case of slander, malicious prosecution, etc., and the rule also does not include acts done with gross carelessness or recklessness showing, utter indifference to the consequences. The decision has been so limited by later cases that it is of doubtful application today.28 The court holds that a passenger may not recover if the conductor in removing a drunken man pushes him against her whereby she is frightened but suffers no bodily injury. The court remarks that a carrier is not bound to anticipate or guard against an injurious result which would only happen to a person of peculiar sensitiveness. The court proceeds to place the matter on a practical basis in the following language: "The law of negligence in its special application to cases of accidents has received great development in recent years. 

The number of actions brought is very great. This should lead courts well to consider the grounds on which claims for compensation properly rest, and the necessary limitations of the right to recover. We remain satisfied with the rule that there can be no recovery for fright, terror, alarm, anxiety, or distress of mind, if these are unaccompanied by some physical injury; and if this rule is to stand, we think it should also be held that there can be no recovery for such physical injuries as may be caused solely by such mental disturbance, where there is no injury to the person from without. The logical vindication of this rule is, that it is unreasonable to hold persons who are merely negli-

gent bound to anticipate and guard against fright and the consequences of fright; and that this would open a wide door for unjust claims, which could not successfully be met. • • "It is hardly necessary to add that this decision does not reach those classes of actions where an intention to cause mental distress or to hurt the feelings is shown, or is reasonably to be inferred, as, for example, in cases of seduction, slander, malicious prosecution, or arrest, and some others. Nor do we include cases of acts done with gross carelessness or recklessness, showing utter indifference to such consequences, when they must have been in the actor's mind.'' 29

A declaration is insufficient which alleges merely that the defendant by a loud explosion in blasting close to the plaintiff's house so frightened her that she became sick, although the declaration also claims that the negligence was gross and that the defendant should have known that the result complained of would follow its act. Plaintiff Jumping from Fright. Where a woman is frightened by an explosion and starts to rise from her chair and trips or stumbles, damages may be assessed for injuries caused thereby, and so if she rose and then fainted and fell. "The principle of the Spade case is confined strictly to cases where the connection of the physical illness with the fright is wholly internal. When the fright reasonably induces action which results in external injury, the defendant may be liable as well as when the impact is brought about without the intervention of the plaintiff's consciousness." 37 Where the plaintiff jumps from his wagon to avoid being hit by a train at a grade crossing and suffers no bruises but feels sick and has pains, it cannot be said as matter of law that his injuries were caused solely by fright, but the jury may find the pains were due to unusual exertion in jumping and to the physical shock caused by the impact of the plaintiff's body with the ground.38 

Where the woman plaintiff is sitting in a street car when flames dart out and burn her clothing and she jumps and is injured, this is not only an assault, but a battery, where the flames come in contact with the clothing of the person, although she may be neither bruised nor wounded. "The phrase 'from without' as used in our cases excludes purely psychological or emotional consequences when they stand alone, but includes all physical injury not resulting solely from mental shock or emotional disturbances. The question, therefore, in each such case is whether the physical injury resulting from the defendant's negligence is in fact one which was not caused solely by mental disturbances. The proof that it was 'from without,' in the sense in which we have just defined that phrase, is not restricted to evidence of the application of violence to the person of the plaintiff." 40 § 901. § 907. Indemnity the Test. In an action for malicious prosecution, if no specific instructions are asked it is sufficient to instruct the jury that they are to give such sum as will indemnify the plaintiff for the injuries he has sustained.2 

§ 908. Natural Results of Service of Process. In an action for malicious prosecution the defendant may be liable for that which would naturally arise from the service of the process or which naturally might be expected to happen as the natural consequence of the service of the process. The defendant was not liable for any acts of the officer done in excess of the authority conferred by the warrant, but was liable for everything done within such authority even though the officer might have been a little more considerate than he actually was.³ § 909. § 914. That Plaintiff had Made Similar Charges. In an action for malicious prosecution the defendant cannot show in mitigation of damages that the plaintiff had instituted similar proceedings against him. "The offer of the defendant to prove, in mitigation of damages, that the plaintiff had instituted a complaint against him, charging him with perjury, is not sustained by any authority cited. The cases of Watts v. Fraser, 7 C. & P. 369, and Fraser v. Berkeley,

Ib. 621, do not apply to a case like this. In the first case it was held that one who is sued for a libel may prove, in mitigation of damages, that he was provoked to the act by a libel of the plaintiff upon him. In the second case it was held that one who is sued for an assault may prove, in mitigation of damages, that he was provoked to it by a libel of the plaintiff upon him. But we find no case where it has been held that such an act as a malicious prosecution is excused or palliated by the fact that the person prosecuted had committed a similar offence against the prosecutor.

Excited feeling can be no apology for entering a court of justice and making or instigating a malicious prosecution. 

It is in the highest degree reprehensible to make the criminal law or a court of criminal jurisdiction an instrument for gratifying private malice or excited passion. The only purpose which the law recognizes as justifiable or excusable, in promoting a criminal prosecution, is to aid the state in the execution of public justice. The evidence offered did not tend to mitigate the wrongful act of the defendant in the least degree." 10 § 915. Loss of Promised Job Too Remote. Where special damages are claimed, the declaration must show how these special damages were occasioned by the slander, and should set forth precisely in what way such special damages resulted from the words relied on.* "If published in writing or in print, the words which tended to expose the plaintiffs to aversion and disgrace, and to disseminate an evil opinion of them in the community, would be libellous and actionable without evidence of special damages. But in oral defamation, unless the falsely spoken words impute such conduct as shows the commission of a criminal offence for which, if true, he may be prosecuted, or charge that he is suffering from some contagious disease which, if known, would bar him from society, or that he is an unfit person to perform the duties of the employment or office exercised or held by him for profit, or that he is wanting in integrity in discharge of the duties of his employment or office, or unless the words cause him to be prejudiced in his profession or trade, the plaintiff must allege special damages resulting from the act complained of or the declaration is demurrable. § 940. Agreement Not to Compete. Substantial damages may be awarded for breach of an agreement not to engage in a competing business in a small place without evidence specifically directed to what the damage would be. The damages, being for breach of an entire contract, must be assessed once for all, and necessarily are largely a matter of estimate,¹ and include all injuries caused thereby.2 In a bill in equity to enforce a covenant not to compete in business the amount of sales made by the defendant's company may be made the basis of damages.³ Where one partner retires from the partnership and agrees that the partnership may include his name for the term of five years he may have a further use of it enjoined, but may not recover profits. 

The plaintiff has not been competed with unfairly and his loss bears no relation to the defendants' gains. He has suffered nothing beyond the infraction of the statutory right of prohibition.*

§ 943. Damages and Profits from Selling Goods Imitating 

Plaintiff's. In a suit in equity to restrain unfair competition the defendant may be found liable for actual damages and profits, if any, realized from the sale of the goods imitated to look like the plaintiff's products. In a bill in equity for the assessment of damages sustained by the plaintiff by reason of the defendant's unfair competition in selling packages made up to look like those manufactured and sold by the plaintiff and under its trade name the court says: "At the argument before us the plaintiff contended that it was entitled to recover from the defendant both the dam- 

5 Parker v. Levin, 285 Mass. 125. "New York Bank Note Co. v. Kidder Press Manufacturing Co., 192 

Mass. 391. 

7 See also ◊ 73 et seq. 

8 Forster Manufacturing Co. v. Cutter-Tower Co., 211 Mass. 219.

$943 

ages which it has sustained from the defendant's wrongful use of its trade name and the amount of the profits realized by the defendant therefrom. We agree that the plaintiff is so entitled, so far as this may be necessary for its full compensation. Regis v. H. A. Jaynes & Co. 191 Mass. 245, 250. 

Forster Manuf. Co. v. Cutter-Tower Co. 211 Mass. 219, 223.

But this does not mean that the plaintiff may recover from the defendant both the amount of the latter's profits as such and also damages assessed upon the theory that the plaintiff, but for the defendant's wrongful acts, would have made the sales which have been made by the defendant, and so is entitled to recover an additional amount for the profits which it has lost. It may not recover a double compensation for the same sales. The plaintiff is not to derive a double gain from the defendant's sales, by recovering in addition to the profits made by the defendant from its sales those which by reason of the same sales the plaintiff has lost the opportunity of making. This would be a manifest injustice. The plaintiff in such a case as this may to be sure have suffered some particular loss or damage for which the receipt of the defendant's profits would not compensate him. If, for example, the defendant has attempted to undersell him, has introduced what sometimes is called a 'cutthroat competition,' thus cutting down the plaintiff's profits without correspondingly increasing his own, or if the defendant has cheapened his production by the use of inferior materials or by unsuitable processes of manufacture, and thus has depreciated the value of the plaintiff's trade name or of the words or symbols to which the plaintiff has acquired a right, or otherwise has injured the reputation of the plaintiff's goods and thereby caused an appreciable loss to the maker, in addition to that caused by the actual sales which the defendant has made, the plaintiff should be allowed to recover for such a loss besides taking the defendant's profits, if the plaintiff has claimed and is allowed such profits. And this plaintiff appears to have suffered

§§ 944, 945 487 

UNFAIR COMPETITION 

substantial damages, exceeding the defendant's profits. But these damages as assessed include the profits which the plaintiff would have realized, if it had made, with certain exceptions, all the sales of infringing goods that were made by the defendant. See L. Martin & Co. v. L. Martin & 

Wilckes Co. 5 Buch. 257, 260, et seq. It follows that the plaintiff may recover only the amount of damages and the amount of the defendant's profits on the excepted sales, being the additional sum of $195.93, with interest.' 999 

§ 944. Payment by Doctor on Return to Practice. Where a physician sells his practice and agrees not to practise in that city again but shall have the right to do so after five years on paying the sum of $2000, this is not liquidated damages or a penalty, but is a sum fixed by the contract which must be paid if he returns, irrespective of the damage suffered.10 

§ 945. Former Employee Taking Customers from Em ployer. In an assessment of damages for unfair competition in selling to customers contrary to an agreement, damages may be awarded for interference with the plaintiff's business within a reasonable area and for selling to customers whom the former employee had served while he was working for the plaintiff.11

In a bill in equity against a former employee of the plaintiff for breach by the defendant of his contract of employment by obtaining and executing orders for work from the plaintiff's customers, the rule of damages is the same as though the plaintiff had brought an action for breach of contract, and the plaintiff is entitled to damages sufficient in amount to compensate him for the loss actually

Therefore the loss which the plaintiff sustained was the difference between what it would have actually cost the plaintiff to execute the orders in question and the contract prices therefor.12 

§ 946. Failure to Give Whole Working Time to Employer. 

In a suit in equity by the employer to enjoin the employee from disclosing or making use of trade secrets, where it is found that the employee has devoted some portion of his working hours to the construction and installation of his own machinery, the bill may be retained for the assessment of whatever damages the employer had suffered from breach of the contract to give his whole working time to the employer. 13

§ 960. Fraud Inducing Partnership. § 962. Fraud of Buyer Inducing Sale. In a bill in equity to rescind a sale of stock by the plaintiff at an inadequate price on account of the fraud of the defendants, the general rule is that the injured party is entitled to be put in as good a condition as he would have been but for the wrong done him. Another rule goes with this, that the consequences for 

13 Hedden v. Griffin, 136 Mass. 229. 

14 Richards v. Todd, 127 Mass. 167. 

15 Merchants' National Bank v. National Bank of the Commonwealth, 139 Mass. 513.

$ 963 

which the wrongdoer is liable are only those which are the direct and proximate results of his wrongdoing. It would be impracticable for courts to attempt to follow to its utmost consequences any wrong that is done. 

In this case the wrong was done when the deceit was practised, and the consequences must be measured as of that date or within a reasonable time thereafter. In a case like this, if the wrongdoer has the stock in his possession, equity will compel him to return it on the plaintiff's putting him in statu quo. If, however, the defendant has not the stock in his possession or control, it would be entering the realms of conjecture and speculation to assume that the plaintiff would have kept the stock if he had not been induced to part with it by the defendant's fraud. 

In this case the defendant was not bound to have the stock in his hands when the bill was brought or at any other time, and until the plaintiff elected to avoid the sale the defendant could rightfully sell and dispose of the stock to an innocent purchaser as he did in this case. The rule of damages here is the difference between the value of the shares on the day when the sale was made and the amount paid by the defendant to the plaintiff, with interest at six per cent from the date of the sale to the date of the final decree. If this defendant had disabled himself from conveying the stock by a sale and transfer after the bill was brought, a different rule might apply.16

§ 964. Damage Necessary in Deceit.18 One of the essen tial elements of an action of deceit is proof of damage, and if no damage appears, no action can be maintained.' 19 § 965. Usual Rule of Damages. In an action for fraud in inducing the plaintiff to purchase, the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of what the plaintiff received and what that value would have been if the defendant's representations had been true.20 In an action by the buyer for rescission of a sale of stock on the ground of misrepresentations, the damages must be limited to the difference between the value of what the plaintiff received and what its value would have been if it had been as represented.21

Where an action for deceit is brought for false representations inducing the plaintiff to buy an interest of the defendant in the stock and good will of a firm, the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the stock and good will purchased at the time of the purchase and its value had the representation been true. The court lays down the following rule: "The rule of damages was rightly stated to the jury. It is now well settled that, in actions for deceit or breach of warranty, the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the property at the time of the purchase, and its value if the property had been what it was represented or warranted to be. . . . This is the only rule which will give the purchaser adequate damages for not having the thing which the defendant undertook to sell him. To allow to the plaintiff (as the learned counsel for the defendant argued in this case) only the difference between the 

18 See also § 12. 

19 Connelly v. Bartlett, 286 Mass. 311. 

20 Vouros v. Pierce, 226 Mass. 175. 

21 McNulty v. Whitney, 273 Mass. 494.

real value of the property and the price which he was induced to pay for it would be to make any advantage lawfully secured to the innocent purchaser in the original bargain inure to the benefit of the wrongdoer; and, in proportion as the original price was low, would afford a protection to the party who had broken, at the expense of the party who was ready to abide by, the terms of the contract. The fact that the property sold was of such a character as to make it difficult to ascertain with exactness what its value would have been if it had conformed to the contract affords no reason for exempting the defendant from any part of the direct consequences of his fraud. And the value may be estimated as easily in this action as in an action against him for an entire refusal to perform his contract." 22 

§ 966. Test Not Simply Difference between Price and Ac tual Value. In an action by a purchaser for deceit in inducing a sale, "the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the property at the time of purchase, and its value if the property had been what it was represented or warranted to be." It is not the rule that the measure of damages is the difference between the value of the property at the time when it is bought and the purchase price. So in an action for deceit in inducing the plaintiff to purchase a farm and milk route the jury must be made acquainted with the conditions of sale and of the parties and to understand what the representations of the

The out-of-pocket rule, on the other hand, gives the difference between the purchase price and the value received. § 967. Secret Profits Not the Test. Rescission. § 970. Where Market Value Illusory. In an action for fraud in the sale of a bond the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the bond at the time of the purchase and its value if it had been what it was represented to be, secured as represented, and on this issue the jury may consider what has happened since the sale. 

The market value of the bond at the time of the sale may have been illusory, because the public also may have been deceived.27 

§ 971. Value of Good Will Misstated. Dealer's Talk. No damages can be awarded because of false and fraudulent representations respecting the value of the good will of goods sold where this was manifestly a declaration of opinion or properly classified as dealer's talk where no sensible person could understand that the value of the good will sold was other than problematical.28

 § 976. Effect of Sale by Purchaser at Same or Better Price.

§ 977. Personal Injuries when Horse Sold is Unsafe. In an action of tort for deceit in sale of a horse it appeared that the defendant induced the plaintiff to buy the horse by false statements that it was perfectly safe for a woman to drive and was not afraid of the cars, that the plaintiff did drive it and it took fright at cars and ran away, injuring the plaintiff, and it was held that the defendant was liable for these personal injuries.34 

§ 978. Recoupment in Horse Trade. In an action of tort for false representations as to the value of the defendant's horse in inducing an exchange, the defendant may recoup by an answer claiming that the plaintiff falsely represented the value of his horse, and is not remitted to a cross-action. 

The court remarks that the principle of recoupment in actions of tort is well settled.35

§ 981. Liability of Co-Owners. Where a part owner of a schooner fraudulently induces the plaintiff to buy her, he is liable for the whole damage caused to the plaintiff although the defendant's share sold is less than the share the plaintiff bought.38

In an action for deceit against two owners of a vessel for fraud in inducing its sale, "The action is for the tort, the wrongful act done by the deceit practised in the sale. 

The damages are not limited to the profit which the vendors or either of them derived from the fraud. If one defendant sold only his half, and by himself or his agent committed a fraud in so doing, he would be answerable for the whole injury which the fraud occasioned, although it might exceed the value of the whole vessel. We have, then, the case of two principals sued for false representations made in the sale of property, one acting for himself, and the other acting by an agent. If the agent employed by one had been a third person, there seems to be no doubt that the two principals could be jointly sued. What difference can it make that one of the principals acted as agent of the other? He is joined in the suit, not as agent, but as another principal. 

37 O'Koomian v. Brandt (Conn.), 126 Atl. 332. This case is discussed and the general rule illustrated in a note in 38 Harv. L.R. 523. 

38 Springer v. Crowell, 103 Mass. 65.

$ 981

"But, farther than this, we think the two owners must be considered as partners in the sale and the fraudulent representations accompanying it; and, upon this ground, are jointly liable. The distinction attempted to be made between that which is done for one part of the chattel and that which is done for the other is rather metaphysical than practical. If two separate owners, each of an undivided half of a carriage, employed the same servant to drive the two halves along a highway, would they not be jointly responsible for his negligence in driving? Yet there it might be said that each employed the man only to drive his separate half. The difficulty is that the careless driving in the one case, and the making a false representation in the other, is an indivisible act. If there is no joint interest in the fruits of the fraud, that is no objection in the case of a conspiracy, where the parties join in the tort, but each for his several advantage. The defendants joined in the act; the one in his own person, for his own profit; and the other, through his agent, representing and binding him by his conduct and statements. In reference to the particular transaction, namely, the joining in doing one thing for their mutual benefit, there would seem to be all the elements of a partnership. " 39 

39 White v. Sawyer, 16 Gray, 586, 589.

§ 982. Seduction of Plaintiff's Daughter.¹ In an action for seducing the plaintiff's daughter the injury to the plaintiff's feelings as a father is but one element in computing the damages, and need not be specially alleged in the declaration. It was early held that "injury to the plaintiff's feelings is an element in computing the damages, as being a natural consequence of the principal injury; and need not be separately averred in the declaration.”3 

In an action by a parent for seduction of his minor child the plaintiff cannot recover unless he shows a loss of services to which he is entitled; but if his right to recover is established, his damages may include compensation for the injury to his feelings and for the dishonor and disgrace brought upon himself and his family.* 

§ 983. Illegality of Plaintiff's Marriage. In an action by a father for seduction and loss of services of his minor daughter the defendant may show that the plaintiff's marriage was illegal and void to show that he was not entitled to the services of his daughter, as bearing on the question of damages. 5 

§ 984. Cruelty of Plaintiff Husband. In an action for seduction of the plaintiff's wife her statements, prior to 

1 See also 449. 

2 Hatch v. Fuller, 131 Mass. 574. 

3 Phillips v. Hoyle, 4 Gray, 568. 

4 Cook v. Bartlett, 179 Mass. 576. 

5 Howland v. Howland, 114 Mass. 517.

$ 984 

the seduction, of her husband's cruelty towards her are admissible in mitigation of damages. The reasons for this result are thus stated by Bigelow, J.: "These were competent, and should have been admitted. 

In actions for criminal conversation, one of the principal grounds on which the husband is allowed to recover damages is, that by the wrongful act of the defendant he has been deprived of the confidence and affection of the wife. 

If the defendant invaded domestic peace, destroyed conjugal felicity, and by his solicitations alienated and seduced the wife's affections from a kind and tender husband, he inflicted a much more grievous wrong, and incurred a far heavier penalty in damages than he would have done if love and harmony and affectionate intercourse had been previously impaired or lost, through the misconduct and cruel treatment of the husband. "The state of the wife's mind and feelings towards the husband before the alleged infidelity is therefore directly in issue, as bearing on the question of damages; and it may be shown, in the usual mode in which proof of such a fact is made in courts of law, by evidence of declarations and statements of the wife, indicating the condition of her affections towards her husband during their cohabitation and prior to the alleged seduction. Such is the rule, whenever it is necessary to show the mental feelings of an individual. The usual expression of them by contemporaneous complaints and admissions is original evidence. They are in the nature of res gestae, accompanying the subject matter of inquiry, and giving character and significance to the acts and conduct to which they relate. By this proof, the true nature of the cohabitation of husband and wife might be best shown; and by confining it to a period of time contemporaneous with their cohabitation, and prior to any misconduct on her part with the defendant, all danger of any improper use of such testimony is avoided. This evidence is not admitted under any exception to the general rules

$505

regulating the competency of evidence, nor for the reason that proof of the facts might otherwise be difficult, but because it falls within the principle, that it is the best and original evidence of the facts.' 998

Joint Liability.¹ If two joint tortfeasors contribute to an injury, they may be sued either jointly or severally, and the plaintiff will be entitled to judgment against each for the full amount, but the plaintiff is entitled to only one satisfaction. Under a statute imposing liability on owners of dogs engaged in injuring sheep, where two or more dogs together attack sheep each owner is liable for the whole damage done, although one of the dogs is owned by the owner of the sheep, but there can be but one satisfaction.3 

§ 986. Settlement with One Joint Tortfeasor. Where the statute creates a right in a wife to recover damages against those who caused her husband to become intoxicated, if several join in the act she can have only one recovery for damages, and a settlement of a claim against one is a bar against the others.* § 987. Covenant Not to Sue. In an action of tort against three joint tortfeasors, covenants not to sue, given by the plaintiff to two of them, do not release the third defendant from liability. The rule of law that a release which dis- 

1 See also § 355. 

2 Corey v. Havener, 182 Mass. 250. Contribution among tortfeasors, cf. 

54 Harv. L.R. 1156. 

3 Inhabitants of the County of Worcester v. Ashworth, 160 Mass. 186. 

4 Aldrich v. Parnell, 147 Mass. 409.

§§ 988, 989 507 

JOINT TORTFEASORS 

charges the liability of one joint tortfeasor releases the others seems to be based on the nature of their liability, which is one and individual, and is necessarily destroyed by the discharge of one, and the basis for the rule does not exist in the case of a covenant not to sue one of several jointly liable. Here the liability is not discharged and the plaintiff's right of action is retained against all the wrongdoers. Such a document should be construed in accordance with the intent of the parties, and where it is evident that the consideration paid to the plaintiff was not intended to be full compensation and the agreement signed by him although in form a release was clearly intended to preserve the liability of those who are not parties to it. This intention is often carried out by construing the agreement as in legal effect a covenant not to sue and not a technical release.5 

§ 988. Selectmen as Joint Trespassers. Where selectmen act without lawful authority they may become trespassers and, being joint trespassers, each is liable for the whole damage. § 989. Promoters Jointly Liable. In a suit in equity by a corporation against one of the two promoters who organized it to recover damages for fraud in the organization and it appears that the two promoters are jointly liable as the fraud was a joint act, and only one promoter is a party to the suit, the division of the profits between the promoters cannot affect the rights of the plaintiff against the defendant, the breach of trust committed being in the nature of a tort which makes them liable for the whole damage, severally as well as jointly." 

5 Matheson v. O'Kane, 211 Mass. 91. Cf. also § 355. " Pinkerton v. Inhabitants of Randolph, 200 Mass. 24. 

7 Old Dominion Copper Mining & Smelting Co. v. Bigelow, 203 Mass. 159.

$ 990 

 § 990. Actions for Death.8 Where actions for death are brought by the same plaintiff against two different defendants and it appears that the death was caused by the concurrent negligence of both, the court does not pass upon the question whether there can be full recovery in both cases. Where the cases are tried together and submitted to the jury under an instruction that there cannot be more than one satisfaction, the plaintiff is estopped to claim more. The question of full recovery here left open was settled in a later decision holding that, where death is caused by the concurrent negligence of two defendants, separate actions must be brought against each and damages assessed in each action without reference to the other, although the amount due can only be recovered once.¹º

§ 991. Personal Injury by Automobile. Medical Expense. 

And the plaintiff says that on or about the second day of January 1921 she was lawfully on Brookline Avenue at or near where said Brookline Avenue is intersected by Verndale Street in the Town of Brookline in the County of Norfolk and said Commonwealth; that while the plaintiff was upon said Brookline Avenue and in the exercise of due care and diligence, the defendant, his servant or agent, operated a certain automobile so carelessly and negligently that the automobile struck the plaintiff with great force and seri-

§§ 992, 993 

ously and permanently injured the plaintiff causing her great pain and suffering; all to her great damage. (This declaration by an unmarried woman is defective in not claiming medical expenses, as pointed out in Braun v. 

Bell, 247 Mass. 437.) 

§ 992. Permanent Personal Injury. 

And the plaintiff says that on or about February 18, 1937 while he was properly a pedestrian upon River Street, at or near the corner of Jay Street, both public highways in the City of Cambridge, the defendant so carelessly and negligently operated an automobile that it struck the plaintiff, knocked him down, and seriously injured him, as a result of which he was seriously and permanently injured, and has suffered great pain both in body and mind, and was put to great expense for medicines and medical attendance, and was and still is prevented from following his usual occupation, and suffered a permanent injury; all to his great damage as he says in his writ. (Under this declaration the plaintiff was permitted to recover for impairment of earning capacity in Doherty v. 

Ruiz, 302 Mass. 145.) 

§ 993. Personal Injuries of Passenger in Street Car. 

And the plaintiff says the defendant is a Street Railway corporation, maintaining, operating and controlling lines of electric street railway on North Beacon Street, in the Town of Watertown, Massachusetts; that on the 18th day of July

A. D. 1903, the plaintiff was lawfully a passenger upon a car of the defendant, on said North Beacon Street, and while so a passenger on said car and while in the exercise of due care, and while the plaintiff was endeavoring to alight from said car, said car was negligently, carelessly and unskilfully operated, by reason of which the plaintiff was thrown to the ground and caused to suffer great and severe bodily injury and anguish of mind.

DECLARATIONS 

All of which is to her damage as in her writ alleged. (This declaration was held sufficient as a basis for evidence of impairment of earning capacity in Millmore v. Boston Elevated Railway Co., 198 Mass. 370.) 

§ 994. Passenger in Street Car Expelled. 

1st Count. And the plaintiff says the defendant is a corporation owning and operating a railroad from Lynn to Boston and particularly from Revere Beach so-called to Boston and is a common carrier of passengers between said places by means of street railway cars drawn by horses over defendant's railroad; that on the 31st day of July 1887 on or about that date at the request of defendant she took a seat in one of defendant's cars for the purpose of being carried to Boston from a place at or near Revere Beach socalled and paid the fare fixed by defendant, to defendant's servant and agent in charge of said car. After proceeding some distance toward Boston defendant's servant and agent in charge of said car required and compelled plaintiff to get out of said car and directed her to take another car for Boston which the plaintiff did do; and after proceeding a short distance further toward Boston defendant's agents and servant in charge of said car caused it to be stopped and neglected and refused to allow plaintiff to ride in said car. 

The defendant, its agents and servants ordered plaintiff to leave said car and forcibly expelled her therefrom contrary to the duty of the defendant. In consequence of her wrongful expulsion from defendant's car, the defendant's neglect of duty in not carrying her to Boston as it was the duty of the defendant to do, and of her walk to Boston in order to reach her home, she was made severely ill for a long time and suffered great bodily pain and anguish of mind to her great damage. The plaintiff avers that she was at all times in the exercise of due care. 

2nd Count. The plaintiff says the defendant is a corporation owning and operating a railroad by means of street railway cars drawn by horses over defendant's railroad

$ 995 

between Boston, Revere Beach so-called and Lynn in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and is a common carrier of passengers between said places. On or about the 31st day of July 1887 the plaintiff at the request of defendant entered one of defendant's cars then about starting for Boston to which place she was intending to proceed and paid the regulation fare established by defendant to Boston to defendant's agent and servant in charge of said car; whereby plaintiff became a passenger entitled to be conveyed to Boston and it became the duty of defendant to convey plaintiff to Boston. But defendant, its agents and servants being wholly regardless of their duty in the matter refused without cause to carry plaintiff and wrongfully compelled plaintiff to leave said car and refused to permit plaintiff to ride upon its cars to Boston although requested by plaintiff so to do. The plaintiff walked to Boston, her home, there being no other way or means of reaching Boston, all which was well known to the defendant, its agents and servants. In consequence of defendant's refusal to convey plaintiff and of her walk home to Boston and her being compelled to leave defendant's cars she was made severely ill and has sustained severe injuries and has suffered great bodily pain and anguish of mind to her great damage. The plaintiff avers that during all that time she was in the exercise of due care. (This declaration was held sufficient to enable the plaintiff to recover for her expulsion and for the walk to Boston in 

Spicer v. Lynn & Boston Railroad Co., 149 Mass. 207.) 

§ 995. Dog Bite. 

And the plaintiff says that on or about March 27, 1929 the defendant was the owner of a certain dog and at said time the said dog attacked and bit the plaintiff and severely injured her and caused her great suffering and loss. (This declaration was held sufficient to enable the plaintiff to recover double damages against the administrator of the defendant in Somers v. Broderick, 281 Mass. 550.)

DECLARATIONS § 996. Damage to Automobile. Loss of Use. 

And the plaintiff says that on or about July 7, 1922 a motor vehicle belonging to him, to wit, an automobile, was lawfully standing on a public highway in the City of Norwich in the State of Connecticut; and that the defendant then and there operated a motor vehicle, to wit, an automobile truck, so negligently, carelessly and improperly that it ran into the plaintiff's automobile and greatly damaged it. (This declaration was held sufficient to enable the plaintiff to recover, not only for the expense of repairs, but also for the loss of use, in Antokol v. § 999. Loss of Prospective Profits. 

And the plaintiff says that by reason of the defendant's false, fraudulent, deceitful and malicious conduct as aforesaid he was prevented from acquiring said 5,000 shares of 

Hawaiian Commercial & Sugar Company stock free and clear and has lost the benefit of his investment in said stock; that the intrinsic value of said stock was and is $100 per share; that 5,000 shares were and are worth $500,000; that the plaintiff received only $150,773 for said 5,000 shares of stock and the plaintiff claims the difference between said sums amount to $349,227 together with interest thereon from the 19th day of February 1902. § 1000. Loss of Profits from Boarding House. 

And the plaintiff says that in November 1928 the defendant was a dealer in meats and provisions and as such owned and conducted the business in Amherst known as The Public Market; that the plaintiff at the time and place aforesaid was the keeper of a boarding house reputed for the service of sound and wholesome food and enjoying the custom of about 60 regular boarders; that for the purpose of serving her boarders therewith as well as partaking thereof herself, which purpose was well known to the defendant, the plaintiff requested the defendant to select, furnish, sell and deliver to her certain sound, fit to be eaten and wholesome fowls, to wit: 4 slaughtered turkeys; and the plaintiff relied on the defendant's skill and judgment to select and furnish turkeys of such quality; that thereby it became the defen-

§ 1001 

dant's duty to select, furnish and deliver to the plaintiff turkeys which were sound, fit to be eaten and wholesome; that the defendant failed to do so and selected, furnished, sold and delivered to the plaintiff turkeys which were unsound, unfit to be eaten, unwholesome and poisonous; that the plaintiff, ignorant of the unsound, unwholesome, unfit to be eaten and poisonous condition of the turkeys, but believing them to be sound, fit for food and wholesome, properly cooked, seasoned and prepared said turkeys to be eaten and served them to her boarders and partook thereof herself. 

In consequence of which the plaintiff was made severely sick and disordered, and suffered great pain of body and anguish of mind and was prevented for a long time from doing her customary work; and her boarders were made violently sick and disordered and in large numbers ceased boarding with the plaintiff, and the plaintiff lost their patronage and the profits ensuing therefrom, and the plaintiff was otherwise greatly damaged in her said business. (This declaration was found sufficient in Hawkins v. Jamrog, 277 Mass. 540.)

§ 1005. Expenses Arising from Defective Boiler. Subrogation. 

And the plaintiff says that on or about the 19th day of March 1898 and prior thereto the defendants were manufacturers of boilers, tanks and similar iron work and were carrying on the business of manufacturing boilers, tanks and similar work in the City of Cambridge in said County of Middlesex; and that the plaintiff at the same time was a manufacturer of rubber goods and similar goods and was carrying on the business of manufacturing rubber goods and similar goods in said City of Cambridge. 

And the plaintiff further says that on or about said 19th day of March 1898 it ordered of the defendant an iron boiler or iron tank of certain size and kind known as a vulcanizer to be used in its business of manufacturing rubber goods and the defendants accepted said order and undertook and agreed to manufacture said iron boiler or iron tank for the plaintiff in a good workmanlike manner and that on or about the fourth day of April 1898 the defendants in pursuance of said order delivered to the plaintiff a certain iron boiler or iron tank which the plaintiff accepted and set up upon its premises in said City of Cambridge believing it to be of good workmanship and air tight and gas tight and safe to be used upon the said premises of the plaintiff in its said business. 

And the plaintiff further says that said iron boiler or iron tank was not of good workmanship and was not air tight, nor gas tight, and was not safe to use upon its said premises, but was of poor workmanship and was dangerous and defective in that the hinge of the door was improperly and negligently constructed and prevented the door from clos-

ing tightly and permitted the escape of the naphtha gas from said iron boiler or iron tank, and that while said boiler or tank was in use upon said premises of the plaintiff, to wit, on April 12, 1898 the fumes and gases from the naphtha used in said boiler or tank by reason of said defect escaped in large quantities and entered the boiler room and other parts of the said premises and ignited and caused an explosion whereby Patrick Grady, John Gallagher,

§ 1008. Liquidated Damages. 

That on September 14, 1921 the plaintiff and defendant entered into a contract whereby the defendant in consideration of the agreement on the part of the plaintiff hereinafter set forth agreed that in the event of cancellation or termination of said lease to New England Motors, Inc. within a year he would give plaintiff a lease expiring October 31, 1925 at a yearly rental of $9,100 "or at defendant's election

§ 1009. Satisfaction. Recoupment. 

And the defendant still further answering says that the plaintiff agreed to accept and did accept a check for $100 in full accord and satisfaction of the plaintiff's demands. 

And defendant still further answering says that if the plaintiff shall offer any evidence tending to prove any of said allegations then defendant avers that the agreement, if any, with plaintiff was that plaintiff was to carefully and skilfully train said horses and to drive the same personally and not allow any other person than plaintiff or defendant to drive them, and defendant avers that said horses were not carefully and skilfully trained but were unskilfully and carelessly trained and the plaintiff hired and procured another person to drive the same and that said horses were negligently and carelessly driven and severely and permanently injured thereby, all to the great damage of the defendant, which damages defendant seeks to recoup in this action. (The court in Sayles v. Quinn, 196 Mass. 492, holds that the allegations as to lack of skill are necessary in recoupment.)
